author: Danilo Arao
title: Peryodiko
content:
Photo from the Kilusang Magbubukid ng Pilipinas

Maganda ang teknolohiya kung mapapakinabangan ng karamihan.

May nagbabasa pa kaya ng peryodiko? Alam pa kaya ng kabataan ang mga katulad na salitang pahayagan at diyaryo?

Baka mas pundamental pa ang tanong: May nagbabasa pa kaya? Totoo bang wala nang masyadong kultura ng pagbuklat ng anumang nakaimprenta dahil mas gusto ng mga taong manood na lang ng bidyo?

Kung sabagay, higit pa sa peryodismo ang isyu. Analog o digital? Nobela o pelikula? Lumang midya o bagong midya? Pero saglit lang. Kailangan ba talagang mamili sa dalawa? Hindi ba puwedeng pagsabayin ang luma’t bago?

Kung gagamit ng ilang salita sa wikang Ingles, hindi ito usapin ng “conversion” kundi “convergence.” Posibleng gamitin ng lumang midya ang bagong teknolohiya para mapalakas ang mga katangian nito. At sa konteksto ng peryodismo, nagdesisyon ang maraming peryodikong gumawa ng mga website at account sa iba’t ibang social media platform.

Para sa mga peryodista, kailangang pumunta kung nasaan ang masa. Ito ang dahilan ng literal na pagbisita sa mga komunidad, lalo na sa mga liblib na lugar na tila napag-iwanan ng kabihasnan. Ito rin ang magpapaliwanag kung bakit pinapatulan pati ang TikTok sa paghuhubog ng opinyong pampubliko. Naglalaan din sila ng oras para makipagtalastasan sa social media kahit na hindi pinapansin ang mga personal na atake.

Dahil sa mabilis na pag-unlad ng teknolohiya, totoo namang lumang-luma na ang mga tinaguriang sinauna. Pero kapansin-pansin ang ebolusyon ng print para isama sa diseminasyon ng impormasyon ang teknolohiyang digital.

Gayundin ang kaso ng mga programa sa radyo dahil mayroon na silang kaakibat na teleradyo para marinig at makita ang balita, pati na ang nangyayari sa loob ng booth habang nagbobrodkast. At para naman sa mga programa sa telebisyon, uso na rin ang simultaneous live streaming.

Ngunit para sa mga lugar na mahina o walang internet signal, patuloy na namamayagpag ang lumang midya. Mas nakadepende sila sa radyo o telebisyon para sa pinakahuling balita. Nakakatulong din naman ang peryodiko para sa dagdag na pagsusuri kahit na hindi agad-agad na nakukuha ang kopya. Kaya hindi naman masyadong nahuhuli sa balita ang mga nasa liblib na lugar basta’t may mga matiyagang magsusubaybay at maghahanap ng paraan.

Maganda ang teknolohiya kung mapapakinabangan ng karamihan. Pero kung ang kalidad at bilis ng internet ay depende sa panggastos, parating mapipilitan ang mahihirap na pagtiyagaan ang mabagal na koneksiyon.

Para sa karamihang naka-prepaid na account lang sa kanilang mobile phone, mas gagamitin ang mga libreng opsiyon para ma-access ang social media accounts pero malamang na hindi maki-click ang link papunta sa buong teksto ng balitang nasa website ng mga organisasyong pang-midya. Kaya ang mangyayari, headline lang o maikling bahagi lang ng balita ang posibleng mabasa.

Anong klaseng opinyon ang mabubuo kung limitado lang ang impormasyon? Hindi ba’t mas mainam na gawing libre ang internet para sa lahat? Bakit kailangan pa kasing pagkakitaan ang teknolohiyang dapat na maging tulay para sa epektibong diseminasyon ng impormasyon?

Pero labas ng internet access, kailangan ding pangalagaan ang mga tinaguriang luma. Patuloy na kilalanin ang ambag ng print, radyo at telebisyon, lalo na ang kanilang paggamit ng teknolohiya sa gitna ng nagbabagong panahon. Hindi hiwalay ang pag-aaral ng bago sa pagkilala ng luma. Katulad ito sa pag-intindi ng kasalukuyan batay sa aral ng kasaysayan.

Uso pa ba ang peryodiko? Tandaang may mga nagbabasa pa naman. Hindi naman mawawala ang print media sa kabila ng pag-unlad ng teknolohiya. Mahalaga pa rin ang tuloy-tuloy na paglilimbag lalo na’t kinakailangan ang malalim na pagsasakonteksto.

Para makipag-ugnayan sa awtor, pumunta sa https://risingsun.dannyarao.com

author: Jordan Humphreys
title: The “two souls” of the Spanish general strike
content:
A 24-hour general strike is set to take place across the Spanish state on 11 November, sparked by recent struggles over housing. In the lead-up to the general strike, 

Red Flag

’s 

Jordan Humphreys

 spoke to Germán 

P. Montañés

, a member of the revolutionary organisation Anticapitalistas, about the unfolding situation.

Red Flag

:

 Rising rents and house prices are affecting people across the globe. Why has it become such a flashpoint in the Spanish state in particular? What is the housing situation like there?

Germán

 

P. Montañés:

 Housing in the Spanish state has been a structural problem for a long time. One of the most visible impacts of the 2008 financial crisis was a wave of mortgage evictions. Today, mortgage-related evictions are less common, but renting has become much more widespread.

Even so, renting remains less common in Spain than in cities like Berlin or New York, where tenant voting blocs have played a major political role. In Spain, home ownership is the norm even among much of the working class. This stems from a strategy popularised during the dictatorship—echoing Margaret Thatcher’s later policies in the UK—summarised by a government minister’s famous quote: “I want a country of homeowners, not proletarians”. This high level of home ownership has somewhat cushioned the crisis; without it, the social situation likely would have collapsed much sooner.

Still, the crisis remains severe for two main groups: young people, who are locked out of home ownership and forced to pay exorbitant rents; and low-income workers and migrants, who face the worst housing instability.

The modern housing movement began around 2008 with anti-eviction campaigns such as the Plataforma de Afectados por la Hipoteca (PAH). Later, tenants’ unions emerged from these struggles—founded in 2017 in hubs like Madrid and Barcelona, and expanding across the Spanish state over the past few years.

A major tipping point occurred in late September, when police evicted 87-year-old María del Carmen (Maricarmen) Abascal from her home in Madrid. She had lived there for nearly 50 years under a rent-controlled agreement, but after an investment fund bought the building, her rent drastically increased. On the fourth attempt, police successfully removed her. This high-profile eviction sparked widespread outrage across the country. In response to the growing public backlash, the prime minister brought the general elections forward to 29 November.

RF

: 

Could you give us a better idea about the tenants’ unions—what kind of organisations are they, and what relationship do they have with the revolutionary left?

GPM:

 The emergence of tenant unions reflects the limits of the previous housing movement, which focused almost exclusively on stopping evictions. The problem with focusing on evictions is that the movement arrives far too late: by the time a family is facing removal, the police are already at the door.

The founding principle of the tenants’ unions was to adapt the most effective elements of trade unions to housing—arriving early to conflicts and organising people sooner. Rather than a diffuse social movement, housing activism needed a formal union. Members pay a monthly contribution, providing a financial base that allows staff to work full time and maintains an ongoing presence.

They also drew heavily on US labour tactics, focusing on entire buildings or properties owned by the same investment fund or landlord family to intervene long before eviction day.

They’ve been very successful recently in Madrid. Around September, they had about 2,000 to 3,000 members, and over the last two months of conflict, that number doubled to roughly 6,000. To clarify: these are financial members, not dedicated militants—there are perhaps 100 to 150 core militants—but the growth is significant.

The mainstream political left has no militant presence inside these spaces and does not control them; it tries to exert influence from the outside through government institutions and political pressure.

The revolutionary left isn’t broadly present either, though our organisation is the only one with a real foothold inside the unions. Our influence extends beyond raw numbers: we’ve maintained a dialogue with the union leadership for ten years. While the leaders come from autonomist or anarchist traditions, key militants in leadership positions allow us to maintain a solid presence. Our goal is to build a revolutionary current inside the …

author: Jerome Small
title: Carroll’s royal commission: an attack on effective unionism in Victoria
content:
The Royal Commission into the Integrity of Major Public and Civil Infrastructure Construction Projects in Victoria was announced by Victoria’s Labor Premier Ben Carroll in August: his first act as the incoming premier. 

Carroll’s announcement was a response to a years-long media campaign against the CFMEU, the main construction union. It was also part of a wholesale lurch to the right by an already neoliberal Labor government. And it is a blatant attack on any idea that unions should act to raise wages. 

If proof is needed, just look at the first day of the current bloc of hearings. I attended the first day of the commission back in September and sat through the proceedings yesterday via livestream.  

Literally the main point of yesterday’s hearing was how terrible it was that the CFMEU stopped a major construction job—the Gap Road level crossing removal in Sunbury—for a day and a half in June 2022, and that this resulted in traffic controllers winning an increase in wages from the award rate (at that time $26 per hour) to around $49 per hour. 

The horror. This equates to a full-time wage of $1,862 per week, slightly above Australia’s average full-time wage of $1,835 in 2022. It’s an OK wage, though no king’s ransom. With allowances, shift and casual loading, and the plentiful overtime that construction sites run on, this can add up to a decent wage if you’re prepared to work long hours.

To listen to Chris Young, the counsel assisting the royal commission, a union winning this sort of wage for a blue-collar worker through industrial action in 2026 is a threat to all that is right in the world. So much so that two weeks of the royal commission’s rather expensive time is being devoted to investigating how this could possibly have come about, with the express intention of ensuring it never happens again. 

Young spent yesterday sifting through the circumstances leading up to this supposed affront to decency. The CFMEU had a lot going in its favour. 

Railway crossing removals happen on a tight timetable, planned up to a year in advance. The two companies doing the work—John Holland and CPB—wanted to deliver the job on time in order to secure further work. The labour market was tight in Victoria. The CFMEU had already been successful in securing enterprise agreements with most of the big companies doing this sort of work in Victoria. From the evidence led by counsel assisting, it sounds like the CFMEU judged the moment perfectly—just like any union which is serious about taking action to raise wages should, and historically has. 

Both the CFMEU and the Australian Workers’ Union (AWU) cover workers working on civil construction projects like level crossing removals, and since 2014 the CFMEU has been trying to expand its coverage at the expense of the AWU. The Victorian Labor government at that time was uninterested in helping the AWU maintain coverage over these jobs—like Gap Road—and over traffic control work in particular. 

This was a positive for the workers at Gap Road, and more broadly. The royal commission was told that Zoom Recruitment, one of the AWU-aligned labour hire companies providing traffic control at Gap Road, was operating on a long-expired enterprise agreement that paid only the legal minimum specified in the construction award. 

This is utterly consistent with the business model of the AWU for the past century or more in construction, which is to undercut the wages and condition of the CFMEU and its predecessor unions. And to their credit, for most of that time, the CFMEU and their predecessors generally ignored the AWU’s claims to coverage on “civil” infrastructure work (roads, rail, bridges and tunnels).

The commission heard yesterday that the Labor government’s largely hands-off attitude to this demarcation dispute in 2022, which effectively favoured the CFMEU over the AWU, may have been because of factional alignments within the ruling Labor Party. This is hardly a crime, or even a novel tactic in Australian union politics.  

The AWU has used exactly the same approach, of translating political clout in the Labor Party into industrial coverage (and vice-versa), for its entire existence. The conservative Shop, Distributive and Allied Union (SDA) follows the same path. The only difference is that the AWU and the SDA have an appalling record of lifting wages—in fact the SDA did the opposite, helping employers undercut legal minimums, until a path-breaking legal case in the Fair Work …

author: Odessa Bishop-McMurray
title: “If they won’t give us a future, we will build one right here” - why the French revolt should inspire high-schoolers everywhere
content:
As one of the organisers of the upcoming nationwide 

Students Say No to Hanson

 demonstration on 12 November, I’ve had to endure a lot of inanity from the media and the right. Amongst snide remarks about the stages of brain development and warnings of the mortal dangers of missing two periods of class, one accusation keeps coming up: that we’re plotting to bring “French-style riots” to Australian cities. 

Right-wing journalists seized on an Instagram post we made on 11 October, conveying the inspiration we draw from French student protesters fighting government austerity and the far right. 

Cue an avalanche of hysterical headlines and news segments: The Murdoch-owned Adelaide 

Advertiser

 warned readers to brace for “walkouts ‘inspired’ by violent French protests”. Pauline Hanson went on Brisbane’s 4BC Radio to rip into us:

“...They are saying they are inspired by what’s going on in France. What? The 

looting

? The 

burning

? The 

destruction

? They’re 

inspired

 by that?”

Well, we’re not sorry for being inspired by French students. Everyone who wants to see a better world should identify with their struggle. 

Young people everywhere are facing a dire future, and revolt is rightly spreading. It’s clear even to some in the establishment that what’s happening in France is part of a global wave of protest with deep roots. As former UK Prime Minister Gordon Brown wrote this week in 

The Guardian

: “A global youthquake is happening. Promises we made young people have been broken—and they know it.”

Both far-right governments and “sensible centrists” are taking us on the same trajectory: more racism, more militarism, and more austerity. 

When states aren’t attempting to re-introduce conscription, as in Germany, they’re funnelling billions into the military-industrial complex while schools crumble. In France, students endure classrooms infested with cockroaches, mould and overcrowding, sometimes numbering 35 students to a class. 

We’ll likely never be able to afford secure housing or sufficient healthcare. We’ve watched politicians choose fossil fuel companies over the habitability of our planet. For many of us, the establishment’s unanimous endorsement of Israel’s genocide in Gaza was the final nail in the coffin.

It’s obvious that the journalists’ and politicians’ pearl-clutching about a few broken Parisian shop windows is a means of avoiding discussion of these issues. And their condemnation of violence rings hollow when they decline to comment on the vastly greater violence that the system inflicts on people daily. 

There’s the violence that is inherent in running such an unequal society. French youth linger without a future in the slums while the richest 500 families own nearly half the country. Schools and hospitals in France are crumbling, but the latest budget announcement includes 54 billion euros in further cuts to public spending. The police systematically brutalise Black and Arab working-class migrants. The high-profile killing of 17-year-old Nahel Merzouk, which sparked a nationwide revolt in 2023, is part of a long history of racialised policing. 

When these injustices generate resistance, there’s one public service the government can guarantee: the bludgeoning of protestors, tear gas, and potentially lethal stun grenades; exploding a student’s hand, breaking another’s jaw and leaving two 16-year-olds blinded for life. 

This is an inherent admission that the ruling class has no genuine plan to improve society. They just want resignation from ordinary people, and when that fails, tear gas is their backup plan.

But French students have shown that resignation gets us nowhere; Our power comes from the streets, and that’s a lesson the ruling class desperately does not want students to learn.

Already, France has shown small glimpses of how these movements can win real gains. While still hoping to crush the movement, the government has already been forced to make concessions. They’ve announced plans to cap class sizes, hire more teachers, and create more university places. This is a tiny fraction of what the movement is demanding, but it proves a timeless truth: a month of rebellion can win more change than decades of asking nicely.

A grassroots student movement in Serbia just ended the 14-year rule of the repressive Vučić regime. In Brazil, thousands of students flocked to the streets to successfully halt the advance of far-right presidential candidate Flávio Bolsonaro.

It seems like …

author: Sagar Sanyal
title: Emergency and autocracy in Modi’s India
content:
The far-right government in India led by Prime Minister Narendra Modi has been increasingly repressive and anti-democratic over recent months. Commentators are asking if the country is in the grip of an ‘

undeclared Emergency

’, a reference to the 1975-77 period of ‘Emergency rule’ by then Prime Minister Indira Gandhi in which activists and trade unionists were simply rounded up and jailed. 

The current repression is a response to the student and youth protests that erupted in the capital, New Delhi, in late July. They were sparked by the Cockroach Janata Party (CJP), a satirical movement that began on social media a couple of months earlier. The scale and intensity of the protests surprised the regime, as did the mocking anti-Modi tenor of popular chants. While the protest demand was for the resignation of the education minister over exam leaks, the protesters were motivated by visceral opposition to Modi, who has ruled since 2014. The police lashed out using the sort of 

force

 that they typically use in repressed regions like Kashmir. Police fired pellet guns, used nail-studded batons and sexually assaulted women protesters. 

Despite the repression, tens of thousands mobilised daily for five days—high school and university students, middle-class and working-class youth. Not only in Delhi, but in dozens of cities around the country. Alongside clips of police brutality circulating on social media, there are clips of youth chasing police off the streets with their sheer numbers and bravado. There are clips of cheeky middle-class youth approaching police who are away from the heat of the action to ask mocking questions like “Dear Mr. Officer, are you planning to tear gas protesters today?” The government is tracking down incriminating and embarrassing recordings of those events and asking social media platforms to 

remove them

.

Public opinion has turned strongly against Modi’s repression. Among the Hindi-speaking, middle-class, upper-caste Hindus who have been the most secure vote base of the BJP, parents now saw their own children being beaten—just for demanding a fair opportunity in college exams! Ultimately, the administration conceded the protest demand to sack the education minister, a humiliating 

defeat

 for Modi. It gave the lie to the “unstoppable strongman” image of him so carefully crafted by pro-Modi big media. 

Less than three months after the July protests, a new protest movement gripped the nation. It demands the resignation of the Chief Election Commissioner of India, Gyanesh Kumar, who has been highly partisan to Modi and his 

Hindu nationalist

 Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) and, according to some parties, rigged state elections in Bihar (May 2025) and West Bengal (April 2026). In West Bengal, the BJP won for the first time due in part to the chief election commissioner disqualifying millions of names from the eligible voters list. Deletions disproportionately targeted Muslims, who are an ideological enemy of Hindu nationalists, and who were also an important vote base of the party the BJP displaced—the Trinamool Congress (TMC). 

Following a late September 

expose,

 which revealed that the chief election commissioner had overruled the protestations of even his fellow election commissioners, the CJP and left student groups took up vote-rigging as a national campaign to channel the energy from the July student movement. Demands for the chief election commissioner to resign have been taken up by all opponents of the BJP. 

When a large protest was called for 

10 October

, the state responded by locking down New Delhi. Around 40,000 paramilitary and police laid siege to a sizeable area around the “designated protest site” of Jantar Mantar in the centre of the city. They blocked roads and shut down local internet mobile services (India is 

among the worst

 states for this). They closed over 40 metro train stations in Delhi and stopped over 200 inter-city trains from reaching Delhi. They threatened activists in their homes on the night before the march, this coming on top of regular arbitrary detention of prominent leaders of the protest movement (from the CJP and the left parties). 

Undeterred

, protestors appeared in their tens of thousands and were again met with batons and tear gas, and thousands were detained.

Sizeable protests have continued sporadically since 10 October, some called by the CJP or student organizations of the left, 

others

 by major opposition parties. The …

author: Rick Kuhn
title: Unemployment: a feature of capitalism, not a bug
content:
Today more than one in ten workers can’t find enough paid labour to live a decent life. And that’s only workers actively looking for a job or for more hours of employment. It doesn’t count those who have given up on finding a job, even though they want one, and survive thanks to friends, family or a measly government payment that isn’t an unemployment benefit.

In September

 the seasonally adjusted

un

employment rate was 4.7 percent;

under

employment was 6.3 percent. According to the Australian Bureau of Statistics, you’re not unemployed if you worked even an hour in the survey fortnight.

To get the Jobseeker Payment or Youth Allowance the un- and underemployed have to follow the Albanese government’s savage eligibility rules, inherited from its Liberal predecessors. If you earn more than a pitiful $75 a week, your payment starts to go down. You must follow the instructions of Workforce Australia and, if you’ve been directed to one, of an outsourced “employment services provider” agency, which profits from government funding.

That may mean applying for a certain number of jobs every “reporting period”, doing training they tell you to do, however meaningless courses about writing job applications or behaviour during an interview might be; or perform “work for the dole”, that would normally be done for much higher award wages. You have to “accept any offer of suitable paid work”, defined by the provider, whether the type of work or its location actually suits you or not.

If you’re single, without kids, the dole is

currently


a princely $413 a week. Certainly in Sydney, you’d be very lucky if less than half of that went on renting a room. And if you’re young, that’s unfortunate: unemployed aged 21 or younger are penalised and get less money than those over 21. Apparently young people don’t need as much shelter, food, clothing, etc. as older people.

Both the unemployment and underemployment rates are rising.

Unemployment is not a bug in capitalism, but a feature. The threat of un- and underemployment – descending into what Marx called “

the industrial reserve army

”—disciplines workers fearful of losing their jobs. The higher the level of unemployment, other things being equal, the less likely they are to take risks by fighting to defend or improve their pay and conditions.

The extent of the reserve army of labour changes in the course of economic cycles: lower during booms, higher in slumps.

Many central banks, like the Reserve Bank of Australia, are bumping up interest rates to slow their countries’ economies down. Their goal is not increased unemployment; that’s a side effect. Their main target is the rate of inflation. High inflation—lack of stability in the purchasing power of money—makes calculations by capitalists about their activities and especially investments more difficult.

In legislation

, the RBA has two goals: “price stability and the maintenance of full employment”. It says that “

[t]hese two objectives usually work together

”. In practice, the bank favours sacrificing jobs to keep a lid on inflation.

But today, high oil prices, due to the USA’s and Israel’s war on Iran, is the main driver of inflation. The RBA isn’t bumping up interest rates to discipline workers, although that’s a side-effect. Governor

Michelle Bullock

said at the end of September that “There is no wage price spiral going on in Australia. Rises in wages are not driving … cost pressures”.

In fact, it is workers who are mainly affected by inflation. Greg Jericho, in the

Guardian

, has illustrated how workers’ real pay has been falling since 2021, compared with the Consumer Price Index by 7 percent; compared with the more appropriate Employee Living Cost Index, by more than 12 percent.

The hostility of most union officials to leading their members in serious struggles to defend, let alone restore or improve their living standards, is mainly to blame.

In his 1972 report

Poverty in Australia

, Ronald Henderson, appointed by the Liberal government of Billy McMahon, calculated a poverty line, marking an “austere” standard of living below which people were in poverty. The Melbourne Institute of Economic Research frequently updates it.

JobSeeker

has consistently been below this line. Today that unemployment benefit is less than half the

Henderson poverty line

. Using 50, let alone 60 percent of median

author: Önder Algedik
title: Seven things you must never say about COP31
content:
COP31 opened in Antalya on November 9 and its two hosts — Türkiye and Australia — have been busy.

Australia’s Labor government, despite being elected on promises to act for the climate, has approved 37 new or expanded fossil fuel projects since 2022.

Since September 2025 it has signed 19 fossil fuel agreements: 20-year liquefied natural gas (LNG) contracts, oil and gas exploration pacts with ExxonMobil, Chevron and TotalEnergies, drilling rights from Syria to Somalia, and a deal with Australia’s Woodside.

On top of those come six nuclear and mining agreements, three of them were signed in Seoul on November 3, six days before the summit opened.

One host approves the projects. The other signs the contracts. Together they will run a summit whose Action Agenda does not name coal, oil or gas even once.

Everything is going smoothly. In Türkiye, censorship helps; at least 1270 X accounts were blocked in September alone and, over the past 20 months, trustees have been appointed to 10 television channels.

So, to keep the hosts comfortable, here are seven things you must never talk about.

1. Don’t talk about fossil philanthropy

In June, the foundations of the companies that change Türkiye’s climate the most, including a refinery, car factory, coal power plant, an electricity distributor and even the operator of Antalya airport, set up “Philanthropy for Climate”. They invited environmental groups to the table. The polluters bring the money; civil society brings the legitimacy. Australians who have watched gas companies sponsor festivals and sport will know the model.

2. Don’t talk about the COP31 bill

COP31 is expected to cost close to US$2 billion. When the host agreement came before Türkiye's parliament in July, one party wrote a dissenting opinion and then abstained. Only five MPs voted “No”. An agreement that cost to the public up to US$2 billion bill passed in near silence.

COP31 is, in a sense, a rubbish summit; “Zero waste” heads its list of themes. In August, as rubbish washed up along the Mediterranean coast, the national debate was only about waste imported from Britain. Meanwhile, according to Türkiye’s statistics office, more than 10 million tonnes of waste was burned in 2024. The sky became the landfill.

4. Don't talk about the fossil deals

Has anyone at COP31 mentioned the deals Türkiye signed while preparing to host it? The energy minister posed for photos at every ceremony. A 20-year LNG contract with Mercuria. Exploration in the Black Sea and Eastern Mediterranean with ExxonMobil and TotalEnergies. A global partnership with Chevron, from Iraq to Venezuela. A stake in Kirkuk’s oil fields. Rights to drill in Syria, Libya, Somalia and Pakistan. And Woodside’s LNG.

When I counted in October, there were 14. Now there are 19.

5. Don’t talk about cities without resilience

On October 14, Istanbul, Sakarya, Kocaeli, Yalova, Muğla and Antalya went under water on the same day. The minister of urbanisation, who is also COP31 president, called it a “disaster”, blamed climate change and moved the topic onto the summit’s “Resilient Cities” theme. Were these resilient cities or cities stripped of their resilience? Between 2002 and 2021, Türkiye laid 603 million tonnes of asphalt and poured close to a billion tonnes of cement. If you must, talk only about river beds and pretend the valley slopes above them were never paved. In three days, everyone forgets.

6. Say ‘conference’, not ‘fair’

COP stands for Conference of the Parties. But it has become a Fair of the Parties. The minister announced that 1.5 million visitors are expected! That is not a venue for negotiation; it is an exhibition ground. As I argued last month, the stands will be busy and the products green. Never call it a fair. Say “climate summit”, a phrase with no actor and no action.

Say “coal phase-out”, but never mention oil. Ask for a coal exit date, which buys the government time. Don’t touch the summit’s global business partner, Koç Holding, which owns Türkiye's oil refineries. Call gas a “bridge fuel”. Australians know this one: Labor’s Future Gas Strategy says gas will be needed to 2050 and beyond.

So here are the seven things we must not talk about: Fossil philanthropy, the public bill, a country turned into a dump, fossil deals, asphalt-and-concrete cities, a summit turned trade fair, and oil and gas.

Nobody has to ban any of this, because we already don’t talk about it. We don't talk about the groups that sit at the table with fossil …

title: Künstliche Intelligenz: KI-Einsatz in der Arbeitswelt – Folgen und Mitbestimmung
content:
Dossier


„… Der Einsatz Künstlicher Intelligenz löse derzeit bei vielen Arbeitnehmerinnen und Arbeitnehmern Sorgen und Ängste aus, so Schmitz weiter. „Selbststeuernde Prozesse führen zu einer neuen Arbeitsteilung zwischen Mensch und Maschine, ohne dass diese bisher ausreichend erforscht ist.“ Drängende Fragen der Kontrolle, der Ent- oder Belastung, der Qualifizierung und der Beschäftigungssicherung müssten geklärt werden. (…) „Künstliche Intelligenz ist Werkzeug, Mittel zum Zweck. KI-Anwendungen müssen der Verbesserung von Arbeits- und Lebensqualität dienen.“ KI-Systeme seien so zu gestalten, dass die Handlungs- und Gestaltungsspielräume der Erwerbstätigen erweitert werden. „Tätigkeiten sind durch gezielte Qualifizierung aufzuwerten. Dies kann durch Tarifverträge flankiert und durch neue Stellenzuschnitte unterstützt werden.“


ver.di-Pressemitteilung vom 9. Dezember 2020


 zur gemeinsamen Studie von ver.di, IBM und Bundesarbeitsministerium, siehe die Studie sowie weitere Beträge zum Thema:


[Die uralte Frage der Produktivitätsgewinne betrifft auch die Künstliche Intelligenz] KI spart Zeit – wer bekommt sie?


„

Künstliche Intelligenz soll Arbeit erleichtern. Doch Zeitgewinne können zusätzliche Aufgaben bedeuten. Wer entscheidet, was Beschäftigte davon haben?


Im Nachbarland ist manches ähnlich: Ein Drittel der Beschäftigten in Frankreich überschreitet regelmäßig seine üblichen Arbeitszeiten. Bei Führungskräften sind es rund 60 Prozent. Das zeigt eine

Untersuchung des Forschungszentrums CEET


, die Angaben von rund 30.000 Beschäftigten aus den Jahren 2019 bis 2023 auswertet.

Wer länger arbeitet, berichtet auch häufiger von weiteren Belastungen. Überstunden und Arbeitsverdichtung kommen zusammen. (…)


Wird gewonnene Zeit zur Erholung genutzt, mit zusätzlichen Aufgaben gefüllt oder für Personalabbau verplant? Darüber entscheiden Personalstärke, Leistungsvorgaben und betriebliche Aushandlung. Doch wenn Unternehmen bereits mit den erhofften Effizienzgewinnen rechnen, stellt sich eine weitere Frage: Wird die Zeit schon verplant, bevor sie überhaupt eingespart ist?

“

Beitrag von Andrej Simon vom 09. November 2026 in Telepolis

 


„Manche haben ihr Team in weniger als einem Jahr mehr als halbiert“: KI durchrüttelt die Arbeitswelt


„

KI produziert Filme, schreibt Code, führt Unternehmen – und vernichtet Jobs in Rekordtempo. Was das für Arbeit, Gesellschaft und Demokratie bedeutet. (…)


Im Silicon Valley entstehen Unternehmen mit Dutzenden oder Hunderten KI-Agenten und einer Handvoll Beschäftigten. Screenpipe.com, das hilft, Computerfunktionen zu automatisieren, hat seinen Umsatz in kurzer Zeit mit nur zwei Beschäftigten von 60.000 Dollar auf 1,5 Millionen Dollar gesteigert und plant keineswegs, weitere einzustellen. Der Traum von San Francisco im Jahr 2026 ist ein Unternehmen mit Millionenumsätzen und nur einem Beschäftigten. Und dieser Traum rückt näher. Ein durchschnittliches Unternehmen in den Vereinigten Staaten oder Italien erzielt rund 250.000 Euro oder Dollar Umsatz pro Beschäftigtem.


Anthropic hingegen kommt auf neun Millionen Dollar pro Beschäftigtem, OpenAI auf 5,6 Millionen. Nicht etwa, weil beide finanziell glänzend dastünden – OpenAI läuft Gefahr, seine gesamten liquiden Mittel innerhalb von neun Monaten zu verbrennen –, sondern weil beide um ihre oberste Führungsebene herum organisiert sind, mit sehr wenigen Untergebenen. Vielleicht sind es schlicht Systeme, die darauf ausgelegt sind, Geld nach oben zu saugen, an die Spitze der Pyramide. Derweil erledigen die KI-Agenten fast alles. (…)


Vor allem unter den Jüngeren und in den Berufen, die der künstlichen Intelligenz am stärksten ausgesetzt sind, bricht die Beschäftigung in Amerika bereits ein. Bei den 22- bis 25-Jährigen in den am leichtesten automatisierbaren Berufen liegt die Zahl der besetzten Arbeitsplätze schon 19 % unter dem Wert, der sich bei einer Entwicklung entsprechend dem Durchschnitt des Arbeitsmarktes ergeben hätte.


Dieser Teil der Auswirkungen kann auch Italien unmittelbar und als Erstes erreichen: Man entlässt niemanden, stellt aber nicht mehr ein und überträgt die Arbeit einer KI. author: anred
title: De la bendición de Devoto al calvario de Marcos Paz: Milton Tolomeo, preso por luchar contra la reforma laboral, inició una huelga de hambre
content:
Milton Tolomeo se encuentra detenido desde hace casi nueve meses en el Penal Federal de Marcos Paz. Sufre esta detención al igual que Eneas Gallo por haber participado en la movilización en contra de la reforma laboral. Los acusaron de terroristas y les dictaron prisión preventiva. E

l acto humanitario del Papa de visitar la Cárcel de Devoto significó una bendición para los poquitos que quedaron allí y un calvario a 50 km de distancia para los que fueron trasladados a Marcos Paz. A los malos tratos recibidos se suma que les han suspendido todas las actividades educativas, no cuentan con médico de planta, no se les entregan los medicamentos recetados, se les han secuestrado efectos personales y hasta su ropa. Están suspendidas todas las actividades recreativas y los talleres, tampoco existe el servicio de cantina y el régimen de depósito de alimentos permitidos cambia continuamente, siempre haciendo prevalecer las prohibiciones.

Las visitas se han acortado y las demoras reducen el tiempo formalmente asignado de tres horas semanales.


Y por primera vez en décadas el Servicio Penitenciario Federal obstaculiza las visitas de los organismos de DD.HH. Esta suma de elementos es lo que llevó al compañero Milton a declararse en huelga de hambre a partir de las cero horas del día domingo hasta obtener una respuesta a sus reclamos.

Por Coordinadora de Presxs Políticxs.


Milton Tolomeo se encuentra detenido desde hace casi nueve meses en el Penal Federal de Marcos Paz. Sufre esta detención al igual que Eneas Gallo por haber participado en la movilización en contra de la reforma laboral. Los acusan de los disturbios que produjo la policía (como lo hace siempre), durante esa marcha el 11 de febrero pasado.


Ni siquiera los detuvieron en el lugar de los hechos, los «identificaron» mediante el ciber patrullaje, que analiza imágenes buscando patrones comunes. Y los fueron a detener en su domicilio o en su trabajo en el caso de Milton. La verdad es que los tenían «marcados», porque tanto Eneas como Milton siempre acompañaron las luchas de jubilados, discapacitados, trabajadores en lucha o despedidos, estudiantes y trabajadores de la eduación.


Los acusaron de terroristas y les dictaron prision preventiva. El mismo aparato judicial que acaba de dictaminar que Adorni no se robó nada y lo deja libre de culpa y cargo, condena de antemano con la prisión preventiva a trabajadores precarizados que no tienen ni donde caerse muertos y los amenaza con dictarles condenas de hasta treinta años de prisión.


De este modo, el acto humanitario del Papa de visitar la Cárcel de Devoto significó una bendición para los poquitos que quedaron allí y un calvario a 50 km de distancia para los que fueron trasladados a Marcos Paz, a lo que llaman Nueva Unidad Carcelaria, que en realidad es una cárcel sin terminar, con un diseño edilicio que tiene por objeto inocultable producir una sensación de agobio durante todo el tiempo.


A los malos tratos recibidos se suma que les han suspendido todas las actividades educativas, no cuentan con médico de planta, no se les entregan los medicamentos recetados, se les han secuestrado efectos personales y hasta su ropa. Están suspendidas todas las actividades recreativas y los talleres, tampoco existe el servicio de cantina y el régimen de depósito de alimentos permitidos cambia continuamentesiempre haciendo prevalecer las prohibiciones.


Las visitas se han acortado y las demoras reducen el tiempo formalmente asignado de tres horas semanales. Y por primera vez en décadas el Servicio Penitenciario Federal obstaculiza las visitas de los organismos de derechos humanos, rompiendo con una práctica histórica.


Esta suma de elementos es lo que llevó al compañero Milton a declararse en huelga de hambre a partir de las cero horas del día domingo hasta obtener una respuesta a sus reclamos.


Pedimos la mayor difusión a este comunicado y también sumar su voz para exigir la inmediata libertad de Milton Tolomeo y Eneas Gallo.

author: Trevor Ngwane
title: African Labour and Liberation
content:
African Labour and Liberation

 brings together the experiences of workers, trade unions and labour movements across the continent to ask what they can tell us about work, power and liberation today. We assembled this collection because of the surprisingly few recent accounts of the emergence of a class politics on the continent. Labour is central to understanding the present political economy of Africa.  More than 90 percent of Africa’s 500 million workers work in informal and precarious jobs in a labour force that will grow rapidly in the next three decades.


The social and political mobilization of workers in multifarious contexts across the continent is imperative to improving their socio-economic conditions. It is necessary to situate Africa’s workers at the centre. This collection starts from the premise that labour struggles are essential to improving the conditions of work and stamping out poverty and inequality that confront most African workers today and form the basis for building new forms of collective power.


This heterodox collec­tion finds six primary patterns prevalent in the struggle for working-class liberation in the post-independence era.


1. Most governments in Africa are comprador-bureaucratic regimes beholden to foreign capital and imperialists’ interests to protect and maintain unequal exchange of trade and the attenuation of demands by the masses for national control over natural resources and production. Comprador-bureaucratic regimes remain loyal to their post-colonial powers and pay fleeting attention to national sustainability, the rights of women, natu­ral ecology, and the ever-growing needs of the masses for health care, education, housing, infrastructure, water, and electricity.


Government legislation to defend popular interests that have been enacted by national assemblies are rarely fully implemented and are likely to be opposed by international banks and lenders, predominantly from the West through structural adjustment programs that undermine evanescent attempts to ameliorate the most significant challenges.


2. Diverse workers’ movements form to resist t the comprador-bureaucratic political economies which formed in the colonial era which most often extract surplus value from workers and natural resources from the continent  through what  Arghiri Emmanuel  identified as

unequal exchange of trade

, and despoiling, and plundering African nations. Control is maintained by local elites attached to state power who are beneficiaries of rentier capitalism. These national elites have welcomed Western powers to establish military bases osten­sibly to establish peace and order.


In most instances, the emergence of violence and disorder were generated by Western military intervention. However, as Samir Amin shows, workers and peasants drive the enduring imperative for the formation of national projects for popular sovereignty, which are often imperfect and challenged by imperialists seeking to maintain the unequal exchange of trade.


3. African states are ruled by comprador state-centric bureaucratic elites who maintain rentier capitalism as the primary source of revenue rather than investing in productive technology. The historical pattern is opposition to the redistribution of wealth and income to the masses.


This process, in which bureaucratic elements seek to transform themselves – sometimes successful sometimes not, but nearly always drawing links to imperial­ism and thereby fusing the bureaucratic and comprador elements – can be seen nearly everywhere. Unquestionably, compliant and often corrupt political elites provide the patina of legitimacy for all practical purposes, for the expansion of inequality.


4. In Africa, racial justice must include an anti-imperialist per­spective which acknowledges the legacy of European colonialism and the protracted nature of imperialism which sustains racial subordina­tion. Markedly, South Africa, a semi-peripheral mineral-rich state, did not redistribute wealth and property with the end of political apartheid and the development of a superficially democratic state. Black South Africans, composing over 80 percent of the country’s 65 million popu­lation, remain marginalized through the 1994 accords, which did not include a redistribution of wealth and resources – causing higher levels of poverty and inequality and impeding the working class from improv­ing its living standards.

author: gavroche
title: Calentamiento social en Italia. Reflexiones sobre la huelga general del 30 de octubre
content:
La jornada del 30 de octubre ha sido formidable. Desde hacía muchos años un paro convocado solo por el sindicalismo de base no registraba un éxito semejante a nivel nacional, con decenas y decenas de manifestaciones locales que llenaron las calles y las plazas. De los distintos relatos emergen algunos rasgos comunes: participación intergeneracional, papel importante del componente estudiantil, pero también amplia participación de trabajadoras y trabajadores, lo que muestra un evidente éxito del paro, aunque luego habrá que analizar los datos de adhesión. Pero sobre todo muchísimos jóvenes y muy jóvenes. Precisamente aquellos, a menudo menores, que el gobierno intenta encadenar a los pupitres de la escuela si no a los pupitres de trabajo o arrojar directamente a las cárceles de menores. El primer resultado evidente de la jornada del 30 de octubre ha sido la inversión del miedo. Las grandes manifestaciones se reapropiaron de la viabilidad de las plazas, de las escuelas, de las universidades y de los lugares de trabajo. Cierto es que no faltó la represión, con cargas en Roma, Turín, Vicenza y Venecia, y en muchas ciudades no faltaron identificaciones masivas y detenciones preventivas. También se difundió la noticia de registros el 31 de octubre, en todo el país, contra más de 60 personas consideradas relacionadas —parece siempre solo en el plano de la llamada "instigación"— con las tensiones de plaza de las semanas anteriores. Pero de hecho el 30, en la jornada del paro, el gobierno decidió no intervenir contra las manifestaciones, e incluso las acciones más o menos simbólicas de bloqueo —especialmente en los puertos— o de ocupación de sedes universitarias, se desarrollaron en la mayoría de los casos sin la interferencia de la policía. Otro claro resultado del paro es el de haber arrinconado las perspectivas interclasistas así como las derivas a la derecha que —por ejemplo en la protesta de los transportistas— habrían podido asumir un papel en las tensiones que están madurando en el país.

Cierto es que el 30 de octubre representa una bocanada de oxígeno: plazas tan numerosas contra la guerra y la carestía abren nuevas posibilidades en un momento en que el horizonte aparece cada vez más sombrío. Pero atención, esta jornada no es del todo una sorpresa. Aunque construida sobre la marcha, sin la habitual preparación que acompaña a una huelga general, es una jornada de lucha que ha sido preparada y organizada precisamente para responder a una situación social que se estaba haciendo cada vez más explosiva.

El mes de octubre, en efecto, ha llevado, como se dice, los nudos al peine. A lo largo de las últimas semanas la impaciencia hacia los efectos de la política de guerra conducida por el gobierno ha encontrado expresión en las calles y en las plazas, aunque de modo fragmentado y con muchos límites y contradicciones. Diversos sectores de la sociedad, para reaccionar a la carestía, han puesto en acto formas de lucha que se han topado con la represión del gobierno. Ante estas señales inequívocas, gran parte de las organizaciones sindicales de base decidieron convocar un paro para el día 30 de octubre, que ha asumido un papel de catalizador de los impulsos madurados en la sociedad y de las protestas que en parte ya habían sido rechazadas por el gobierno con la represión. La jornada de paro había nacido sobre rieles distintos de campañas políticas distintas, pero ambas concentradas en la oposición a la guerra. Por un lado, el paro plurisectorial convocado por la USI en el marco del paro internacional contra la guerra lanzado por la internacional anarcosindicalista CIT; por otro, el paro internacional de los puertos contra la guerra, que en Italia es promovido por USB y OR.S.A., pero que ve participar a decenas de organizaciones en todo el mundo, entre ellas también la CGT Mar y Puertos en España. Ante las primeras señales de tensión en torno a la cuestión del encarecimiento de los carburantes, la USB decidió proclamar el paro general para el 30. Después de mediados de octubre era claro para todos que esta fecha habría podido asumir un papel mucho más extenso, uniendo, y no solo como mero eslogan, al tema de la guerra la cuestión social que estaba explotando en las calles. Así, hacia el 30 de octubre decidieron converger, tanto con adhesiones como con sus propias convocatorias, todas las demás siglas de base. Esto no ocurrió sin dificultades, tanto técnicas, debidas a la ley antisindical 146/90, como político-sindicales, debidas …

author: cnt.es
title: 13 de noviembre. Mesa redonda: ‘Comités revolucionarios e inteligencia libertaria en la retaguardia antifascista durante la GCE’
content:
El próximo

13 de noviembre

, viernes, a las

19:00

, retomamos la programación cultural en torno al

90 aniversario de la Revolución Social

. Para ello organizamos una mesa redonda titulada:

Comités revolucionarios e inteligencia libertaria en la retaguardia antifascista durante la Guerra Civil Española

.

 Contaremos con la presencia de dos especialistas en la cuestión, el investigador madrileño

Fernando Jiménez

, autor, entre otros interesantes títulos de

El mito de las checas. Historia y memoria de los comités revolucionarios (Madrid, 1936)

, y el historiador catalán

Dani Capmany

, autor de

El eco de las muletas. Una aproximación a Manuel Escorza del Val

 y

Quemar a Troncoso. Inteligencia libertaria en la Guerra Civil Española

.


Con esta mesa redonda pretendemos abordar un tema espinoso, el de

la seguridad en la retaguardia antifascista durante la Guerra Civil Española

, que, sin embargo, empieza a ser estudiado de manera rigurosa por distintos investigadores e investigadoras.


En un

contexto revolucionario

 como el que se vivió en la zona antifascista a finales de julio de 1936,

las estructuras de seguridad, control policial e inteligencia militar y civil, se vieron sacudidas de manera radical por el impulso revolucionario de la clase trabajadora

. Las organizaciones obreras, con los sindicatos

CNT y UGT a la cabeza

, no solo tuvieron que asumir un esfuerzo de guerra para el que, en buena medida, no estaban preparadas hasta ese momento, sino que tuvieron que hacerse partícipes del

control de retaguardia

, ya no solo para impedir la acción de la quinta columna, sino también para

defender las conquistas revolucionarias

 e impedir la discrecionalidad en las incautaciones, toma de fábricas, gestión de los abastos, etc.

title: Hennepin County Charges Far-Right Influencers Following Election Fraud Stunt
content:
Minneapolis, MN – Hennepin County Attorney Mary Moriarty

announced

 felony charges of identity theft and unlawful voting against far-right influencers James O’Keefe and Cam Higby

on Wednesday

, Oct. 28.


“Before the August 11 primary election this office was very clear that reports of unlawful activity related to the election would be investigated and charged if appropriate,” Moriarty said during a press conference held on Oct. 27.


The charges stem from a series of videos produced by the duo during the Minnesota primary election on Aug. 11, where the two attempted to document what they alleged was a flaw in the state’s voter registration system that allows voters to prove their residence by having neighbors vouch for them. 


In the videos, Higby and O’Keefe, representing O’Keefe’s Florida-based Citizens Justice League, provide the names of actual voters in the area to poll workers but stop short of signing the oath to receive the ballot.


“Minnesota law states clearly that no individual shall intentionally misrepresent their identity in applying for a ballot,” Moriarty said, addressing the fact that neither man actually received a ballot. “The charges filed today are appropriate to address the conduct of Mr. O’Keefe and Mr. Higby.”


Read the charging complaints at the end of the article or click the name:

Cam Higby

 /

James O’Keefe


The vouching system in Minnesota is rarely used, accounting for less than 0.6% of all votes cast during the 2024 election, according to Moriarty. The system is most often used among those who live in senior living facilities, where residents often do not obtain drivers licenses updated with the facility’s address.


Despite this, both men disguised themselves as Muslim women and visited polling locations across Minneapolis. 


In one video published Aug. 14 Higby made a clear case for election fraud against himself. In it, he appears dressed in a niqab, with the area around his eyes painted a shade of brown, while attempting to vote under his assumed aliases, all of which were the real names of registered voters.


Throughout the video, Higby repeatedly asks the poll workers if the potential voter being vouched for needs a form of identification. At the first polling location, the poll worker tells him the other person needs one.


“No,” Higby said in a forced accent. “We don’t have ID. We no have pocket.”


If a voter is being vouched for at a polling place, they still need to provide either their Minnesota driver’s license, an ID card number or the last four digits of their social security number,

according to the Secretary of State website

.


Poll workers immediately reported Higby and O’Keefe’s group after their visits,

Minnesota Secretary of State Steve Simon told KSTP News later that day

.


“Their apparent goal was to cast doubt on one or more Minnesota election laws that have been in force for over fifty years,” Simon said in a statement. “Instead, they revealed their ignorance of how those laws actually work – while putting themselves in legal jeopardy.”


O’Keefe defended his and Higby’s actions that day by citing his earlier work with Project Veritas “investigating” the 2012 and 2016 elections in New Hampshire.


Project Veritas, founded by O’Keefe in June 2010, was

described by the Southern Poverty Law Center

 in 2022 as a “hard-right propaganda group that engages in sting operations.”


Related – 2025:

Newly Revealed FBI Document Confirms Collaboration Between DC Police and Discredited Far-Right Group Project Veritas


In New Hampshire in 2012, O’Keefe’s group visited a polling location and requested the ballots for numerous dead people whose names had yet to be culled from voter rolls. The state opened a criminal investigation into O’Keefe and his group,

quietly dropping the charges the next year

.


The strategy used in Minneapolis in August of sending somebody into a polling location under false pretenses dressed in a burqa is not entirely new to O’Keefe. During the 2016 presidential election, a female Project Veritas journalist dressed in a burqa entered a New York City polling location and requested the ballot of Huma Abedin.


On Oct. 26, two days before Hennepin County announced the charges, the two attempted the same investigation in Florida, both still dressed as Muslims.


In 2010,

O’Keefe pleaded guilty

 to entering federal property under false pretenses, for which he was ordered to pay a $1,500 fine and placed on three years’ probation …

author: labor4pal
title: The Teamsters’ Midterm Disaster (Joe Allen)
content:
The Teamsters’ Midterm Disaster

Despite a post-election effort to perfume up the performance of the Teamsters’ in the recent midterm elections, a string of high profile endorsements, many with the blessing of its General President Sean O’Brien went down to a thumping defeat. The historic ‘blue wave’ changed the color of the electoral map in the United States and raised political hopes for many people that a change in direction in the country is possible. Trump’s second term was a nightmare and saw a dramatic shift to the left by many working class people.

Liz Shuler, president of the sclerotic and long declining AFL-CIO captured some of this feeling when she boasted:

“This blue wave was union-made. The billionaires had the money in this election, but working people had the power. The people who make this country run issued a clear mandate last night. Speaking with a unified voice, workers demanded that their elected leaders fight to raise their wages and lower costs, expand access to health care and unions, hold billionaire CEOs accountable, and check the Trump administration’s attacks on their freedoms. The labor movement is ready to work with these newly elected members of Congress, governors and state legislators on a bold agenda to deliver real change for the working class.”

Whether workers get real change after many failed blue waves during the last twenty years, is another question, but can Sean O’Brien make the same claims as Shuler? With a necklace of far right creeps hung around the Teamsters’ neck going down to glorious defeat, most notably Greg Abbott in Texas and Vivek Ramaswamy in Ohio, it is hard to see how the Teamsters have any credibility with anyone, anywhere. It’s worth asking out loud a question that many people have asked privately, are the Teamsters trying to be the most hated union in the United States?

The Teamsters’ midterm disaster has been foretold for several years now. Soon after the Teamsters settled their overhyped 2023 contract with United Parcel Service (UPS), Sean O’Brien, the union’s General President elected in 2021, had a string of chummy meetings with far right political figures in Washington, D.C. with then Senator J.D. Vance and Missouri Senator Josh Hawley. O’Brien was then invited to Mar-a-Largo by then former President Donald for an amiable meeting and photo opportunity. Trump was then invited to the Teamsters’ headquarters in Washington. For all this outreach to the far right, O’Brien was rewarded with a prime time speaking slot at the 2024 Republican Convention.

From there, it just got worse, as documented by Current Affairs contributor Hank Kennedy in his article, Sean O’Brien Sold Labor to Trump, and Got Nothing:

Under O’Brien the Teamsters went on record supporting the president’s pick for Secretary of Labor, Lori Chavez DeRemer, and O’Brien himself wrote an op-ed calling her “The Pro-Worker Choice for Labor” in Compact. Under questioning, DeRemer admitted she no longer supported the section of the PRO Act weakening state anti-union right-to-work laws. This bothered O’Brien not a bit. On Fox, he said that he and his bosom buddy Josh Hawley were working on a version of the PRO Act that “may not include [a ban on right-to-work]” O’Brien seemed to say that right-to-work laws could be “what works” for certain states. At least, that’s how the vehemently anti-union National Right to Work Committee interpreted his remarks in a post on X.

DeRemer resigned in disgrace, but was a guest of Sean O’Brien, whom she called her “good friend,” at the recent Teamsters convention in Las Vegas.

The Teamsters didn’t formally endorse Trump or the Democratic presidential candidate Vice-President Kamala Harris, but the non-endorsement of Harris was seen as a victory by Trump. Speaking to reporters, Trump said of the Teamsters decision not to endorse a candidate: “It’s a great honor. They’re not going to endorse the Democrats. That’s a big thing.” Most people following union and Teamster politics saw it as a backhanded endorsement of Trump.

“Sean O’Brien is not the first Teamster leader to have endorsed right-wing politicians hostile to organized labor,” Kennedy argued. “The Teamsters endorsed Richard Nixon, Ronald Reagan, and George H.W. Bush, usually in a cynical effort to stave off federal investigations and indictments of corrupt leadership. As far as is known, there’s no such cloud hanging over O’Brien’s head. He walks this road to perdition under his own steam.”

content:
Sommes-nous dans une situation pré-autoritaire ou pré-révolutionnaire ? L'insurrection est-elle un devoir en plus d'être un droit ? Faut-il articuler l'émeute au moment électoral ou pas du tout ? Nous nous posons ces questions avec Tristan Garcia (L'autorité est un chantage, 2026) et Patrice Maniglier (La terre ou le monde. Divergences cosmopolitiques. Avec Étienne Balibar. 2025).


À voir lundi 9 novembre :


Quand Marc Crépon affirme sur

C politique

boomer

 – évoque pour lui la tarte à la crème du nihilisme des

Possédés

 de Dostoïevski, il ne se rend peut-être pas compte de l'hilarité universelle qu'il suscite chez à peu près tout le monde. Lorsque l'historien, professeur au collège de France, Patrick Boucheron, dans un entretien de Libération, le 31 octobre : dénonce ceux qui continuent de

« croire que la violence émeutière est toujours émancipatrice »

 et pose le constat que nous sommes en situation pré-autoritaire et pas prérévolutionnaire. Il ne se doute pas que nous rions tout autant.


Lundimatin

 n'a que faire des tautologies nihilistes et des dissociations sociales-démocrates. Notre position a toujours été celle de l'

Encyclopédie des émeutes

 : « Ce qui est intéressant dans l'émeute n'est pas une cause, mais un possible » (BE, II, 54). « Toute tentative des pauvres modernes pour organiser le débat sur le monde commence par une émeute : 1789, 1848, 1871, 1917, 1968, et en 1978 en Iran et au Nicaragua. » (BE, II, 55) C'est pourquoi l'émeute est pour nous « le début possible de la fin du monde » (55) et, en général, « un début de débat » sur cette fin (55). Toute émeute ne conduit pas à une insurrection ou une révolution, mais « il n'y a pas de révolution ni d'insurrection qui ne commencent par une émeute. » (55).

title: Feindbild Antifaschismus: Inflationärer Einsatz von Öffentlichkeitsfahndung
content:
Feindbild Antifaschismus: Inflationärer Einsatz von Öffentlichkeitsfahndung


Ende Oktober 2026 hat das Landeskriminalamt Baden-Württemberg eine Öffentlichkeitsfahndung gegen Antifaschist*innen gestartet, gegen die es wegen schweren Landfriedensbruchs ermittelt. Damit droht ein neuer Dammbruch, indem dieses schwer wiegende Repressionsinstrument inflationär gegen Linke eingesetzt werden könnte.

Initiiert hat die Fahndung die Kriminalpolizei Heidelberg, der das regionale Dezernat Staatsschutz – die Politische Polizei – angegliedert ist. Sie ermittelt gegen rund 40 Antifaschist*innen, die an einer körperlichen Auseinandersetzung mit Rechten am 29. August 2026 in Mannheim beteiligt gewesen sein sollen. Der konkrete Straftatbestand, der ihnen vorgeworfen wird, ist schwerer Landfriedensbruch – ein Pauschalvorwurf, der einen individuellen Tatnachweis obsolet macht und die bloße Anwesenheit in einer Gruppe verfolgt. Der Paragraf wird häufig angewandt, um nach Demonstrationen oder anderen Aktionen dutzende oder gar hunderte Aktivist*innen zu kriminalisieren.

Indem auf der Homepage des Landeskriminalamts 13 Fotos von Beschuldigten veröffentlicht wurden, ist eine neue Stufe der Repression gegen Antifaschist*innen erreicht: Nur vereinzelt wurde diese massive Maßnahme bisher im Kontext von linken Protesten eingesetzt. Dass es hier in erster Linie um Einschüchterung und Abschreckung geht, zeigte eine erste Hausdurchsuchung in diesem Verfahrenskomplex, bei der die Einsatzkräfte rabiat auftraten.

„Dass das Landeskriminalamt Baden-Württemberg die Beschuldigten an den Online-Pranger stellt, zeigt, dass im Kampf gegen Antifaschismus alle Dämme brechen“, erklärte Hartmut Brückner vom Bundesvorstand der Roten Hilfe e. V. „Ob nach Blockaden, Demonstrationen und Aktionen, ob bei Öffentlichkeitsarbeit oder schlichtweg gegen antifaschistische Einrichtungen und Infrastruktur: Kaum ein Repressionsinstrument wird ausgelassen, um Aktivist*innen und die gesamte Bewegung einzuschüchtern und von weiterem Engagement abzuhalten. Umso wichtiger ist es, die Betroffenen nicht alleinzulassen, sondern im Repressionsfall solidarisch zu unterstützen. Wir sind alle Antifa!“

author: Julius Gavroche
title: The Hot Potato Changes Hands Again
content:
On the 2026 Midterm Elections


from the

CrimethInc.

collective, 06/11/2026


Ultimately, the Democrats are no more capable of addressing the root causes of popular anger than the Republicans. State power will continue to swing back and forth more and more wildly between different parties until our rulers consolidate an autocracy or we manage to effect revolutionary change.


As we anticipated

in April

, the death knell of the Trump era has rung. Despite being

historically unpopular

, Democratic politicians won a sweeping victory in the November 2026 midterm elections. Many are describing the rout as an “

extinction-level event

” for the Republican Party.


All this should feel familiar. Only two years ago, when Democrats lost the 2024 elections, pundits across the political spectrum rushed to declare the collapse of the Democratic Party. Summarizing a widespread perception, one

expert

 claimed that


“Fundamental shifts are occurring in the body politic that have left Democrats on the wrong side of the popular vote, congressional races, and the country’s shifting demographics.”


Two years later, people are saying the same things about the Republican Party. The backlash against Republicans in this year’s election eclipses the gains they made in 2024. Yet the pendulum has been swinging wildly back and forth between parties for over a decade now—and it could be that the wildest swings have yet to come.


For all the talk of political polarization, loyalty to political parties is at its

lowest

 in decades. Since at least 2016, anger at the status quo has been the most powerful force in politics; Democrats like Hillary Clinton and Joe Biden who attempted to present themselves as its defenders have learned that the hard way. Likewise, Donald Trump has only able to win elections when he is not in office. Whenever Trump represents the ruling order, he draws the same backlash that he once managed to channel.


Since 2014, we have argued that state power itself has become a hot potato that burns whoever holds it. In a globalized economy, in which governments can no longer mitigate the impact of capitalism on their citizens without investors taking their money elsewhere, no party is able to hold state power for long without losing credibility with voters. Similarly, the challenges of maintaining position as a waning imperial power inevitably undercut the legitimacy of whoever controls the state: just as the genocide in Gaza damaged the Biden administration’s support, Trump’s

war with Iran

 has contributed to driving away voters.


Similar things are taking place all around the world.

British politicians

 have also seen rapid reversals in fortune. The centrist parties that have long ruled Germany and France are in precipitous decline. One Latin American government after another has swung to the far right, but that hardly indicates a

social consensus

 in favor of

any political camp

.


Only countries under continuous autocratic rule, such as Russia, Belarus, China, and North Korea, are excepted from the hot potato pattern. Donald Trump has made no secret of his desire to establish a similar state of affairs in the United States. Yet even in Hungary, which Republicans took as a model for their illiberal aspirations, the long-running autocratic government ultimately lost control. The same has occurred in Poland and, more recently, Serbia. Wherever voters have an opportunity—however narrow—to demand change, they do so—however arbitrarily and capriciously.


With no prospect of improving life for his rank-and-file supporters, Trump’s solution was to

inflict violence

 on their behalf, offering them the vicarious thrill of watching the state cause harm to others as an outlet for their frustration.

Less bread, more circuses

.


Republicans and Democrats—trash and recycling.


It might have worked—if ordinary people had not courageously taken the streets to interfere. We owe Trump’s failure to those who assembled at

Tesla dealerships

 in spring 2025, who

rose up

 against federal agents and the National Guard that June, who confronted Immigration and Customs Enforcement mercenaries in

Chicago

,

Minnesota

, and elsewhere. As we previously saw in

the movement against police and white supremacy

, when people take risks in solidarity with others, this makes it possible for more people to experience empathy where previously, they only felt dissociation and apathy.

author: Jakob Reimann
title: „Renn oder Brenn“ – Brandanschlag gegen propalästinensische Aktivistin Lisa K.
content:
Am Freitagabend [30.10.26] brannte es in der Wohnung von Lisa K. in Leipzig-Connewitz. In den Wochen zuvor wurden im Kiez Graffitis mit expliziten Morddrohungen gegen das Mitglied des FLINTA*-Teams des Fußballvereins Roter Stern Leipzig gesprüht. Im Vereinsvorstand haben proisraelische „Antideutsche“ erheblichen Einfluss. Eine Rekonstruktion der Ereignisse von etos.media-Redakteur Jakob Reimann.


UPDATE: In einer ursprünglichen Version des Artikels waren zwei Funktionäre des Vereins Roter Stern Leipzig mit Klarnamen genannt. Auf Wunsch der betroffenen Mitglieder des FLINTA*-Teams wurden diese entfernt.


Manchmal folgen Worten eben auch Taten. Am Freitagabend brannte es in einem Mehrfamilienhaus in der Wolfgang-Heinze-Straße in Leipzig-Connewitz. Die Wohnung im dritten Stock war zu dem Zeitpunkt leer – die Bewohnerin Lisa K. war nicht vor Ort. In den Wochen zuvor waren im Kiez Dutzende Graffitis mit Morddrohungen gegen die palästinasolidarische Aktivistin gesprüht worden: „Lisa K. renn oder brenn“, lautete eine davon.


Um 19.22 Uhr ging der Notruf bei der Leitstelle ein, berichtete die Leipziger Volkszeitung; 30 Minuten später wurde der Brand als gelöscht gemeldet. Die Feuerwehrleute mussten sich gewaltsam Zugang verschaffen. Bereits zuvor hatten die Bewohner das Haus verlassen. Verletzt wurde niemand. Mit Spezialfiltern musste der Rauch entfernt werden.


Die Kriminalpolizeiinspektion führe Ermittlungen wegen des Verdachts eines Branddelikts, erklärt ein Polizeisprecher gegenüber etos.media. Der oder die Täter müssten in die Wohnung eingebrochen sein und hätten in allen Räumen Brandbeschleuniger verteilt, erzählt Lisa K. im Gespräch. Fotos und Videos des Tatorts liegen der Redaktion vor, werden aus Achtung vor K.s Privatsphäre jedoch nicht veröffentlicht. Sie zeigen schwere Brandschäden im Eingangsbereich der Wohnung und in einem zweiten Raum. Die Einrichtung wurde in weiten Teilen zerstört und die Wohnung komplett verwüstet. Dies deutet neben Einbruch und schwerer Brandstiftung auch auf Vandalismus hin. Solidarische haben einen Hilfsfonds für Lisa K. eingerichtet.


Am frühen Sonntagmorgen brannte es in einem weiteren Haus in Connewitz, berichtete die Leipziger Volkszeitung. Ein Kinderwagen im Hausflur in der Bornaischen Straße wurde in Brand gesetzt. Auf der Fassade des Hauses stand ein Soli-Graffiti: „We stand with Lisa.“ Es wurde später von Unbekannten übermalt.


*„Stell dich dem Plenum“*


Dem Brandanschlag ging über Monate hinweg eine Reihe von Ereignissen voraus, die womöglich in direktem Zusammenhang mit der zerstörten Wohnung stehen. In der Nacht zum 17. September und in drei weiteren Nächten wurden insgesamt mehr als 80 Graffitis im Umfeld des Vereins und in Lisa K.s Connewitzer Kiez gesprüht. Sie enthielten gewaltverherrlichende, rassistische, frauenfeindliche und teils extrem verstörende Inhalte. Darunter waren zahlreiche Todeswünsche bis hin zu Morddrohungen:


– „Häng dich auf Lisa K.“


– „Lisa K. renn oder brenn“


– „Antisemiten raus aus dem RSL. Lisa K. nimm dir einen Strick“


– „Anti-Lisa Aktion Antisemiten raus aus dem RSL!“


– „Lieber 100 Nazis im Kiez als Lisa K.“


– „Lisa K. raus aus dem RSL“


– „Lisa K. stell dich dem Plenum“


– „Lisa K. töten!“


– „Lisa K. totknüppeln“


– „Lisa K. jagen!“


– „Lisa K. wir kriegen dich!“


– „Antisemiten töten. Lisa K. stell dich!“


– „Lisa K. raus aus dem Kiez!“


– „Bald 1 Raum Whng unter der Erde für Lisa K.“


– „Lisa K nach Gaza deportieren“


– „Vergewaltigung in Gaza für Lisa K.“


– …


Es werde „unter anderem wegen Sachbeschädigung und Bedrohung ermittelt“, erklärt ein Sprecher der Polizeidirektion auf Anfrage. Die verschiedenen Handschriften legen nahe, dass es sich um mehrere Täter handelt. „Lisa K. renn oder brenn“ impliziert eine Verbindung zum Brandanschlag. Der mehrfache Bezug zum Roten Stern lässt womöglich auf Personen aus dem RSL-Umfeld schließen, etwa die Aufforderung „Lisa K stell dich dem Plenum“.


Auf dem Plenum am 24. September habe die RSL-Sicherheitsbeauftragte laut mehreren Anwesenden mit Nachdruck erklärt, sie erwehre sich dagegen, dass die Person/en aus dem Verein stammt/en. Worauf sich diese Ansicht stützt, ließ sie offen. title: The Hot Potato Changes Hands Again : On the 2026 Midterm Elections
content:
Ultimately, the Democrats are no more capable of addressing the root causes of popular anger than the Republicans. State power will continue to swing back and forth more and more wildly between different parties until our rulers consolidate an autocracy or we manage to effect revolutionary change.


As we anticipated

in April

, the death knell of the Trump era has rung. Despite being

historically unpopular

, Democratic politicians won a sweeping victory in the November 2026 midterm elections. Many are describing the rout as an “

extinction-level event

” for the Republican Party.


All this should feel familiar. Only two years ago, when Democrats lost the 2024 elections, pundits across the political spectrum rushed to declare the collapse of the Democratic Party. Summarizing a widespread perception, one

expert

 claimed that


“Fundamental shifts are occurring in the body politic that have left Democrats on the wrong side of the popular vote, congressional races, and the country’s shifting demographics.”


Two years later, people are saying the same things about the Republican Party. The backlash against Republicans in this year’s election eclipses the gains they made in 2024. Yet the pendulum has been swinging wildly back and forth between parties for over a decade now—and it could be that the wildest swings have yet to come.


For all the talk of political polarization, loyalty to political parties is at its

lowest

 in decades. Since at least 2016, anger at the status quo has been the most powerful force in politics; Democrats like Hillary Clinton and Joe Biden who attempted to present themselves as its defenders have learned that the hard way. Likewise, Donald Trump has only able to win elections when he is not in office. Whenever Trump represents the ruling order, he draws the same backlash that he once managed to channel.


Since 2014, we have argued that state power itself has become a hot potato that burns whoever holds it. In a globalized economy, in which governments can no longer mitigate the impact of capitalism on their citizens without investors taking their money elsewhere, no party is able to hold state power for long without losing credibility with voters. Similarly, the challenges of maintaining position as a waning imperial power inevitably undercut the legitimacy of whoever controls the state: just as the genocide in Gaza damaged the Biden administration’s support, Trump’s

war with Iran

 has contributed to driving away voters.


Similar things are taking place all around the world.

British politicians

 have also seen rapid reversals in fortune. The centrist parties that have long ruled Germany and France are in precipitous decline. One Latin American government after another has swung to the far right, but that hardly indicates a

social consensus

 in favor of

any political camp

.


Only countries under continuous autocratic rule, such as Russia, Belarus, China, and North Korea, are excepted from the hot potato pattern. Donald Trump has made no secret of his desire to establish a similar state of affairs in the United States. Yet even in Hungary, which Republicans took as a model for their illiberal aspirations, the long-running autocratic government ultimately lost control. The same has occurred in Poland and, more recently, Serbia. Wherever voters have an opportunity—however narrow—to demand change, they do so—however arbitrarily and capriciously.


With no prospect of improving life for his rank-and-file supporters, Trump’s solution was to

inflict violence

 on their behalf, offering them the vicarious thrill of watching the state cause harm to others as an outlet for their frustration.

Less bread, more circuses

.


Republicans and Democrats—trash and recycling.


It might have worked—if ordinary people had not courageously taken the streets to interfere. We owe Trump’s failure to those who assembled at

Tesla dealerships

 in spring 2025, who

rose up

 against federal agents and the National Guard that June, who confronted Immigration and Customs Enforcement mercenaries in

Chicago

,

Minnesota

, and elsewhere. As we previously saw in

the movement against police and white supremacy

, when people take risks in solidarity with others, this makes it possible for more people to experience empathy where previously, they only felt dissociation and apathy.


The grassroots resistance that emerged in response to the Trump administration stands in stark contrast to the way that …

Dossier


„In der Bundespolitik ist das Entsetzen über den Erfolg der AfD bei der Bundestagswahl noch immer groß. Die soziale Dynamik ziele darauf ab, den öffentlichen Raum für alle Personen einzuschränken, die nicht in ein rechtes Weltbild passen, beispielsweise durch dominantes Auftreten von AfD-Abgeordneten im Kommunalparlament – und durch Bedrohungen und Gewalt. (…) Exemplarisch für [die] AfD-Strategie stehen die Attacken auf das Bundesprogramm „Demokratie leben“ des Bundesministeriums für Familie, Senioren, Frauen und Jugend, das zivilgesellschaftliche Initiativen und Vereine fördert, die sich für Demokratie und gegen Extremismus engagieren…“  

Artikel von Elisa Pfleger in den »Blättern« 4/2025


 und mehr daraus/dazu:


U-Turn vom Rotstift? Bund will nach eigenem Sparkurs Demokratieprojekte in Sachsen-Anhalt gegen AfD absichern – zivilgesellschaftliche Organisationen warnen seit Monaten vor den Folgen


„Der Bund will Demokratieprojekte in Sachsen-Anhalt gegen den Wegfall von Landes- und Kommunalmitteln unter einer möglichen AfD-Regierung absichern. Dafür sollen zusätzliche Förderwege erschlossen werden, auch außerhalb des Programms „Demokratie leben!“. „Wir wollen tragfähige Lösungen finden, damit Engagement und Beratungsangebote auch dann fortbestehen können, wenn die Unterstützung durch das Land oder einzelne Kommunen wegfallen sollte“, erklärte das Bundesbildungsministerium am Mittwoch. Bereits bestehende Fördermöglichkeiten sollten

geöffnet oder weiterentwickelt


 werden. Es geht auch darum, Projekte weniger abhängig von der Zustimmung einzelner Länder oder Kommunen zu machen. Ein neues Budget oder konkrete Förderzusagen nannte das Ministerium nicht. (…) Dabei plant die Bundesregierung selbst Einschnitte bei der Demokratieförderung. Nach dem

Haushaltsentwurf für 2027

Davon sind 167,4 Millionen Euro für das Programm „Demokratie leben!“ vorgesehen. Damit werden Träger, Projekte und Initiativen gefördert, die in der Demokratiebildung und Extremismusprävention aktiv sind. Hinzu kommt ein umstrittener

Umbau von „Demokratie leben!“

  

, den Bundesministerin Karin Prien (CDU) bereits im Frühjahr eingeleitet hatte. Zwei bisherige Programmbereiche mit rund 200 Projekten laufen Ende des Jahres in ihrer bisherigen Form aus.
