author: Sharon Lerner
title: Trump Admin Giving $1M to Group Studying Crime Against White South Africans
content:
The new award comes after the administration cut human rights funding to nations in crisis.

Support justice-driven, accurate and transparent news — make a quick donation to Truthout today!

After slashing funding for programs that documented atrocities and protected human rights abroad, President Donald Trump’s State Department is now granting one of its first new human rights awards to a controversial South African organization that promotes the disputed notion that white farmers are a violently targeted, persecuted group, according to multiple sources knowledgeable about the funding.

The group expected to receive the nearly $1 million award, AfriForum, is a nonprofit that advocates on behalf of Afrikaners, a subset of South Africa’s white population. The organization says its members, who have a “God-given calling,” fight for Afrikaner interests and self-governance. The money will be used to “document hateful rhetoric and violent acts” against Afrikaners and other minority populations in the country.

The new award comes from a State Department bureau tasked with promoting democracy and human rights internationally. Until last year, those funds were mainly spent in poor and authoritarian nations — to fight corruption in the Democratic Republic of Congo, for example, or combat child exploitation and sexual abuse in Afghanistan. Since Trump returned to office, his appointees have transformed the bureau, gutting its staff, canceling programs and reorienting some of its funding toward conservative causes in Europe.

Samuel Samson, who was appointed as a deputy assistant secretary to the State Department bureau by Trump, has claimed the U.S. has a “civilizational” connection to Afrikaners, who descend primarily from Dutch migrants and predominantly speak Afrikaans. Samson, who has met with far-right leaders in Europe since joining the administration last year, has framed the U.S. government’s financial support for Afrikaners as grounded in “a common heritage, a common culture, a common way of life, shared history and ultimately a common anthropology.”

There’s a long shared political history between Afrikaner groups and white nationalists in the U.S., said Audie Klotz, a political science professor at Syracuse University who has studied those connections. But, she said, “There’s no heritage connection here. It’s pure scientific racism. In the history of U.S. immigration, there’s no direct connection between South Africa and the United States.”

AfriForum met with the Trump administration in February 2025 to plead for help. The group told officials that Afrikaners are subject to racial discrimination and murders that are more frequent and asked the administration to “act strongly against hate speech that incites violence” against them, according to a statement.

South Africa is plagued by high rates of violence, and some Afrikaners have been tortured and murdered. But independent researchers have found those killings represent a tiny fraction of murders across the country, whose victims are disproportionately people living in poor urban areas, where residents are predominantly Black. Official government statistics, and two formal inquiries into the matter, do not reveal a pattern of targeted violence against Afrikaners.

But Trump subscribes to the idea that white farmers face a “genocide” and has cited disproportionate violence against them as a reason for punishing Africa’s wealthiest nation. In February 2025, he issued an executive order that cut off hundreds of millions of dollars of aid to South Africa and welcomed Afrikaners to the U.S. as refugees. Since then, the administration has opened the doors to more than 16,000 white South Africans while halting virtually all other immigration. Officials recently told Congress they plan to invite as many as 17,500 Afrikaner refugees to the U.S. in 2027.

AfriForum did not respond to specific questions for this story but said that “our understanding is that the allocation has not yet been finalised. Should the allocation indeed be awarded to AfriForum, we will make a public announcement in this regard.”

The new award is the administration’s latest show of support for the Afrikaner cause. The white South African group governed the nation for decades under a brutal system of segregation known as apartheid, which kept the Black majority an impoverished underclass until the system was dismantled in 1994. author: Clare Hymer
title: Could the Way the Greens Set Policy Be About to Change?
content:
Could the way the Green party of England and Wales makes policy – and who gets to call the shots – be about to change?


Ever since

the motion stating that Zionism is racism

 passed at Green conference in October, senior figures have taken to legacy media outlets to claim that the vote shows the party’s internal democracy isn’t working. 


In an act with more than a whiff of the Corbyn-era Labour right, former co-leader and MP for Waveney Valley Adrian Ramsay told Laura Kuenssberg at the weekend that the Greens are at risk of being overrun by the “hard left”. Ellie Chowns MP has said she wants to make sure her party is not

“vulnerable to capture by extremists”

, while Green trailblazer Caroline Lucas has raised

concerns about “entryism”

. 


But it’s not just the Greens’ old guard who think the party needs a shake-up. Leader Zack Polanski wrote in

a Guardian article

 after the conference that the party’s democracy must “evolve” to meet the Greens’ newly expanded membership, “creating wider engagement for members, giving leaders more responsibility to set… strategic direction, and making our processes as robust and accessible as possible”. This was followed by

a “joint leadership statement”

 last week which said a working group had been set up, and the first proposals would likely be voted on at the party’s conference in spring 2027.


As it stands, the Greens have a one-member-one-vote system: any member, regardless of how long ago they joined the party, can vote on policy and changes to the party’s constitution. This direct democracy, which is distinct from the other mainstream parties in Britain, is cherished by the membership – and any group of members who organise well around conference can change party policy, be that to declare that Zionism is racism, or for the Greens

to ditch their longstanding opposition to nuclear power

. 


The recent murmurings around change have got some members worried. An

open letter

 to Polanski and co. circulating on social media this week insists that the party sticks with the one-member-one-vote model, and that “members will not accept any move away from this model”. Meanwhile, Greens for Palestine – the members behind the Zionism is racism motion – put out

a statement

 against those seeking to “subvert the Green party’s member-led democracy because they fear a loss of control”.


Russell Warfield, author of the new book

The Green Socialist: Zack Polanski and the Battle for Britain’s Future

, told Novara Media he doesn’t think Polanski’s calls for improvements to the party’s democracy are, unlike for others, “a knee-jerk reaction to fix the ‘problem’ of the Zionism motion”. But for as long as the leadership’s proposals are unspecific, Polanski risks being seen to be in a coalition with those most vocally opposed to the motion. Members are likely wondering if their leader is –

like Ramsay

 – in favour of a delegate system more similar to Labour, whereby local parties select members to send to conferences.


On Wednesday, Greens Organise, a group of ecosocialist party members,

published a model motion

 aimed at improving how conferences run and better engaging members – one it hopes will be uncontroversial. It also

called for proposals

 for the more fundamental matter of how (and crucially if) the party’s democracy should be reformed. Co-deputy leader Rachel Millward told Novara Media the leadership welcomed this initiative, in addition to a forthcoming consultation of the wider membership.


Greens Organise said: “Any changes must serve the purpose of building a mass, ecosocialist party – not a reaction to any one policy… We should not leave it to [the leadership] to decide.”


The good news for those in the ‘change nothing’ camp is that anyone wanting to see a major reform through will have a tough time. First, they’d need a two-thirds majority. Second,

many have wrangled over the party’s internal workings before

 – and yet its core structure remains the same as 30 years ago. (Warfield noted that it’s an odd reversal that the veteran Greens “clamouring” for the current review “roughly correspond to the cohort who most resisted it last time”.)


“I think it’s unlikely this is going to be easily resolved,” Warfield said.

title: Alemania: la solidaridad con Palestina no es negociable
content:
Líder de Die Linke, Elif Eralp, y manifestantes pro Palestina en Alemania (Ibrahim Ibrahim entre ellos). Foto © Instagram / @eliferalp – Wikipedia


Die Linke fue la fuerza más votada en las últimas elecciones para la Cámara de Diputados de Berlín y de las asambleas de Consejales de Distrito el 20.09. Se desplegó una campaña de agresión, odio y mentiras, ya durante la campaña electoral, que se intensificó luego de la victoria. Obtuvo 25,7 % de los votos, seguido por CDU (derecha cristiana) con el 18,8 % y el partido Grün/Verde alcanzó el 14,3%. Pero como no se llegó a la mayoría, la izquierda podrá gobernar solo si se forma una coalición. CDU se negó rotundamnete a una coalción con la izquierda. Tras semanas de discuciones y peleas mediáticas, siguen sin ponerse de acuerdo sobre los puntos más candentes, que son los puntos claves, por los que muchas personas -sobre todo de origen migrante- habían depositado su voto a favor a Die Linke y son la no criminalización a la solidaridad con Palestina y la expropiación de los inmuebles.

Por Ana Muro, corresponsal de ANRed en Alemania.


El programa para las elecciones que presentó Die Linke decía entre otros puntos: “Deben fomentarse los proyectos contra el racismo antipalestino. Las restricciones a la libertad de expresión, de ciencia y de reunión, así como a otros derechos fundamentales, deben investigarse en profundidad en relación con esta forma específica de racismo y debe combatírselas.”


“La libertad de reunión debe protegerse con más fuerza frente a las restricciones estatales. (…) Condenamos la violencia policial y las restricciones desproporcionadas a la libertad de reunión y de expresión, como las que recientemente han afectado a manifestaciones solidarias con Palestina o aactivistas climáticos. (…) Queremos sacar a la autoridad de reuniones de la Policía de Berlín.”


El 8 de octubre se publicó el “acuerdo“ sobre el inicio de las conversaciones exploratorias entre Die Linke Berlín, Bündnis 90/Die Grünen y el SPD, entre los partidos que es posible una coalición. Ese acuerdo refuerza la represión, porque la definición de antisemitismo que utiliza es tan amplia que cualquier crítica a la política de ocupación, asentamientos, apartheid y genocidio del Estado de Israel queda incluida.


Ese acuerdo además fortalece a la policía y al Verfassungsschutz (Oficina para la Protección de la Constitución), amplía su presupuesto y sus competencias, y los refuerza como garantes de unapolítica de orden público que lleva tres años criminalizando y reprimiendo la solidaridad conPalestina.


Naturalmente los votantes se sienten traicionados


El acuerdo le da poder al SPD y a los Verdes, para decidir entre las voces aceptables y las que deben silenciarse, es decir, aquellas que no se ajustan a la Staatsräson, al apoyo incondicional de Alemania hacia Israel. Ambos partidos tienen una trayectoria bastante manchada en la historia. Los verdes en los 80′ empezaron militarizando la política exterior alemana y el SPD, a pesar de ser concebida con sociales, boicoteó la revolución en 1918 de la mano de Friedrich Ebert.


El arca política no quiere que gobierne un partido de izquierda, por ello a través de este acuerdo quieren un partido más débil, más dócil, divido, para poder frenar el tema que realmente le preocupa a la derechay al centro político: la expropiación de las viviendas. El monopolio inmobiliario tiene un poder inmenso y ejerce presión en los políticos.


La campaña de desprestigio a militantes concretos como Ferat Koçak y Vanessa Emde (ambos son los que más se solidarizan con Palestina) y a la izquierda en general, no apunta a combatir el antisemitismo real, sino a castigar cualquier voz que critique la política de ocupación, de asentamientos y de apartheid del Estado de Israel, o que cuestione la razón de Estado alemana. A su vez, se acusa a Die Linke por tener conecciones con Ibrahim Ibrahim e Issa Remo, ambos acusados de estar al frente de un clan criminal. Ibrahim Ibrahim es un activista de origen palestino y representante del Comité Nacional palestino unificado, se lo vincula con el Frente Popular para la Liberación de Palestina (considerada por EE.UU. y la UE como organización terrorista).


El tema Palestina, ya fue un punto de inflección en toda Alemania, pero también dentro de toda laIzquierda. Die Linke expulsó en 2025 a Ramsis Kilani, un activista de origen propalestino, su familia fueasesinada en un ataque aereo israelí en la franja de Gaza en 2014. Luego de más …

title: Özgür Sevgi Göral: France’s dilemmas also exist in Turkey - Part Two
content:
ANF spoke to academic Özgür Sevgi Göral, who is currently in Paris and has participated in the demonstrations, about the historical foundations of the protests and their potential.


Part one of this interview can be read

here

. 


When you compare these protests with the history of social movements and youth activism in Turkey, what similarities or significant differences do you see? Is the possibility of their influence spreading to Turkey limited, or what factors might increase that possibility?


This is a very difficult question. Youth movements in Turkey constitute a very broad field, and although I try to follow them, they are not my primary area of research. Therefore, I do not think I am in a position to compare the two countries in this respect. Perhaps I can offer just a few observations. Turkey has witnessed powerful youth movements, although they have been heavily suppressed, particularly over the past decade. We can assume that the racialised capitalist regime in which we live, and its various manifestations, have also generated considerable dissatisfaction among young people in Turkey. Moreover, even under Turkey's extremely harsh political conditions, youth movements have repeatedly emerged and made themselves visible over the past ten years. However, we know that for particular grievances or isolated political revolts to develop into powerful political mobilisation, there must be an accumulated history and tradition of struggle capable of protecting and developing itself. There must also be different political organisations operating at various levels, sometimes reaching agreements with one another and sometimes coming into conflict. I do not know to what extent such conditions exist or are possible in Turkey today, although there are certain emerging centres of struggle.


On the other hand, I think that rather than speaking of the protests spreading from one country to another, we can speak of a certain "simultaneity". Simultaneity, a concept frequently used in the literature on political and social movements, suggests that movements in different parts of the world during the same historical period can inspire one another in terms of political programmes, repertoires of mobilisation and demands, and that revolutionary ideas can travel across geographical boundaries. This could also apply to Turkey at a moment when the repertoire of street protests has some room to expand. However, the state's security strategy and policies against the accumulated experience of the Kurdish struggle, particularly the rapid criminalisation of forms of political violence and their framing through the concept of "terrorism", have unfortunately also proved effective among different political and social movements. Therefore, I cannot determine whether this wave of protests might produce rapid consequences for youth movements in Turkey through an effect of simultaneity, or what possibilities might exist for such a development. I am sure that my colleagues who are active in this field and study these movements have much more to say on the subject than I do.


Do these protests offer the prospect of lasting social and political transformation?


I think this question is extremely important, not only in relation to these protests but also in terms of the situation that widespread mass protests and uprisings have faced for some time. The latest youth uprising began on a broader scale than previous ones. However, in France and many other countries, it is debatable how successful such uprisings have been in producing concrete political and social transformation, despite all their potential. This movement also faces the dilemma your question points to. The central issue here is the dual nature of the demands of the groups driving the movement. There is a tension between those who prioritise short-term problems concerning the existing education system and those who focus on how wealth and resources should be distributed and on the broader prospect of anti-capitalist transformation. For now, it is difficult to say that this uprising has a programme and organisational structure based on a broader emancipatory perspective extending beyond its concrete demands. The government currently appears to have taken a step back by announcing that it will abolish Parcoursup, the university admissions system, in 2028. However, unless a strong and sustained bloc of political struggle can be established, it could introduce essentially the same …

author: Nick Everett
title: Will Israel’s election outcome make life better for Palestinians? Not likely.
content:
In the lead-up to Israel’s 27 October election, media headlines declared this would be the most “consequential” in Israel’s history. At stake is the fate of Benjamin Netanyahu, Israel’s longest-serving prime minister, who faces corruption charges at home and an international arrest warrant for war crimes in Gaza.

Israeli politicians debated the cost of living, the independence of the judiciary, conscription of ultra-Orthodox Jews into the military, a state inquiry into security failings on 7 October and Israel’s growing isolation abroad. Not up for debate was Israel’s Gaza genocide, nor the massive expansion of Israeli settlements, settler violence and military invasions in the West Bank, nor Israel’s seizure of territory in southern Lebanon and Syria. 

This was a contest between two blocs, a pro-Netanyahu coalition of far-right and ultra-Orthodox parties against an alliance of centrist and right-wing Zionist parties seeking to depose him, led by retired General Gadi Eisenkot, the former military chief of staff. A third bloc, made up of the two Arab-majority parties, the Joint List and Ra’am, was initially barred from participation by Israel’s Central Elections Committee before the supreme court overturned the ban.

Right-wing parties Likud and Otzma Yehudit petitioned for their exclusion, accusing the Arab-majority parties and candidates of denying Israel’s existence as a Jewish and democratic state, supporting armed struggle against Israel or inciting racism. A ban was, however, upheld against Sami Abu Shehadeh, leader of the Palestinian nationalist Balad party and one of the Joint List candidates, on the grounds that he had supported armed struggle against Israel. 

The evidence? An opinion piece published in 

Alaraby

 on 8 October 2023, in which Abu Shehadeh described the previous day’s Hamas-led attack on Israel as a “significant historical event”. 

Accusations of “inciting racism” against Ra’am and the Arab List are of course rank hypocrisy coming from Netanyahu and his coalition partners who have 

called for

 the “total annihilation” of Gaza’s cities and the burning of Lebanon, as well as the death penalty for Palestinians accused of “terrorism” offences.

On the eve of the election, Netanyahu’s social media posts drew attention to long queues of Palestinian voters at polling stations and urged Likud supporters to come out and vote.

“If we don't wake up now, we'll find ourselves with a government of Mansour Abbas and Ahmed Tibi”, he said, referring to the leaders of the two Arab-majority parties.

Netanyahu’s coalition ally and Jewish supremacist Itamar Ben-Gvir described the level of Arab voter turnout—people exercising their democratic right to vote—as “crazy”. As national security minister, Ben-Gvir has armed Israeli settlers and established a paramilitary police force in the West Bank.

Basel Smotrich, another Jewish supremacist Netanyahu ally, and leader of the Religious Zionism party, announced he had suspended his election day campaigning to convene an emergency meeting to discuss what he described as unusually high turnout among Arab voters, alleging voter fraud. 

While Netanyahu failed to win this election, he remains far from defeated. His ruling coalition, dominated by Likud, will likely secure 53 of the Knesset’s 120 seats, a major drop from the 64 seats he won in 2022, and significantly short of a majority. However, the opposition bloc is trailing with 48 seats. The opposition’s only pathway to power is to govern with the support of the two Arab-majority parties, the Joint List and Ra’am, which together secured an additional 19 seats (nearly double the ten they secured in 2022).

This would not be unprecedented. In 1993, the Oslo Accords were signed by a minority Israeli government with the support of the Arab List parties.

In 2021, Ra’am leader Mansour Abbas broke with the Arab List to join an eight-party coalition, the first time an Arab-majority party had joined an Israeli government. For Abbas, this was an opportunity to secure some short-lived investment in Palestinian communities inside Israel, while turning his back on the elephant in the room: the Israeli occupation. The coalition collapsed within a year following defections from its right flank.

Abbas has declared his intention again to seek a coalition that can unseat Netanyahu. His Islamist Ra’am party put a Jewish former police chief in second position on its slate. However, such overtures have so far been rebuffed.  …

author: Shireen Akram-Boshar
title: Trump Calls Immigration Policy “Too Tough,” Then Promotes Stephen Miller
content:
The new chief of staff has shaped some of Trump’s most draconian immigration policies, including family separation.

Honest, paywall-free news is rare. Please support our boldly independent journalism with a donation of any size.

In a “60 Minutes” interview that aired on Sunday evening, President Donald Trump admitted that Republicans’ massive defeats in the midterm elections resulted from widespread frustration with the war on Iran, as well as his immigration policies.

Reiterating that he “was not on the ballot” — as if to suggest that support would have been higher for him personally — Trump said that Americans “didn’t like the war” and “the fact that gasoline went up,” claiming he “had it down at a low” prior to launching the war. In Trump’s assessment, public opposition to his war on Iran is reducible to gasoline prices.

Trump also stated that Republicans’ massive losses during the midterm elections were due to “a great dislike, incredibly, for Israel” — characterizing growing opposition to the U.S.’s relationship with the genocidal state as mere “dislike.”

Trump then said that his immigration policies may have also affected the midterms, and that he may have been “too tough.”

“I think I got an A+ for closing up the border,” he said. “I get very high marks for getting the bad ones out. But I get hurt because we also took people that had good jobs, that created one violation, or breaking of the law, and that was that they came into the country illegally. And there’s a large group of people [that] think they should be allowed to stay.”

“So you think your deportation policy went too far?” asked CBS News’s Ross Douthat.

“I think it might be too tough,” Trump replied.

In the interview, Trump acknowledged a central contradiction in his administration: that he is caught between the priorities of his far right base, who “would like everybody taken out” [of the country], and the general population, which rejects his brutal policies.

Shortly after his “60 Minutes” interview on Friday, Trump announced that he was promoting political advisor Stephen Miller to White House chief of staff — suggesting that he does not, in fact, plan to soften his approach to immigration enforcement. Miller is known as the hardline, white nationalist architect of Trump’s mass deportation policies, including his policy of family separation.

Over the past year of his administration, Trump has been forced to temper the most overt aspects of his immigration crackdown, after Immigration and Customs Enforcement’s (ICE) brutal “Operation Metro Surge” in the Twin Cities brought about widespread resistance, particularly after immigration agents killed Minneapolis residents Renee Good and Alex Pretti. As a result of widespread opposition, mass protests, and even a general strike in the Twin Cities, Trump replaced Department of Homeland Security (DHS) Secretary Kristi Noem with Markwayne Mullin, who promised that DHS operations would be less visible and stay out of the headlines.

While subsequent ICE operations have not been as brazen as that of Operation Metro Surge, the agency’s strategy has not fundamentally changed. In New York City in July and August, ICE’s “Operation Rotten Apple” resulted in the arrests of some 2,200 people — more than the amount detained by ICE during Operation Metro Surge earlier in the year. The New York City operation, however, managed to evade the same level of pushback, as ICE agents remained less visible, arriving in unmarked cars and detaining and disappearing people quickly, before resistance could emerge.

Trump also stated in the “60 Minutes” interview that he would work with Democrats on immigration. Indeed, his categorization of immigrants as either hard workers or “rough,” “drug dealers” and “killers” echoes rhetoric that has been key to both Republicans’ and Democrats’ approach to immigration since the 1980s — and to bipartisan “comprehensive immigration reform” policies that have increasingly ceded ground to the right.

While voters rejected Trump’s policies in the midterm elections, it is little surprise that Trump has offered to work with Democrats on immigration, as they do not represent an actual alternative to the criminalization, deportation, and precarity offered to undocumented immigrants and asylum seekers.

Meanwhile, the president’s promotion of Miller suggests that even as Trump’s own popularity falls, his aggressive deportation tactics are likely to continue.

title: ICE Agent Falsely Accused Federal Defender of Helping Client Evade Arrest and Deportation
content:
Minneapolis, MN — It was supposed to be another routine court appearance.


Assistant Federal Defender Michael Deates and his Salvadoran client settled inside the Minneapolis courtroom on April 28. ICE Deportation Officer Michael O’Neal sat inside the gallery when he heard a familiar name: Ezequiel Portillo-Rodriguez.


He pulled out his government phone and then searched for the name. A Certificate of Nonexistence (CTNE) that he filed in April 2025 popped up. To O’Neal, this meant that there were no official records of Portillo-Rodriguez ever holding a visa, green card or U.S. citizenship. He texted agent Blake Willwerscheid, asking if he knew about the case. Willwersheid told him that Homeland Security Investigations (HSI) Special Agent Brubaker was in charge of the case. A prosecutor later testified that this HSI Agent thought he was talking to an agent Witt in St. Paul.


Had O’Neal looked through court records he would have found something more relevant than a CTNE. On Sept. 2, 2025, Portillo-Rodriguez started his six-month stint inside the notorious Golden State Annex in McFarland, Ca. He filed an asylum claim while inside the private immigration jail run by GEO Group. Attorneys wrote that Portillo-Rodriguez had a “fear of persecution and torture” if he were deported back to El Salvador. Two weeks later an asylum officer denied this claim.


An immigration judge overturned that denial on November 7, 2025, finding his fears credible.


Portillo-Rodriguez filed a habeas corpus petition on Jan. 26, 2026. His attorney Deborah Czuba filed an emergency motion for a temporary restraining order on March 12. Four days later the government decided not to contest the review.


In California, U.S. District Judge Dale Drozd declared that the government had violated Portillo-Rodriguez’s Fifth Amendment Due Process rights by subjecting him to indefinite detention without a proper hearing.


On March 18, Judge Drozd issued an injunction releasing Portillo-Rodriguez and barring ICE from re-arresting him on immigration charges.


A month later, O’Neal was texting his boss, Supervisory Detention and Deportation Officer Nicholas Carey, looking for a green light to arrest Portillo-Rodriguez. He got no response while court was in session. Once the hearing adjourned, O’Neal cornered the prosecuting attorneys, asking if this was a case where Enforcement and Removal Operations (ERO) was barred from placing a detainer. The prosecutors told him they didn’t know.


O’Neal then approached U.S. Deputy Marshal Cassandra Stone, telling her he planned to take Portillo-Rodriguez into custody. Stone told him an arrest could be made at the U.S. Probation and Pretrial Services office. O’Neal claimed that Deates was standing close enough to eavesdrop.


“Deates was listening to the conversation I was having with Deputy Marshal Stone, made eye contact with me, then told his client Portillo-Rodriguez they needed to leave and follow him downstairs,” O’Neal wrote.


Deates denied this in his sworn declaration.


“I did not overhear, and had no knowledge at the time of, any conversation,” he wrote.


Deates and Portillo-Rodriguez walked downstairs to eat lunch at the Federal Defender’s Office. O’Neal rushed to the courthouse cellblock. He called Carey, demanding an immediate administrative warrant. Minutes later, Carey emailed a signed Form I-200 straight to O’Neal’s inbox.


The plainclothes task force scrambled to spring a familiar trap. O’Neal left the courtroom with Deputy Marshals Cassandra Stone and Gnika. Stone went to the Marshals Office to scan the live security video feeds, spotting Deates and his client in the public lobby.


By the time O’Neal and the marshals rushed down to the ground floor, the lobby was empty. The marshals searched the interior corridors while O’Neal glanced out a window. He caught sight of the pair walking along the sidewalk next to Minneapolis City Hall toward the light rail platform.


The three rushed outside before a red light stopped them at the intersection of 3rd Avenue and 4th Street. The light turned green. Trains departed in both directions. O’Neal saw Deates standing alone on the light rail platform. Portillo-Rodriguez was on his way back home to California.


After the failed trap, O’Neal contacted Special Agent Brubaker for an update. Brubaker informed him that Portillo-Rodriguez had been released in California on a habeas corpus petition.


The next day O’Neal sent a memo to Assistant ICE Field Officer …

title: La derrota del trumpismo: ¿un canto de cisne o un cisne negro?
content:
LA DERROTA DEL TRUMPISMO: ¿UN

CANTO DE CISNE

 O UN

CISNE NEGRO

?


Por Rafael Bautista S.


Mientras el futuro más temible llegue,


lo único que nos devuelva la luz será


esta velita prendida que supimos


cuidar en plena oscuridad.


Ya con la cabeza fría, conviene profundizar analítica y prospectivamente lo que se ha de jugar en estos casi dos meses de transición hacia las más temibles opciones que se pondrán en movimiento, una vez que el Estado profundo ha decidido prescindir del episodio Trump. Por cuestiones de sobrevivencia discordante –como ya señalamos– entre dos opciones supremacistas de restauración del liderazgo imperial

[1]

, la derrota de Trump no limpia el panorama sino lo enrarece aún más.


Todos saben que los demócratas son rusóbos, para empezar, y eso no augura un cese de la amenaza nuclear sino la radicaliza, como ya se está observando en los últimos movimientos beligerantes de la OTAN, Inglaterra y Alemania

[2]

 contra Rusia. El AIPAC, por cuestiones ya de sobrevivencia del Estado sionista, más aún cuando perdió Netanyahu, hará uso de su fuerte influencia entre los demócratas

[3]

 para continuar la política nuclear contra Irán y el exterminio de los gazatíes y los palestinos en general (Líbano, Siria y Cisjordania). Lo cual, además de la prolongación del genocidio palestino, no hace sino continuar, por otros medios, la política expansiva (aunque cada vez menos posible, como la inutilidad de los bombardeos recientes de parte de USA e Israel a Irán) del Estado sionista.


Tampoco los inmigrantes verán otro panorama más alentador con los demócratas, cuando fue la administración “demócrata” de Obama, por ejemplo, la que más cantidad de deportados produjo. De boca para afuera, los demócratas harán de Trump el chivo expiatorio que necesita la restauración imperial para justificar su continuidad. Creyendo que la limpieza de la imagen imperial podrá ofrecerle demagógicamente al mundo, otra cosa que no sea una nueva versión de la continuidad de “un mundo basado en reglas” para los demás y excepciones para el Imperio.


En ese contexto, pondremos a consideración el panorama que sugiere Alexander Dugin y nuestro comentario a lo que creemos, una de las descripciones más cercanas a lo que se viene. En sus propias palabras

[4]

, si Trump pierde irremediablemente el control del Congreso: “la venganza de los demócratas contra Trump y sus seguidores

no se parecerá a nada de lo que hemos visto antes

”. Los demócratas no pasarán por alto, lo que significó el desmantelamiento de los brazos administrativos y operativos de su poder de influencia nacional y global, cuando se creó la Oficina de Eficiencia Gubernamental, el DOGE, y se inició la desarticulación de la Agencia de los Estados Unidos para el Desarrollo Internacional, la USAID (desde donde se operó la restauración derechista –una vez desarticulada por la “primavera democrática”– en Latinoamérica, en favor de la tutela demócrata gringa). Esa era una de las vías que permitió la injerencia de los intereses que representa, por ejemplo, George Soros. Por eso, no es casual la sincronía de la ola de protestas en Europa

[5]

 y el triunfo demócrata en USA. Hasta el triunfo de Lula se explicaría, en parte, por esa caída de las piezas de dominó que sostenía al trumpismo, a nivel global (rival en la jefatura de un nuevo orden mundial que destaca otro tipo de intereses, sobre todo financieros, que tienen en Soros un actor reconocible).


Dugin, en tono de socarrón señala: “realmente creyeron que Trump cumpliría sus promesas y que el Estado profundo estaba a punto de ser erradicado de raíz”. Pero Trump, que nunca generó el contexto para la realización del golpe definitivo, ahora tiene, en el Congreso (tanto en diputados como en senadores, además de gobernadores), la mayoría necesaria para que el globalismo, que intentó atacar, reorganice filas con sus portavoces y comiencen el contraataque.


Ya algunos analistas en geopolítica preguntan si quien ganó en las “midterm” fue, en realidad, Soros. Pero éste es sólo el actor expuesto y si algo manifiesta el

poder duro

 es la no exposición. Éste

poder duro

 (o Estado profundo) actúa creando la objetividad que se constituye en escenario, una vez que ya ha mudado a otro tipo de realidad, teniendo a todos ocupados en el escenario conveniente que el poder produce para desplegar mediáticamente conspiraciones para el disfrute masoquista del morbo político. Con esos fines se viene activando la alerta, en 33 países …

title: Saki: Turkish citizens top the list of deportations from Europe
content:
Deportations across Europe have accelerated following the implementation of the new Pact on Migration and Asylum. These measures have begun to affect not only undocumented migrants but also asylum seekers and political refugees who have been granted asylum.


The adoption of the pact has been followed by an increase in deportation orders targeting Kurdish refugees in particular. Numerous Kurdish political refugees have begun to be returned to Turkey from the European countries where they reside. Refugees, including politicians, poets and writers, face trials carrying potential prison sentences of several decades under cases brought against them after their return to Turkey.


Peoples' Equality and Democracy Party (DEM Party) MP Özgül Saki spoke to ANF about recent developments affecting migrants in Europe and the growing number of deportation orders.


'The price of the crisis is poverty, massacres and displacement'


Özgül Saki said that pressure on refugees had intensified following the implementation of the new Pact on Migration and Asylum on 12 June 2026. She added said: "Following its entry into force on 12 June, the Council of the European Union (EU) formally adopted a new regulation known as the Return Regulation on 1 October 2026, aimed at accelerating the deportation and return of irregular migrants who have no legal right to remain.


We must first recognize that since 2013, we have been witnessing mass migration on a scale unprecedented in previous periods. The period of conflict that began with ISIS attacks in Syria and Iraq, Israel's genocidal policies against Palestine, the escalation of tensions between Ukraine and Russia into a prolonged war, the Taliban's return to power in Afghanistan and US attacks on Iran have displaced millions of people. In my view, the underlying cause is the imperialist capitalist system's continued reliance on war as a regional strategy to resolve its own crises. The price of this crisis continues to be paid by the peoples of the region through poverty, massacres and displacement.


We are witnessing the re-emergence of colonial reflexes. Efforts to remain protected within Europe's own borders are proceeding alongside expansionist ambitions beyond them. Concepts described as 'European values,' such as human rights, democracy and equality, have lost their meaning. We are confronted with a Europe dominated by governments that regard everything as permissible in the name of 'security' and 'defense,' are turning toward fascism and envision a white Europe.


There is a widespread expectation that migration statistics will increasingly be used as a political tool, particularly amid the rise of the far right in Germany, the Netherlands and France. The prominence of 'returns,' 'border security' and 'irregular migration' in election campaigns indicates that this right-wing and fascistic trajectory will continue. As a result, a deliberate anti-migrant political agenda is being implemented through new, multilayered mechanisms of pressure on refugees."


'Restrictions begin at the border'


Özgül Saki said that, according to the Council of the European Union, the regulation adopted on 1 October expands member states' powers to carry out deportations.


Saki continued: "We have already begun to see the serious consequences of the new legislation in recent months. The coming period will bring highly unfavorable conditions both for migrants already living in European countries and for those seeking to apply for asylum.


The Council of the European Union stated that the new rules adopted on 1 October will complement the Pact on Migration and Asylum and contribute to its implementation. The regulation gives member states greater scope to carry out returns and allows for the establishment of 'return hubs' in countries outside the EU. This means that people who have been issued return decisions and are deemed to have no right to remain in the EU may be transferred to these centers under agreements or arrangements concluded with the relevant non-EU countries


Eurostat figures and recent EU data show that asylum applications across the EU have declined by approximately 24 percent. However, this decline has been achieved by deliberately making the application requirements more complicated from the outset. author: Justin Garson
title: Seeing BPD in a Positive Light: An Interview with Dr. Shay Welch
content:
P

eople often take psychiatric drugs because there’s something about themselves they don’t like—extreme low mood, threatening voices, or panic attacks. But many who’ve been diagnosed with borderline personality disorder (BPD) take drugs for the sake of others. They’re repeatedly told that their very personalities are disordered, pathological or just intolerable. This message is profoundly stigmatizing. It can contribute to isolation, loneliness, and even suicidal thoughts.


In September 2024, I talked with

Dr. Shay Welch

, a philosophy professor at Spelman College. Welch, who’s been diagnosed with BPD, truly writes from an insider’s perspective—a perspective that’s nearly absent from the academic literature.


Shay Welch


Her recent paper, “

Am I Safe Enough for You Now? BPD and the Forced Erasure of Personal Identity

,” describes how people with BPD often feel forced to erase who they are to make others feel safe. We discuss ways of promoting more positive messaging around BPD, and creating a more tolerant and accepting society.


The title of her paper captures a theme that ran throughout our conversation: “treatment” for BPD is often less about alleviating the diagnosed person’s suffering than about making them more tolerable to other people. She describes medication levels that kept rising to make other people more comfortable, and a research literature built almost entirely around people in crisis. She also describes what would make life better: a cultural shift that would see, in BPD, not a defective kind of person, but just a different kind of person.


Justin Garson: There’s this idea that people take psychiatric drugs to manage parts of themselves that are inherently distressing, like being depressed or anxious. But as you point out in your paper, people with BPD often take medications for the sake of others. You describe how other people want to “erase—literally—who we are for their own comfort.” Can you say more about this idea of taking drugs to erase one’s personality?


Shay Welch:

 It’s true that you have these categories of social anxiety, panic attacks, and chronic deep depression, and those can interfere with somebody’s ability to thrive. But then you have these “identity” disorders, like BPD and bipolar and schizophrenia, which make other people very uncomfortable. When it comes to bipolar, or BPD, or schizophrenia, the institutions or the medical field itself will try to medicate it completely out of them. And then you just completely eliminate the person. These people are like, “I’m not a person. I am so medicated, I don’t exist as an individual.”


So, we are constantly trying to back off the medication to hit a point where we’re still satisfying other people, but reclaiming more of our actual identity. But that’s when people say, “you’ve come off your meds too much, and now you’re not functioning well in society and you need to go back on your meds.” And then people like us are like, what do I do? I’m terribly unhappy, but it’s me versus all of them. That causes many people to isolate themselves.


For example, a lot of bipolar people really love their mania. They accomplish so much, and their lives are so colorful, when they’re in the manic state. Then they have to go into the depression state. But sometimes they’ll tolerate the depression for the mania—especially if your manic state is longer than the depressive state. But other people don’t like that. For others, it’s too intense or erratic.


Garson: That makes sense. My dad was bipolar and he was on medication mainly because people didn’t like his manic episodes. In general, he didn’t like medication—he enjoyed having those emotional extremes.


But it seems to me—and this is something you get at in your paper—that for schizophrenia or bipolar disorder, there’s a sense that “we’re treating your symptoms,” like hallucinations or manic episodes. Whereas for BPD, the “problem,” as it were, is you. The message is that your very personality is at fault.


Welch:

Right. What makes these “personality disorders” is that there’s a problem with your personality. I’ve often been told that I’m too boisterous for other people. Even when I medicate, I project my voice. I’m very straightforward and very blunt, but I’m always enthusiastic, like, let’s go. I’m driven. Before I was medicated, people didn’t like that.


And it’s true that when you’re not medicated for borderline, you do have these spillovers. I spent my whole life having random …

title: In Their Own Words: The Senior Reform and Tory Figures Who Have Lauded Trump
content:
U.S. President Donald Trump suffered a spectacular setback in the country’s midterm elections this week, with Democrats taking control of Congress and the Republicans losing races in their traditional heartlands.


The election was a rebuke to Trump’s increasingly

unpopular presidency

. Voters expressed frustration with the cost of living and the economy, while the U.S.-Israeli war with Iran – which has driven up fuel prices – has proven to be a major political liability.


Trump’s political fortunes have also been damaged by his administration’s aggressive immigration enforcement. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE), the agency at the centre of his mass deportation drive, has become a flashpoint and an emblem of Trump’s autocratic rule.


Yet, across the Atlantic, some of the UK’s most senior right-wing politicians have spent recent years enthusiastically praising Trump, celebrating his political leadership, and seeking to emulate his policies.


Reform UK

 leader

Nigel Farage

 has repeatedly presented himself as one of Trump’s most enthusiastic international allies. At a Conservative Political Action Conference (CPAC) event in February 2025, he

declared

 that Trump is “the bravest man I know”.


Farage also

described

 the president’s 2024 election victory as a source of inspiration for his own political ambitions. “This is all going to blow back and help us. We are now topping every opinion poll in Britain, and we are going to win the next general election,” he said.


With Reform

falling in the polls

 and the party facing

police

parliamentary

 investigations, that prospect now seems increasingly unlikely.

At the

 (ARC) conference in February 2025, Badenoch

referenced

 her party’s defeat at the 2024 general election and her subsequent election as Tory leader, saying: “People ask me what difference new leadership will make? Well, take a look at President Trump.”


She continued: “He’s showing that sometimes you need that first stint in government to spot the problems, but it’s the second time around when you really know how to fix them.”


And this enthusiasm has extended beyond rhetoric. Reform and Conservative politicians have embraced Trump’s calls for expanded fossil fuel extraction, praised his drive to slash the state, and proposed British versions of his immigration enforcement operation.


Meanwhile, as revealed by DeSmog, influential right-wing Westminster pressure groups have

accepted $20 million

 from U.S. sources, including major Trump donors, over the past decade – while MPs have received more than £300,000 for attending Trump-aligned events since the 2024 UK general election.


‘Drill, Baby, Drill’


Few policy areas illustrate the ideological alignment between Trump and Britain’s right-wing parties more clearly than oil and gas.


Trump began his second presidency by demanding that Britain abandon restrictions on North Sea extraction. On 3 January 2025, he

posted

 on Truth Social: “The UK is making a very big mistake. Open up the North Sea. Get rid of Windmills!”


And his administration has made expanding domestic fossil fuel production a central policy objective, encapsulated by the slogan “drill, baby, drill”.


The Conservatives and Reform have both echoed that mantra, arguing that Britain should maximise extraction from its

dwindling

 North Sea reserves rather than pursue a transition away from fossil fuels.


In September 2025, Badenoch met Trump at the White House. Afterwards, she made clear that the North Sea had featured prominently in their discussions.


The Conservative leader

wrote

 on the social media platform X: “Not surprised Trump was so emphatic. It’s all we spoke about last night. We have to get our oil and gas out of the North Sea.”


She added: “We have to make the most of our natural resources. It’s mad to leave billions of £ in there.”

 to scrap the 2050 net zero emissions target that the Conservative Party introduced in office.

title: Formalising the RSF: EU Policies and Sudan’s Search for Funds
content:
The Rapid Support Forces (RSF) are one of the two armed parties in the current war in Sudan. Despite their historic collaborations with multiple domestic and external actors, everyone is washing their hands of them. In this piece, I will try to make sense of the RSF and conclude by associating its institutionalisation with the convergence of goals between Sudan and the EU in the 2010s.


It depends on where you stand to identify the root causes of the formalisation and institutionalisation of the RSF. In 2003, when the war broke out in Darfur, Sudan’s western region, the Sudanese Armed Forces (SAF) received a

humiliating shock

. The Sudanese government then mobilised Darfurians, who know the geography of the area and who were mobile enough to cope with the insurgents’ tactics. The rebel groups were mostly from non-Arab ancestries, while the bulk of the counterinsurgent militias were Darfurian Arabs including Mohammad Hamdan Dagalo ‘Hemedti’ (the current leader of RSF) and others. The counterinsurgency campaign was successful militarily, but against the backdrop of this ‘‘succes’’ the campaign left damaging results. The International Criminal Court (ICC) issued an arrest warrant,

in March 2009

, for Al-Basheer, then the president of Sudan,  for war crimes and crimes against humanity during the counter insurgency. What is relevant here is the governmental admiration for this model received despite the associated ethical and reputational costs. The informal militias were deployed outside of Darfur and grew in size, and in 2013 they were given an official identity as the ‘RSF’ and attached to the National Intelligence and Security Service (NISS).


The RSF was considered by many as a

coup-proofing

 tool. Al-Basheer was an army officer and seized power through a military coup. As an insider, he knew what a strong army could do for a dictator’s throne. The NISS received better treatment than the army, elevating it to a

rival status

 with the SAF, something that caused angst within SAF ranks. In November 2012, authorities foiled a coup that had the former chief of NISS,

Salah Goush

, as the putschist. Again, the playbook was revisited and this time the rising player was RSF. Hemedti would subsequently

quip

 that

‘Sudan has no army but us.’


Making Sense of the RSF


The key decisions leading to the formulation of the RSF took place between 2013 and 2014 in Sudan and Europe.  In Sudan, Al-Basheer’s regime was experiencing a difficult time. On the 27

th

 of January 2014, Al-Basheer

addressed the nation

 in what was known as the ‘National Leap Speech’.  He considered

four prerequisites

 for the country to leap forward: Peace, free and rule-abiding political community, lifting the Sudanese from poverty into prosperity, finally reviving the ‘Sudanese Identity’. In addressing poverty, Al-Basheer zeroed in on sanctions as a major hindrance in the alleviating poverty in Sudan.


To the north, Europe was facing what it described as a ‘Migration Crisis’. In November 2014, the EU-Horn of Africa Migration Route Initiative, known as the

Khartoum Process

, was established.  It was meant to be a platform for political cooperation between Horn of Africa and Europe regarding migration routes.  In November 2015, the Valletta Summit action plan was issued.  This plan served as a marriage of convenience between the Sudanese government and the EU. The latter wanted to address migration, while the former was keen to achieve the leap goals through partnering with a global power like the EU.


The government started drafting and amending acts eagerly to prove itself as a reliable partner in the addressing migration. In January 2014, it issued the

Asylum Regulating Act

 2014, repealing

The Regulation of Asylum Act 1974

.  The new act imposed more restrictions on the movement of refugees in Sudan.  They were not allowed to move outside their registered residence without permission. The law vested authority in the Minister of Interior to establish, close or transfer any refugee camp.


18 months later, the

Sudan’s Passports and Immigration Act 2015

 was passed.  Harbouring aliens who are not eligible to reside in Sudan was now considered a crime. Those found guilty were subject to two years imprisonment and a fine. The same act considered involvement in human trafficking an offense resulting in imprisonment for between five to ten years, and the court had the right to confiscate any property used in trafficking.  None of …

title: Bigger, Stronger, More Violent: The EU’s Plans for Frontex
content:
On 27 October 2026, the European Commission presented its proposal for a new Frontex Regulation. The proposal would massively expand Frontex’s powers, staff, budget and activities, both inside and outside the EU. At the same time, some of the already very weak Fundamental Rights safeguards will be further weakened.

We oppose this proposal of the new regulation and call for an International Action Day on 18 December 2026, asking groups in all countries to participate however they can.

 Find here the callout for the Action Day and below our analysis of the new regulation proposal. 


1. Tripling Frontex’s border force and massively increasing its funding


What are the planned changes?


The EU wants to increase Frontex’s standing corps from 10,000 to 30,000 officers by 2041. This includes creating a new European Border and Return Reserve, made up of national officers trained by Frontex.


Frontex officers would also receive more powers to act independently. They could intercept people at borders, search vehicles and belongings, identify people for deportation and carry out deportations by air, land or sea.


The proposal also removes the general requirement for national border guards to be physically present when Frontex officers use force. 


The rules on the use of force would also change. The specific requirement that handcuffs are used only on people who pose a danger to themselves or others would be removed and replaced by broader criteria. The same applies to the use of batons and pepper spray. The use of service dogs would be explicitly allowed, while several specific safeguards concerning the oversight of force would be removed from the annex.


The European Commission has proposed a budget of €11.9 billion for Frontex for 2028–2034. The reform adds additional possibilities for Frontex to access more funds, including a duty for the Commission to consider the Agency as a priority partner when engaging third parties in Union funded projects. 


Frontex would also be able to help determine priorities for EU research and innovation funding while receiving funding from the same programmes.


Why is this problematic?


This would mean a massive expansion of the EU’s militarised border regime, with more officers, more equipment and more powers to stop, detain and deport people on the move. For people on the move this will mean more violent and deadly borders. 


Billions of euros would be spent on strengthening border enforcement instead of providing housing, healthcare, education and support for people on the move.One year of Frontex’s proposed budget could instead fund: 


A year of schooling for 121,000 students (Germany 2024)


More than 5,000 energy-efficient social homes (Barcelona)


A year of healthcare for 3,800 people (EU average cost 2023)


EU resettlement support for more than 125,000 people 


More than 725,000 basic German language courses at Goethe institute 


More than 1,400 rescue ships like SOS Humanity


The expansion would also strengthen the border-industrial complex, including the arms and security industry that profits from border surveillance and enforcement.


2. Turning Frontex into the central EU deportation agency


What are the planned changes?


Frontex would become the central EU agency for planning, coordinating and carrying out deportations. It would be involved in practically every step of the deportation process, from identifying people and obtaining travel documents to organising deportation flights and so-called reintegration assistance. A new Return Coordination Centre would be established within Frontex to coordinate these activities.


A new SIRENE office would give Frontex access to additional information from the Schengen Information System concerning deportations and refusals of entry.


A new hit/no-hit system would allow Europol and Eurojust to check whether Frontex holds personal data relevant to their work, further conflating migration and security issues.


Frontex would be able to restrict people’s rights to access, correct or erase their personal data under certain conditions. The proposal would also facilitate systematic transfers of deportation-related personal data to third countries.


Under Articles 63 and 64, Frontex could support deportations starting from countries outside the EU. This includes deportations carried out under the laws of those countries, even when there is no deportation decision from an EU member state.


Member states would have to …

title: Perdió Trump y los demócratas recuperan el control de las Cámaras: velorio en la Casa Rosada
content:
Los demócratas dominarán el próximo Congreso. Consiguieron triunfos en estados en disputa como los de Iowa, Kansas, Maine, Carolina del Norte, Ohio, Carolina del Sur y Texas, que le permitirán controlar el Senado. La votación general donde superan a los republicanos por más de diez puntos le permitirán obtener una amplia mayoría que se expresará en la Cámara de Representantes (Diputados), que se renueva por completo. La derrota de Trump ha sido un golpe muy fuerte para el gobierno argentino, que se ató a su destino político, y que fue correspondido por el gobierno estadounidense con apoyos políticos y financieros en momentos clave.

Por Guillermo Cieza, para Huella del Sur.


En el Senado, según los últimos conteos, los demócratas habrían obtenido 54 curules y los republicanos apenas retienen 44. En la Cámara de Diputados la diferencia será aún más aplastante. Los demócratas obtendrían 231 representantes, contra 139 de los republicanos.


El deterioro económico de la mayoría de la población estadounidense y sus promesas incumplidas de acabar con las guerras, bajar el precio de los combustibles y publicar el archivo Epstein, parecen haber sido decisivas en estas elecciones. La marea azul (demócrata) parece haberse asentado en el fuerte apoyo del voto latino (una comunidad asediada por las deportaciones), en el cambio de voto de los jóvenes y en la ruptura de sectores rurales con la gestión (por razones económicas y morales).


Gina Hinojosa será la primera latina en gobernar Texas, un estado de fuerte ascendencia republicana. Lo mismo sucederá en California donde se impuso Xavier Becerra, por amplio margen. Otra de las sorpresas fue el triunfo de Abdul El Sayed que ganó en Michigan y se convirtió en el primer senador musulmán de EEUU.


También hay un crecimiento del ala izquierda del Partido demócrata. Janeese Lewis George, miembro del partido Socialista Democrático de América (DSA) ganó las elecciones a la alcaldía de Washington DC, la capital del país. El resultado fue abrumador. La candidata socialista democrática obtuvo el 84% contra su rival republicana, Rhonda Hamilton, que obtuvo el 10,3%.


La derrota del gobierno republicano que se estima en una cifra no inferior a 10 puntos, y la pérdida del Congreso, coloca al presidente Trump en una situación muy complicada, por las dificultades legislativas que tendrá en el futuro y porque estallará en su propio partido una feroz interna para sucederlo.


El gobierno de Argentina también ve agravar sus dificultades. Apoyó a Bolsonaro que perdió las elecciones en Brasil y después se fugó con ayuda de Milei, creando un importante conflicto con el principal socio comercial de nuestro país. Ahora advierte que su mentor y sostén en Estados Unidos se ha convertido en un “pato rengo”, que ha perdido carisma y poder. Finalmente advierte que en las elecciones estadounidenses el voto joven se volcó mayoritariamente a la oposición y que este fenómeno ya está empezando a producirse en la Argentina.


Para finalizar y reducir un poco el triunfalismo que se ha apoderado de distintos sectores de la oposición en la Argentina, habría que recordar que en Estados Unidos tanto demócratas como republicanos comparten los siguientes acuerdos.


1. El gran enemigo a derrotar es China. Debilitar y tratar de cortar la expansión de esta nueva potencia emergente es la prioridad. El tiempo juega a favor de China que crece mucho más rápido que Estados Unidos, y que está armando una política de alianzas que pueden deteriorar la vigencia del dólar como moneda rectora de los intercambios internacionales. La guerra, que es cada vez más impopular en Estados Unidos y lo empieza a ser en Europa, se les presenta a las elites occidentales como la única forma de evitar la pérdida de la hegemonía mundial.


2. En el actual declive estadounidense, producto de las derrotas que están sufriendo en otros puntos del mundo, tanto republicanos como demócratas avalan la política de replegarse y hacerse fuerte en lo que considera su patio trasero (Nuestramérica). En la Argentina lo que no puede sostener Milei, lo intentarán con Patricia Bullrich, con Massa, Picheto o promoviendo a algún otro dirigente dentro del peronismo que se reporte a la Embajada. author: Joshua Carroll
title: Home Office Unlawfully Blocks Gaza Children From Joining Families in UK
content:
The Home Office is refusing to allow mothers and their children trapped in Gaza to join family members in the UK, even after a judge said the government’s position is unlawful.


The two women, who have five children between them aged seven and under, were told to submit biometric information as part of a security check to obtain family reunification visas.


But the application centre where they would need to submit fingerprints and other information has been closed since the start of Israel’s genocide in October 2023.


On 30 September, a judge in the immigration and asylum chamber of the upper tribunal ruled that the Home Office, by refusing to waive the biometric requirement for these families, had unlawfully applied its unsafe journeys policy.


In her ruling, judge Fiona Lindsley said the mothers and children – who have been granted anonymity – “have too little food and are suffering from malnutrition. They dare not go to US aid collection points as they are aware that people have been killed by Israeli forces at these places.”


She said the children’s fathers, who are based in the UK, were also suffering severe psychological hardship. One has been diagnosed with PTSD due to his experiences in Gaza “coupled with the continuous threat” to the survival of his wife and children, she added.


The Home Office has appealed the judge’s decision and a hearing is set for 16 December. But the Greater Manchester Immigration Aid Unit (GMIAU), whic

h


represents the families,

 said th

at process will further delay reunification and put the families “in grave danger” in Gaza.


“The children are all traumatised,” said Decla Palmer, a lawyer from GMIAU. “They have gone to bed every night to the sound of bombs, suffering from nightmares, with rats and mice crawling around their tent. The mothers are completely exhausted and without hope.”


“Every day the families remain in Gaza, they are at risk of death,” said GMIAU.


Surgeons who have worked in Gaza have said Israeli forces

 deliberately and systematically

 kill children. Dutch newspaper Volkskrant last year

published testimony from doctors

 who had encountered at least 114 children with multiple bullet wounds in the head and chest.


A Home Office spokesperson told Novara Media that “enrolment of biometrics enables comprehensive checks… to identify individuals who may pose a threat to national security, public safety or immigration controls.”


Ghassan Ghaben of the British Palestinian Committee, an advocacy group, said the government was applying a double standard against Gazan families.


“The UK has shown in other situations that, when there is the political will, rules can be adapted to the realities of war – and in this case, genocide,” he said. “The Ukraine Family Scheme recognised that ordinary immigration procedures were not appropriate in the circumstances and enabled people to reunite with their families.”


Since the Russian invasion in 2022, Ukrainians and their children have been able to live and work in Britain under special temporary humanitarian visas.


“Palestinians have been asking for a similarly practical response since 2023, yet the response has instead been to maintain or introduce even stricter barriers,” said Ghaben.


He added there was “a real contradiction” between the shift in rhetoric about Gaza from Andy Burnham’s Labour government and its treatment of the families. 


“The home secretary has recently announced the reopening of the UK Resettlement Scheme, and spoken about creating safe and legal routes for people fleeing persecution,” he said.


“Yet at the same time, the Home Office is continuing to fight against the reunification of Palestinian mothers and young children with their fathers who are already in the UK.”


During the genocide in Gaza, the UK has

allowed weapons

 sales to Israel, flown spy flights over Gaza, allowed

military planes to depart

 from its bases bound for Israel and

refused to investigate British nationals

 who joined the Israeli military.


Home secretary Shabana Mahmood was accused last month of


giving people in Gaza “false hope”

 after announcing a new safe route to the UK for Palestinian refugees. The route only applies to those who have

already escaped to Lebanon or Jordan

 and will benefit only a few hundred people a year.


Last year, the government suspended a programme that allowed people granted asylum in the UK to bring their family members over.

author: Unknown
title: Socialist Strategy within the Architecture of Power
content:
The artwork in this dossier, produced by Tricontinental: Institute for Social Research, depicts three forms of power: social power in magenta, governmental power in yellow, and systemic power in cyan. Where these forms overlap, new colours emerge, representing their different configurations and interconnections within a broader architecture of power. This composition invites us to consider how power is organised, contested, and transformed through processes of emancipation.


When a radical government takes office with a mandate for transformation, the next morning it will have to confront banks that remain in private hands, mines under corporate control, private mainstream media, and public administration governed by inherited procedures. Capital can postpone investment, transfer money abroad, close factories, hoard essential goods, dismiss workers, and speculate against the currency. The havoc wrought on the economy and population can then be presented as proof that transformation is impossible, all while the government is held responsible for a crisis produced or intensified by forces beyond its control.


This reality reveals a central problem for socialist strategy. Taking governmental office can be an important step toward systemic transformation, but misunderstanding these two forms of power as one and the same can have dangerous consequences. A clear analysis of where power resides and how its different forms interact is necessary to avoid patterns that have plagued revolutionary processes across the world.


An electoral victory may be mistaken for a revolutionary event when a left-wing party has taken office even though the wider state apparatus, the economy, and the institutions that shape common sense remain largely beyond its control. Conversely, a socialist movement may possess considerable social strength without being able to translate that strength into governmental authority or changes to the structures of the state and economy.  The ruling class exercises power through its control over production and the structures that reinforce it, while the working class exercises collective power through strikes, demonstrations, and the organisations it builds through struggle. To use a single word – power – for all these different capacities can confuse political strategy. In this dossier, we therefore distinguish three related forms of power as an analytical framework for debate and discussion:


Social power

 is the organised capacity of a class or political bloc to act collectively, reproduce material life, and contest the ruling class’s command over society. It is built through institutions of struggle and cooperation such as trade unions, peasant and women’s organisations, cooperatives, community structures, cultural and media projects, political education, and political parties. Through these institutions, a class or political bloc can struggle to reshape common sense and establish moral and intellectual leadership.


Governmental power

 is the capacity to assume governmental authority, whether through elections, insurrection, or another political rupture, and to use executive, legislative, and administrative institutions to pursue a programme. It provides access to important instruments of administration and policy but does not, by itself, amount to control of the state or the wider system.


Systemic power

 is the capacity to transform the class character and institutional form of the state, bring the major means of production and the social surplus under democratic authority, and reorganise the relations through which society reproduces itself. It includes state power but cannot be reduced to it because capitalist social relations are reproduced beyond the formal institutions of the state – through property, finance, the world market, colonial relations, culture, and social reproduction – and many of these relations exceed the reach of any single government or national state.


These forms are analytical distinctions, not sealed compartments, and do not constitute a fixed sequence. They overlap, develop unevenly, and can pull in opposite directions. Governmental power may become a bridge between organised social power and systemic transformation. It may also weaken popular organisation and reconcile it to the existing system. The central strategic question is therefore not which form of power matters but how the three can be connected in a process of emancipation.

On 25 October, the “Student List” won a projected 140 of 250 seats in the Serbian parliament, defeating the ruling party that has been in power for 14 years. The electoral victory comes on the back of a student movement that began on 1 of November 2024, when a newly renovated canopy fell at the railway station in Novi Sad and killed sixteen people. Since then, people in Serbia have organised mass protests and assemblies.

We reached out to Klasna Solidarnost (Class Solirarity), founded in Belgrade in 2016, which grew out of an anarcho-syndicalist movement. Its members continue to participate in student occupations while critiquing electoral strategies. They are also active in antifascism, solidarity with Palestine, antimilitarism, support for workers, and the “Solidarna kuhinja” free kitchen, as well as political analysis and publications.

The mainstream media has presented the student movement as “decentralised” and highlighted the appointing of non-politicians to parliament; is this an accurate reflection of the movement now?

The appointment of non-politicians to parliament is one of the main talking points of the Student List. There were over 160 candidates with PhDs on the list, which was highlighted as a key reason why the new government should be “better” than the old one in which it turned out that even some ministers had fake PhD diplomas. The Student List basically has a technocratic structure and by what we’ve seen so far, it aims to create a “government of experts” which is perfectly in line with the dominant neoliberal ideology that convinces us that the society will be better as a whole if we have experts leading the government.

For us as anarchists, this of course is a fairy tale because we know how technocratic governments ended in countries like Italy and Greece in the last 10-15 years, where they simply ushered in the most brutal neoliberal reforms, bringing down the life standard of the working class even more than their predecessors. And this is actually one of the key elements that show us there probably won’t be much improvement in the working class’s life standard.

During the Student List’s electoral campaign, the focus was on defeating the political mafia regime of the SNS (Serbian Progressive Party), which had been in power for 14 years. The movement focused on the regime’s criminal acts and massive corruption scandals, but it barely mentioned any economic measures to improve the everyday lives of the working class.

Now that the SNS regime is finally gone, it remains to be seen what the economic policy of the new government will be, but from what we’ve heard so far, there isn’t any mention of substantial changes in the economic position of Serbia as a client-state of the European Union, and a partial economic partner of the US, China, and Russia.

title: City of Blood Part [Part IV] – Special Edition: Gen Z regelt – Phase 2
content:
“Ich hab so Heimweh nach dem Kurfürstendamm


Berliner Tempo, Betrieb und Tamtam


Hätt ich auch wo ′ne Wohnung, und wär sie noch so neu


Ich bleib Berlin, meiner alten Liebe treu”


Hildegard Knef – Heimweh nach dem Kurfürstendamm


“…fragt sich, wer in der Gruppe der proletarischen Mieter noch weniger als andere zu verlieren hat, das heißt auch die Nase schon so voll genug hat, so verelendet sind, dass ihnen nichts anderes bleibt als den Kampf aufzunehmen. Das sind die kinderreichen Familien, das sind die von Exmittierung bedrohten Familien, das sind die dem Proletariat und Subproletariat angehörigen Jugendlichen.”


Ulrike Meinhof u.a. – Vorläufiges Strategiepapier Märkisches Viertel¹ (1970)


Nun denn, der Klassenkampf ist zurück in der Stadt. Nachdem die “Wohnungsfrage”, die über Jahrzehnte den direktesten Ausdruck des sozialen Antagonismus in Form der “Häuserkämpfe” repräsentierte, vom ewigen Partizipationszirkus der “Mieteraktivisten” von ‘Kotti und Co’ bis ‘DW enteignen’ und dem identitären Gebaren der Berliner Szene so lange durch den Fleischwolf gedreht wurde, bis am Ende nur noch alle zur Wahlurne rennen, um die PdL an die Regierung zu bringen, artikuliert sich ein vager Antagonismus erneut auf den Strassen.


Die Geschehnisse beim ersten Aufschlag der GenZ Revolte auf deutschen Boden, die Kloppereien mit den Bullen im Prenzlberg, die Riots im Hamburger Bahnhofsviertel und auf Frankfurts Edelmeile, die diversen bundesweiten Halloween Scharmützel mit den Bullen sind nicht zu begreifen ohne zumindest eine vage Vorstellung von der Neuzusammensetzung der Klasse und den sozialen Verwüstungen des Corona Ausnahmezustandes. Wie die anonymen Autoren des Konspirationistischen Manifests² schrieben: “Wir wollen Rache!”. Die Ausschreitungen³, die sich zum Jahreswechsel 22/23 über das gesamte Berliner Stadtgebiet erstreckten und den Bullenapparat vorführten, waren genau das: Ein Bedürfnis nach Rache aus tiefstem Herzen. Unmittelbar, unvermittelt und kalt genossen. Das die deutschen Linken und Anarchisten in großen Teilen diese Aktionen nicht verstanden haben oder sie zu einer rein ‘antirassistischen’ Antwort umdeuteten hat eben sowohl mit ihrem unmaterialistischen Verständnis von “Politik machen” als auch mit ihren unaufgearbeiteten Verstrickungen in die orchestrale Inszenierung des Corona Ausnahmezustandes zu tun.


Nun also bauen sie wieder Molotows im Märkischen Viertel [4] und legen sich mit den Bullen an. Und ein Hauch von Frankreich weht durch die kalten grauen Straßen von Berlin, wo sich die Luxusgeschäfte auf dem Kurfürstendamm an Halloween hinter Sperrholzplatten verschanzt hatten. Doch der Spuk ist noch nicht an ihnen vorbei gegangen. Unter dem Motto ‘Gen Z regelt – Phase 2’ wird jetzt für den 14. November zu einer Ansammlung um 17:00 Uhr am Charlottenburger Savignyplatz aufgerufen, der Aufzug soll von dort über den östlichen Kurfürstendamm bis zum S-Bahnhof Halensee ziehen.


“J’ai deux passions


La fanfare, la révolution


Vive les blocages, les sabotages


Les ZAD et les manifs sauvages”


So singen sie derzeit in Frankreich im Tränengas und natürlich wäre es vermessen die vorrevolutionäre Stimmung im Mutterland der Aufstände mit der Situation hierzulande zu vergleichen, aber angesichts den zwei Optionen, die derzeit zur Disposition stehen: Eine rechtspopulistische/faschistische Eroberung der staatlichen Macht oder die Verteidigung des Status Quo in der breiten ‚antifaschistischen Front’ bis sehr weit ins bürgerliche Lager hinein – ist jede soziale Irritation die mit dieser Dichotomie bricht, einen Raum jenseits davon erschafft, nicht zu gering zu schätzen. Das wirkliche Elend ist dass alles einfach so weiter geht, selbst der Wortführer der Klimakollapsprepperblase, der wahlweise mal Anarchist, dann wieder doch Marxist ist, ruft ja nun zur aktiven Unterstützung der realpolitischen Machtoption einer PdL geführten Landesregierung auf und genau hier führt sich das ganze Geraune von der “nicht aufzuhaltenen Katastrophe“ ad absurdum. Nicht weil wir nicht auf eine klimatische Katastrophe zusteuern würden, sondern weil die einzige Perspektive, diese Katastrophe aufzuhalten, die Rekonstruktion einer revolutionären Vorstellungswelt und ihre materielle Umsetzung ist. Nicht das reale Einrichten in den Zuständen, egal was für einen radikalen Farbanstrich man seinem persönlichen Survival-Kit verpasst.

content:
