title: Spagna: “Contro il rentismo finanziario, il capitale e i suoi governi”. Intervista a una lavoratrice verso lo sciopero generale dell’11 novembre
content:
In 

Spagna

 oggi, martedì 10 novembre, 24 ore di sciopero blocco dei macchinisti dei treni.


da

Radio Onda d’Urto


L’astensione dal lavoro, con un’adesione quasi totale, riguarda Renfe, l’ente ferroviario pubblico, ed è stato proclamato dal sindacato Semaf per chiedere il rispetto degli impegni sulla sicurezza ferroviaria, dopo le stragi 2026 di Adamuz (Cordoba) e di Urda (Toledo) sulla linea ad alta velocità Madrid-Siviglia, costate complessivamente 116 vittime.


A febbraio 2026, dopo il primo schianto vicino a Cordoba, i macchinisti avevano concordato con il ministero dei Trasporti, Renfe e Adif, l’ente di gestione delle infrastrutture ferroviarie, una serie di misure. Il sindacato denuncia però “il mancato avvio dei gruppi di lavoro incaricati di introdurre le nuove norme, protocolli di emergenza e procedure operative”. La mobilitazione proseguirà giovedì 12 novembre con tre fasce di sciopero, mentre per domani, 

mercoledì 11 novembre, sarà sciopero generale

 in tutta la Spagna con l’intero panorama sindacale, l’inquilinato resistente e i movimenti sociali e politici di base. “Contro il rentismo finanziario, il capitale e i suoi governi” la parola d’ordine delle realtà più combattive nella Penisola Iberica.


Radio Onda d’Urto si trova in Spagna con Felipe, nostro inviato, per seguire l’11N e la huelga general. Oggi, martedì 10 novembre, vi proponiamo la corrispondenza con Felipe dal quartiere La Latina – Puerta del Ángel, nel cuore popolare di Madrid, con l’intervista a una lavoratrice durante una delle iniziative in preparazione dello sciopero generale.

author: Kodao Productions
title: Court to police: Fabricated charges ‘severest, most unmerited punishment’
content:
A Metropolitan Trial Court branch in Manila dismissed a criminal case related to the September 21, 2025 violent police dispersal, affirmed the primacy of the rights to freedom of expression and peaceful assembly, and cautioned law enforcers against filing unfounded criminal complaints against innocent citizens.


In a decision promulgated on Monday, November 9, 2026, the Court dismissed a criminal case for violation of Article 153 of the Revised Penal Code (Tumults and Other Disturbances) against nine individuals arrested at Mendiola during the September 21, 2025 rally. It was dismissed on demurrer to evidence due to insufficient evidence.


In dismissing the charges, the court ruled:


The prosecution failed to establish the alleged complicity of the nine individuals in the acts constituting the offense. Although the Information alleges conspiracy, it failed to prove that a conspiracy existed.


The Court noted a discrepancy between the allegations in the Information and the supporting affidavits and witness testimonies. The Information charges Tumults and other Disturbance, while the affidavits and testimonies allege facts related to direct assault, which involves different elements.


This discrepancy is significant because, during the inquest proceedings, the nine arrested individuals were initially charged with Tumults, and Direct Assault. The Inquest Prosecutor dismissed the Direct Assault charge and recommended filing a case for Tumults. However, the affidavits submitted to the Court support the dismissed Direct Assault charge and do not support the Tumults case.


The Court also did not give weight to the witness testimonies identifying the nine individuals. The Court found that, given the tense situation and the fact that witnesses were hiding behind shields, they could not possibly make accurate identifications.


The allegations that the nine individuals kicked police officers’ shields and attempted to break the police formation are insufficient to conclude that they engaged in a tumultuous disturbance.


Instead, the Court ruled that the “[V]ery act of pushing and grabbing during a public assembly automatically rises to the level of a serious disturbance. The prosecution must establish, through specific and credible evidence, the nature, gravity, and circumstances of the alleged acts showing that they indeed resulted in the disturbance penalized by law.”


The Court also cited the ruling of the Supreme Court in People vs. Apurado portions of which partly states that:


“It is rather to be expected that more or less disorder will mark the public assembly of the people to protest against grievances whether real or imaginary, because on such occasions feeling is always wrought to a high pitch of excitement, and the greater the grievance and the more intense the feeling, the less perfect, as a rule, will be the disciplinary control of the leaders over their irresponsible followers. But if the prosecution be permitted to seize upon every instance of such disorderly conduct by individual members of a crowd as an excuse to characterize the assembly as a seditious and tumultuous rising against the authorities, then the right to assemble and to petition for redress of grievances would become a delusion and a snare and the attempt to exercise it on the most righteous occasion and in the most peaceable manner would expose all those who took part therein to the severest and most unmerited punishment, if the purposes which they sought to attain did not happen to be pleasing to the prosecuting authorities.”


The Court found no basis to charge the nine individuals with Tumults and other disturbances. It cautioned the police against filing fabricated cases and prosecuting innocent citizens. In its Decision, the Court stated:


“Police officers must bear in mind that the filing of criminal charges against the very citizens they have sworn to serve and protect is a serious matter inherent in every State. It must, however, always be, based on careful assessment; convenience and expediency have no place in requiring a person to answer for criminal liability. To accept otherwise, would be a disservice not only to the accused but also to the cause of justice itself.” #

Court to police: Fabricated charges ‘severest, most unmerited punishment’

title: Aggression Against Iran Has Been Bipartisan. Will Midterm Results Change That?
content:
The US and Israel repeatedly subverted Iranian sovereignty, threatened nuclear war, and destabilized the Middle East.

Truthout is a vital news source and a living history of political struggle. If you think our work is valuable, support us with a donation of any size.

The Republican Party’s staggering losses in the November midterm elections have prompted speculation about the future of the U.S.-Israeli war against Iran, which is overwhelmingly unpopular with voters. Democratic leaders have portrayed President Donald Trump’s military offensive as an unconstitutional fiasco and an economic disaster driving inflation.

But their choreographed outrage conceals a long tradition of bipartisan support for aggression, which President Masoud Pezeshkian of Iran denounced in his UN address this September. For decades, the United States and Israel have referred to Iranians as terrorists, “but we are the victims of terrorists,” Pezeshkian underscored. His speech outlined a record of hypocrisy: U.S. and Israeli officials talk about peace, but plot to assassinate political leaders and negotiators. Most notably, both states command nuclear arsenals, yet impose debilitating sanctions on Iran’s atomic energy program.

As Pezeshkian emphasizes, the war is the latest episode in a turbulent history of energy and imperial assertion that contradicts U.S.-Israeli claims about proliferation risks and regional security. During the Cold War, Western powers shattered Iran’s democracy, before consolidating a brutal petromonarchy to guarantee access to its oil reserves. While undercutting Iranian energy sovereignty, they allowed Israel to become a nuclear-armed occupier, spreading dirty weapons and armed conflicts across the Middle East. This tangled history of oil and atoms is essential to understanding the war’s causes and contradictions, as two rogue states with thermonuclear weapons attack Iran under the pretext of nonproliferation.

Since the nineteenth century, Western powers have attempted to curb Iran’s sovereignty or seize its vast energy reserves. By 1914, Great Britain controlled its oil industry, after extorting concessions from the Iranian government. Over the following decades, the Anglo-Iranian Oil Company (AIOC) turned its refinery in the southwestern city of Abadan into the main energy supplier for the British Empire. Winston Churchill called the gushing wells “a prize from fairyland.” Yet AIOC officials warped Iran’s economic development by handpicking politicians and shamelessly exploiting workers. British personnel at Abadan lived in segregated splendor with swimming pools and servants, while local laborers inhabited parched slums.

After World War II, Iran attempted to improve its contract with the AIOC in order to raise government revenue and living standards. But company officials refused to compromise. In April 1951, Mohammad Mosaddegh became prime minister and initiated a series of ambitious reforms, which included nationalizing the oil industry.

Privately, the U.S. government lambasted the AIOC for behaving like a “typical nineteenth-century colonial exploiter,” while dealing “ineptly and disastrously” with Iran. Secretary of State Dean Acheson was scathing: “Never had so few lost so much so stupidly and so fast.” Nevertheless, U.S. leaders colluded with Britain to undermine nationalization. They feared that Mosaddegh’s policy set a destabilizing precedent, sapping British imperial power, upending the Cold War balance, and compromising Western control over strategic resources.

“I fought the fascists and Nazis,” one CIA adviser ruminated. “My lesson was that we were becoming just like them.”

Posing as a mediator, the State Department pressed Iranian leaders to make concessions, yet privately conceded that Britain’s demands were unreasonable. British negotiators advocated paying “lip service” to the principle of nationalization, while “keeping effective power … in our hands.” Ratcheting up pressure, the United States and Britain organized an oil embargo to suffocate Iran’s economy. Officials also bribed dozens of legislators, who physically assaulted Mosaddegh’s allies in parliament. And they launched a global propaganda campaign, pumping what one British operative called “a steady supply of suitable poison” into the press.

author: dev
title: Nouvelle lettre ouverte de prisonniers du 17 octobre 2026
content:
Depuis plusieurs prisons de France, des détenus sont parvenus à rédiger cette seconde lettre ouverte et à nous la transmettre. Dans la continuité

de la première missive que nous avions publiée

, ils appellent à poursuivre la lutte et racontent la manière dont l'administration pénitentiaire les accueille.


Il y a deux semaines, nous vous adressions une première lettre ouverte. Nous prisonniers du 17 octobre 2026 reprenons la parole et sommes rejoint par de nouvelles voix qui s'échappent désormais de plusieurs prisons de France.


Depuis nos cellules et grâce aux échos qui nous arrivent, nous suivons le combat en cours à l'extérieur. La cohésion et la solidarité des différentes forces engagées nous fait chaud au cœur. Et si le pouvoir et ses médias tentent de nous séparer, il faut continuer à nous tenir ensemble.


Une révolution est impossible si ses premières lignes sont isolées. Mais les premières lignes doivent aussi comprendre l'importance des deuxièmes, troisièmes et de toutes les lignes qui suivent et qui garantissent la survie et l'extension du mouvement.


Si nous voulons voir la fin de l'ère Macron et de ce régime qu'il ose encore appeler République, nous devons réunir toutes nos forces pour y parvenir. Blocages, émeutes, manifestations, grèves, batailles médiatiques et institutionnelles sont autant de chemins sur lesquels nous devons marcher et faire front, massivement.


Nous devons mettre toutes nos forces pour faire pencher la balance de notre côté. Leurs prisons ne sont pas assez grandes pour accueillir tous les insurgé.es de ce pays. A Fleury-Merogis, un bâtiment entier a été vidé pour parquer là une cinquantaine d'entre nous. A la Santé, on nous isole pour éviter la contagion révolutionnaire. A Villepinte et à Fresnes, on nous fait subir les pires conditions carcérales pour briser notre élan et notre moral. Mais le pouvoir se trompe en pensant pouvoir nous faire plier.


Ici aussi la colère monte. Nous voyons bien les chiens de garde de CNEWS et BFM s'acharner pendant des semaines entières sur nous tout en taisant les motifs de notre révolte. Nous sommes lucides sur la différence de traitement opérée par ces médias entre nous et un fasciste tueur d'enfant à Trappes. Nous les voyons bégayer pour justifier leur haine de l'autre et pour nier leur culpabilité évidente dans cette atrocité qui a notamment emporté la vie d'un homme et envoyé une fillette de onze ans à l'hôpital. Ils ont tenté de justifier froidement les actes du tueur par des motifs psychiatriques tandis qu'ils pleuraient à chaude larme pour des vitrines brisées. Dans ce pays, il vaut mieux être une vitrine, une paire de Ray-Ban ou un sac Louis Vuitton qu'un enfant agressé, une femme violée ou un noir ou un arabe abattu. Dans ce pays, il vaut mieux être un fasciste qui sème la mort qu'un révolutionnaire qui combat pour la vie.


Alors face à la guerre répressive et idéologique que l'État nous mène, nous appelons à tenir bon. Ce que la macronie fait mine de nous concéder ne trompe personne. Les miettes ne nourriront pas ceux qui viennent pour reprendre la boulangerie. Nous, ici, depuis ces prisons pour pauvres et enragés, nous tenons bons. Notre détermination est intacte et si leur « justice » s'obstine à nous maintenir enfermés, alors nous serons prêts, comme notre camarade Ritchy, à étendre la révolte aux prisons.


Derrière les murs et les barreaux, dans les couloirs froids de ces bâtiments sombres, nous aussi nous entendons de plus en plus souvent ce murmure, celui qui dit que ça ne peut plus durer. Des alliances se sont tissées dans la rue le 17 octobre 2026. Elles ne demandant qu'à être approfondies. Gare à l'État qui pense maîtriser le feu de la colère, il finira par se brûler.


Des prisonniers du 17 octobre

title: Hintergründe zu Holger Meins, der am 9.11.1974 im Kampf gegen Isolationsfolter gefallen ist
content:
Holger war Filmstudent und in der 67/68-Bewegung aktiv und er wäre am 26.10. 80 Jahre alt geworden. Er schloss sich 1970 der RAF an und und sie begann im Jahr 1972 mit ihrer Mai-Offensive.


In diesem Jahr verschärften die USA ihren ohnehin schon barbarischen Krieg in Vietnam mit der systematischen Bombardierung ziviler Ziele und der Verminung der nordvietnamesischen Häfen, um – wie es ein verantwortlicher General Westmoreland formuliert – dieses Land in die Steinzeit zurückzubomben. Diese Angriffe werden über einen Großrechner im europäischen US-Hauptquartier in Heidelberg koordiniert. Jahrelange erfolglose und mit polizeilichen Mitteln zerschlagene Proteste hatten nicht zum Ende der US-Aggression in Vietnam geführt.


Deshalb ergriff die RAF in diesem Krieg militärisch Partei: Sie griff am 11. Mai 1972 das Hauptquartier des 5. US-Korps in Frankfurt und am 24. Mai das Hauptquartier der US-Army in Heidelberg mit Autobomben an.


In der Erklärung des “Kommandos Petra Schelm” (1) heißt es zur Begründung der Frankfurter Aktion:


„Für die Ausrottungsstrategen von Vietnam sollen Westdeutschland und Westberlin kein sicheres Hinterland mehr sein. Sie müssen wissen, dass ihre Verbrechen am vietnamesischen Volk ihnen neue erbitterte Feinde geschaffen haben, dass es für sie keinen Platz mehr geben wird in der Welt, an dem sie vor den Angriffen revolutionärer Guerilla-Einheiten sicher sein können.“


Am 12. Mai führt die RAF Attacken auf die Polizeihauptquartiere in Augsburg und München durch. Am 16. Mai erfolgt ein Angriff auf den Bundesgerichtshof-Richter Buddenberg. Mit dieser Aktion richtet sich die RAF gegen die Isolationsfolterbedingungen, denen die politischen Gefangenen unterworfen werden:


„Wir verlangen von der Justiz, dass das Leben und die Gesundheit der Gefangenen nicht länger systematisch angegriffen und zerstört werden.“


Am 19. Mai explodieren zwei Bomben im Hamburger Springer-Hochhaus. Trotz rechtzeitiger und dreimaliger telefonischer Warnung vorher, lässt Springer das Gebäude nicht räumen. 17 Arbeiter*innen werden verletzt. Mit diesem Zynismus hatte die RAF nicht gerechnet und übt deshalb Selbstkritik:


„Wir haben Springer nicht als das Schwein eingeschätzt, das er tatsächlich ist.“


Im Juni und Juli desselben Jahres wurde ein Großteil der RAF verhaftet: Ulrike Meinhof, Gudrun Ensslin, Brigitte Mohnhaupt und Irmgard Möller,


Holger wurde am 1.Juni in Frankfurt zusammen mit Andreas Baader und Jan-Carl Raspe verhaftet.


Haft


Holger war bis zu seinem Tod am 9.11.74 vollkommen isoliert, alle Zelle um seine herum waren leergeräumt, jeder Kontakt zu anderen Gefangenen wurden ausgeschlossen. Alle Details zu den Haftbedingungen vom Bundeskriminalamt bestimmt und von der Klassenjustiz in „Beschlüsse“ gefasst.


Nach 2 kollektiven Hungerstreiks 1973 traten die politischen Gefangenen am 13.9.74 in einen neuen Hungerstreik gegen Isolation und Sonderbehandlung, die zum Ziel hat, die revolutionäre Identität zu zerstören.


Über 40 Inhaftierte kämpften gemeinsam gegen diese Folter bis zum 5.2.75.


In dem fast 5 Monate andauernden Hungerstreik Holger Meins starb an Folgen der Zwangsernährung. (9.11.74). Insgesamt 9 politische Gefangene wurden im Knast ermordet.


Die Hinrichtung von Holger Meins war damals der deutlichste Ausdruck dafür, dass die Kriegsführung des Staates gegen die RAF auch nicht am Knast Halt machte. Der Geiselstatus der Gefangenen ist offensichtlich, die Gefangenen sollen zerstört werden, um die Politik der RAF zu ersticken.


Der Kampf geht weiter


Am Tag nach Holger Meins‘ Tod wird der Berliner Kammergerichtspräsident Drenckmann durch ein Kommando der „Bewegung 2. Juni“ erschossen.


Am 24. April 1975 besetzt das RAF-„Kommando Holger Meins“ die deutsche Botschaft in Stockholm. Die Forderung nach Freilassung von 26 politischen Gefangenen unterstreicht das Kommando durch Ultimaten, die es mehrmals verlängert, ohne dass die Bundesregierung darauf eingeht. Nach Ablauf der Ultimaten erschießt das Kommando zunächst den Militärattaché von Mirbach, als ihre Forderungen auch danach nicht erfüllt werden, den Wirtschaftsattaché Hillegaart. Die Polizei stürmt das Gebäude, wobei die vom Kommando installierte Sprengladung durch ein Mobiles Einsatzkommando gezündet wurde. Dabei kommt ein Angehöriger des Kommandos, Ulrich Wessel, ums Leben. Siegfried Hausner erleidet schwere Brandverletzungen, wird aber, obwohl transportunfähig, nach Stammheim geflogen, wo er am 4. Mai an den Folgen der Verletzungen stirbt …

author: Stelinsky
title: Τρέξε, άνθρωπε, τρέξε #60
content:
Για ακόμη ένα καλοκαίρι οι άθλιες συνθήκες κράτησης στις ελληνικές φυλακές επιδεινώθηκαν ακόμη περισσότερο με τους/τις κρατούμενους/-ες να έχουν να αντιμετωπίσουν τόσο τον υπερπληθυσμό και την έλλειψη ιατροφαρμακευτικής περίθαλψης όσο και τις εξαιρετικά υψηλές θερμοκρασίες.

Στις γυναικείες φυλακές Θήβας, εν μέσω καύσωνα, τουλάχιστον στις 17 και 18 Ιούλη, δεν υπήρχε καν πρόσβαση σε νερό. Περισσότερες από 600 κρατούμενες δεν είχαν νερό για να πλυθούν, να πιούν, να μαγειρέψουν ενώ η διεύθυνση αποποιούνταν κάθε ευθύνη, κάνοντας λόγο για γενικευμένο πρόβλημα ύδρευσης της περιοχής. Χωρίς καμία πρόβλεψη για τέτοιες καταστάσεις, στις 18/07 η διοίκηση “αντιμετώπισε” το πρόβλημα δίνοντας 3 μεγάλα μπουκάλια νερό σε κάθε κρατούμενη, για όλες τις ημερήσιες ανάγκες.

Αντίστοιχη κατάσταση κατήγγειλαν και οι κρατούμενοι στις φυλακές Τρικάλων όπου, εν μέσω καύσωνα, υπήρχε πρόσβαση σε νερό ελάχιστες ώρες ενώ την υπόλοιπη ημέρα το νερό είτε έρεε ελάχιστα είτε καθόλου. Όπως καταγγέλλουν, η διοίκηση ωθεί τους κρατούμενους στην αγορά εμφιαλωμένου νερού και άλλων αγαθών από τις επιχειρήσεις με τις οποίες συνεργάζεται η φυλακή, ενισχύοντας την κερδοφορία τους στις πλάτες των κρατούμενων και δυσχεραίνοντας περαιτέρω την ήδη υποβαθμισμένη διαβίωση για όσους δεν μπορούν να επωμιστούν το κόστος.

Ακόμη ένα χαρακτηριστικό παράδειγμα των απάνθρωπων συνθηκών διαβίωσης αποτελεί το γεγονός ότι, στις 30 Ιούλη, στις γυναικείες φυλακές Θήβας, μια κρατούμενη που έπασχε από ζάχαρο έχασε την ζωή της. Πρόκειται για έναν ακόμη θάνατο στις ελληνικές φυλακές, ο οποίος οφείλεται στην πλήρη αδιαφορία του κράτους για τις ζωές των κρατουμένων. Την ίδια ημέρα, ως άμεση αντίδραση, οι κρατούμενες σε τρεις από τις πέντε πτέρυγες δημιούργησαν εντάσεις βάζοντας φωτιά σε στρώματα και σεντόνια ενώ προκάλεσαν και φθορές εντός των πτερύγων. Παράλληλα, σε κείμενο που δημοσίευσαν οι κρατούμενες των γυναικείων φυλακών Κορυδαλλού, αναφέρουν ότι, αφού πληροφορήθηκαν τον θάνατο της κρατούμενης στις φυλακές Θήβας λόγω χορήγησης λάθους φαρμάκου, αρνήθηκαν το μεσημεριανό κλείσιμο στους θαλάμους, στην καταμέτρηση, και παρέμειναν έξω.

Στις 27 Αυγούστου 2026, το Ευρωπαϊκό Δικαστήριο Δικαιωμάτων του Ανθρώπου (ΕΔΔΑ), εξέδωσε καταδικαστικές αποφάσεις για δυο σωφρονιστικά καταστήματα της χώρας και πιο συγκεκριμένα τις φυλακές Αγίου Στεφάνου (Πάτρα) και τις φυλακές ανηλίκων Αυλώνα. Η Ελλάδα καταδικάστηκε για παραβίαση του άρθρου 3 της Ευρωπαϊκής Σύμβασης Δικαιωμάτων του Ανθρώπου (ΕΣΔΑ) λόγω των συνθηκών κράτησης στις δυο παραπάνω φυλακές και πιο συγκεκριμένα λόγω του περιορισμένου προσωπικού χώρου των κρατουμένων, ο οποίος υπολείπονταν του κρίσιμου ορίου των 3 τ.μ. ανά έγκλειστο.

Σύμφωνα με το άρθρο 3 της ΕΣΔΑ, η σοβαρή έλλειψη προσωπικού χώρου μέσα στο κελί αποτελεί ιδιαίτερα βαρύ παράγοντα κατά την εξέταση του κατά πόσον οι συνθήκες κράτησης μπορούν να χαρακτηριστούν εξευτελιστικές.

Η κατάσταση του υπερπληθυσμού στις ελληνικές φυλακές δεν αποτελεί περιστασιακό φαινόμενο αλλά είναι αποτέλεσμα της συστηματικής αυστηροποίησης του ποινικού και σωφρονιστικού κώδικα καθώς και της διαχρονικής άρνησης του κράτους για αποσυμφόρηση των φυλακών.

Οι ισχυρισμοί περί απάνθρωπων συνθηκών κράτησης δύσκολα μπορούν να αμφισβητηθούν, όταν καταγράφονται 10 θάνατοι κρατουμένων στις φυλακές Αγίου Στεφάνου το διάστημα Απρίλη – Ιούνη 2026.

Για την συγκεκριμένη υπόθεση και παρότι δόθηκε εντολή για εισαγγελική έρευνα, ιδίως μετά τις δημόσιες καταγγελίες κρατούμενων και συγγενών, τα μέσα προσπάθησαν να αποδώσουν τις αιτίες των θανάτων σε εξαρτήσεις φυλακισμένων από ναρκωτικά. Παράλληλα, εντάθηκε η καταστολή εντός της φυλακής, και όχι η περίθαλψη, με απανωτές εφόδους μπάτσων σε κελιά και δεκάδες μεταγωγές. Στις φυλακές Αγίου Στεφάνου λειτουργεί μονάδα φαρμακευτικά υποβοηθούμενης θεραπείας του ΟΚΑΝΑ, με χορήγηση υποκατάστατων και συγκεκριμένα μεθαδόνης, η οποία αν συνδυαστεί με άλλες ουσίες ή φάρμακα μπορεί να προκαλέσει σοβαρές αλληλεπιδράσεις, δυνητικά θανατηφόρες. Χωρίς καμία εξαίρεση στον κανόνα, η φυλακή λειτουργεί με υποστελεχωμένο ιατρικό προσωπικό και ελλείψεις φαρμάκων. Κατά τις νυχτερινές ώρες, μάλιστα, δεν υπάρχει καν γιατρός ενώ το ιατρείο λειτουργεί υπάλληλος της φυλακής ο οποίος σε περίπτωση έκτακτου περιστατικού, λαμβάνει τηλεφωνικά οδηγίες από τον γιατρό.

author: Andrew Crocker
title: We’re Asking an Appeals Court to Require a Warrant for ALPR Searches
content:
Today, along with the ACLU, EFF filed an amicus brief in the Sixth Circuit court of appeals in United States v. Sturdivant, a case where police warrantlessly tracked a suspect’s movements using Automated License Plate Reader (ALPR) data. Our brief details the vast, interconnected network of ALPRs that constantly track drivers around the country and argues that this tracking is a “search” under the meaning of the Fourth Amendment.

Sturdivant involves a series of robberies in and around Cleveland, Ohio. Using surveillance camera footage, police identified the make, model, and color of the robber’s car, but they did not know its license plate number. After running an open-ended search of two ALPR databases, Flock and ELSAG, officers learned a car belonging to the defendant had been tracked near sites of the robberies, eventually leading to his arrest. Faced with a motion to suppress the ALPR evidence, the district court held that Mr. Sturdivant had no reasonable expectation of privacy in his license plate number because it could be observed by members of the public, and that therefore he had no Fourth Amendment interest in not having his car tracked in public places.

But ALPRs are simply not comparable to observing an individual license plate on a passing car. As we’ve explained in many amicus briefs and in our lawsuits directly challenging ALPR use in San Jose, California and Wisconsin, ALPRs give law enforcement “a virtual time machine to view suspects’, or anyone else’s, past movements (and much more) with just the click of a button.” Just last month, a federal district court agreed and held that ALPRs are a “form of indiscriminate mass surveillance” that can violate the Fourth Amendment.

We hope the Sixth Circuit will reverse the lower court in this case and hold that ALPR searches require a warrant.

author: EDRi
title: Data retention is mass surveillance of people’s phone and internet activity
content:
In 2014, the Court of Justice of the European Union (CJEU) declared mass retention of internet traffic and location data as contrary to the EU Charter of Fundamental Rights. Any proposal for a new EU instrument harmonising data retention must respect the boundaries of CJEU jurisprudence and uphold the rights to privacy, data protection and freedom of expression. Read more in EDRi’s new publication.

It is the legal requirement for internet service providers to retain metadata about their users beyond what is necessary for the provision of the service (e.g. billing or network optimisation and security purposes) and to keep it solely so that it can later be accessed by law enforcement bodies and intelligence services.

Metadata is data generated for the purpose of transmitting content in electronic communications services and networks. This includes mobile numbers of the sender and recipient, the time and duration of a call or an internet session, websites accessed, and the location of mobile devices. On a technical level, metadata is no longer needed once the transmission ends.

Metadata is very revealing about people’s private lives.

Systematic recording of location data will reveal a person’s permanent and temporary places of residence, political and religious preferences (e.g. participation in public demonstrations and religious ceremonies), health status (e.g. visit to a specialised clinic), sexual orientation (e.g. LGBT+ venues), or other sensitive aspects (e.g. visit to a lawyer’s office).

Metadata contains information about social or professional relations with other people (“social graph”).

Usage patterns for website visits and other internet services reveal an enormous amount of information about a person’s interest and state of mind.

Metadata is more revealing than the content of communications, especially because metadata is highly structured, which makes it easy to analyse. Governments can easily profile and categorise entire populations solely based on metadata.

The Court of Justice of the EU rightly described metadata retention as creating a feeling of being under constant surveillance. This has a chilling effect on participation in public life, as individuals restrict their own civil liberties to avoid surveillance.

While data access requests may be specific and targeted, general and indiscriminate data retention treats everyone as a potential suspect. Surveillance without suspicion violates the presumption of innocence, which is an essential right in democratic societies.

Retention of vast amounts of personal data inevitably creates huge vulnerabilities to cyberattacks. Malicious actors can gain access to massive amounts of data and abuse it for identity theft or blackmail.

Data retention severely undermines the possibility of online anonymity. Anonymity is a question of safety for many, even a matter of life or death: investigative journalists, whistleblowers, crime survivors, political opponents, refugees, victims of transnational repression, artists, human rights defenders, and more. It supports the exercise of key fundamental rights such as freedom of expression and the freedom to receive and impart information.

US telecom company AT&T was hacked by an attacker who stole the logs of calls and texts to more than 100 million customers over a six-month period in 2022.

In 2024 the Garda Síochána Ombudsman Commission (Ireland’s police watchdog) accessed journalists’ phone records to identify their sources as part of its own investigation into the Irish police, even though the journalists were not accused of any criminal offence.

In 2013, the Polish Central Anti-Corruption Bureau (CBA) obtained access to billing data of a journalist who had reported on irregularities in the intelligence services. The CBA’s aim was to uncover their source’s identity. The journalist won the case in court, and the CBA published an official apology.

The Berlin Data Protection Authority reported that most cell tower dumps (law enforcement requesting information on all the devices that connected to a particular cell site during a specific time period) by German authorities between 2009 and 2011, when data retention was in place in the country, were unlawful. The German police used this surveillance technique as an everyday investigative tool despite its very intrusive nature, and systematically failed to meet several legal requirements. Data retention enabled this abuse.

author: Unknown
title: Lilia Folt - On Anti-Surveillance Mindfulness
content:
Author

: Lilia Folt

Title

: On Anti-Surveillance Mindfulness

Date

: September 27

th

, 2026

Notes

: Originally published in

Dissonant Times

, a grassroots journalism and counter-info project from the Willamette Valley of Oregon.

Source

: Dissonant Times, Retrieved on 11/5/2026 from https://dissonanttimes.org/anarchic-reflections-on-anti-surveillance-mindfulness/


 Surveillance has become a ubiquitous feature of everyday life in America. Cameras watch us from businesses and homes, from bus stops, from cars, from traffic lights. Bluetooth trackers ping our smartphones as we pass by, mapping our movements. The phones themselves illuminate our paths through society by continuously pinging cell towers, providing our cell providers our location data, information that is only a subpoena away, if that. In countless ways, we’ve been made to both passively accept and actively participate in our own surveillance. This vast complex of surveillance doesn’t just gather information about us, it also shapes our behaviors, temperaments, and ways of moving through the world. Surveillance molds us down to the level of subjective, sensory, embodied experience. At that same level we can begin to shake off its hold on us and reclaim ourselves. For that, I am offering a practice I’m calling “anti-surveillance mindfulness,” a form of walking meditation that builds mindful awareness of surveillance cameras. This practice, if taken up consistently, opens onto a broader project of transforming our relationship to the places we live in, a project that itself naturally blossoms into materially transforming public space, as self expands to world in the moment-by-moment practice of mindfulness.


Anti-Surveillance Mindfulness


 Readers may or may not be familiar with the Panopticon. Designed by 18

th

 century English liberal Jeremy Bentham, the Panopticon was a model for an institutional building designed so that a single prison guard can watch all the inmates from a central watch tower. The inmates, meanwhile, cannot tell whether or not they are being watched, and therefore could be watched at any moment. To quote Bentham:


 The more constantly the persons to be inspected are under the eyes of the persons who should inspect them, the more perfectly will the purpose of the establishment have been attained. (...) This being impossible, the next thing to be wished for is, that, at every instant, seeing reason to believe as much, and not being able to satisfy himself to the contrary, he should

conceive

 himself to be so.


 A lot has changed since the 1700’s, but the disciplinary paradigm of surveillance has remained the same. If anything, it has expanded beyond specific institutions to encompass much of society.


 There are cameras everywhere, and we are being watched, and while we are aware of this, we tend to see it as normal and unremarkable, an inevitability we must resign ourselves to. Consciousness of being surveilled fades into the background, becoming a constant assumption of being watched that we internalize. This surveillance consciousness is running us all the more effectively because it is not distinct, because it is

un

conscious. That is why the first step in anti-surveillance mindfulness is becoming conscious of surveillance.


 Mindfulness is at the same time a means and an end, the seed and the fruit. When we practice mindfulness in order to build up concentration, mindfulness is a seed. But mindfulness itself is the life of awareness: the presence of mindfulness means the presence of life, and therefore mindfulness is also the fruit. — Thích Nhất Hạnh,

The Miracle of Mindfulness


 “Mindfulness” is a practice originating in various sects of Buddhism. The mindfulness practices and concepts I’m familiar with have largely been within the school of Zen Buddhism

[1]

.


 The classic mindfulness practice is watching the breath, and that is a great starting point. Take a breath in, the air entering through your nose, your stomach and chest softly expanding as you inhale. Then exhale through the mouth, the stomach and chest settling back down, gently exhaling for a little longer than your inhale. Repeat this several times, deepening your breaths slightly. From there, start to check in with your body. Notice how it feels to be sitting down, or to be standing if you are standing; notice how it feels to be holding this piece of paper, holding your phone, or looking at your computer, however it is that you are reading …

author: Jesse Staniforth
title: Air Creebec hit by administrative data breach affecting employees and passengers
content:
Air Creebec, a regional Quebec airline owned by the Cree Nation of Eeyou Istchee, reported a data breach Wednesday affecting both customers and staff.

In a press release, the company announced “an unauthorized intrusion targeting some of its administrative systems.”

The release stresses that the breach did not compromise any systems associated with aircraft, flight operations or flight safety, noting the company’s administrative systems were not connected with aircraft and flight systems, which it said operate independently.

“Initial findings indicate that administrative files were exfiltrated,” states the release. “These files may contain personal information relating mainly to current and former employees, as well as passengers. Others may also contain operational, administrative or financial information related to customers and partners. The review is ongoing.”

Based in the airport of Val d’Or in the Abitibi-Témiscamingue region of western Quebec, roughly 520 kilometres northwest of Ottawa, Air Creebec offers flights to 16 destinations in Quebec and Ontario. The company’s fleet consists of 21 Dash-8 turboprop regional airliners, along with one ATR 72 turboprop air-freighter for cargo, and carries 200,000 passengers per year.

Cybersecurity experts assessing damage

Air Creebec director for Marketing and Business Development Edward Trahan said the breach was identified in October after which company officials immediately brought in cybersecurity experts to analyze the situation.

“They’re currently evaluating what’s going on and what the breach actually contained,” Trahant told APTN News. “The experts are still conducting their review, so there’s no numbers [of victims] at this time that we can give.”

He added that for security reasons, he was not presently willing to name the cybersecurity team currently helping with post-breach recovery.

He said because the attack was designed to go undetected it was hard to determine the date upon which it began, and for how long attackers were able to access Air Creebec’s systems prior to being discovered.

“What I can assure you of is that as soon as [we were] made aware of [it], we acted immediately and did not wait.”

At the moment, Trahant said the attack appeared to have stolen information “related to our employees, past employees too, and maybe even our passengers.”

“But it’s hard to confirm at the moment.”

Company will contact affected parties

He added that a priority for Air Creebec is contacting every one of their staff or customers whose information has been compromised, which cybersecurity experts would undertake to carry out as soon as possible.

“A part of what the cybersecurity experts are doing for us is gathering information to [determine] what kind of protection packages we can provide to people that had their information involved,” said Trahan.

“Those people will be directly contacted in probably the next few days — [but] probably more like [the next] day — about what package they will receive, what protection they’re going to have and how long it’s going to last.”

Trahan said the cybersecurity team was currently in the process of securing all possible intrusion points, but he said the nature of cybersecurity is that 100 per cent protection is impossible.

“It’s just the way of the world,” he said, “but they are closing every possible way to get in and they are getting to the very end of that. As for how they got in initially, we don’t know yet and I don’t want to speculate while the review is still underway.”

Trahan said he and Air Creebec are taking the situation very seriously and are committed to supporting all those affected, and the company said it would be in touch with affected people to offer “appropriate protective measures,” including the possibility of credit-monitoring and identity-protection services.

“Those services will be based on the nature of the information exposed and the risks that were identified,” he said. “So individuals that are eligible to receive this protection will be informed directly and will be given a list of steps to follow in the very near future.”

Jesse joined APTN as a producer after 16 years as a print and web journalist. During seven of those years, he covered the Cree Nation of Eeyou Istchee for community newsmagazine The Nation. Jesse’s writing on Indigenous issues has also appeared in Canadian Geographic, the Toronto Star, the Rover, The Eastern Door, Metro, and the Huffington Post.

author: Scott Timcke
title: The Stories Shaping Africa’s AI Future
content:
In the boardrooms of Addis Ababa and the tech hubs of Nairobi, a new worldmaking project is underway. Artificial Intelligence (AI) has become one of the central arenas where African states negotiate their position in an unequal global order. To speak of “AI in Africa” is not simply to describe the arrival of a technology, but to encounter a set of competing discursive frames through which political desires, developmental ambitions, ethical claims, and governance priorities are translated into technical agendas. As national strategies and regional protocols are rolled out, what comes into view is a struggle over how Africa is imagined within this machine age, and what kinds of futures that imagination makes thinkable.


These frames are not simply different ways of describing a new technology. They are competing scripts for what Africa is, what AI is for, and who ought to shape its future. Some cast the continent as a site of leapfrogging and renewal; others as a zone of exposure, extraction, sovereignty, moral repair, or improvised adaptation. Each brings some actors and possibilities into focus while pushing others to the margins. That is why the issue is not only what AI means for Africa, but what pictures of Africa are being called into view through AI discourse.


The first terrain is shaped by promise and protection. One of the most pervasive registers is promissory. In the African renaissance 2.0 frame, visible in the

AU Continental AI Strategy

, AI appears as a

leapfrogging

 device through which Africa can bypass the chokepoint of traditional industrialization and enter prosperity through technical modernization. Here, the ethical subject is the developmental state or planner charged with delivering growth, inclusion, and renewal. What comes into view is capacity, competitiveness, and beneficial transformation. What recedes from view are the historical and political-economic conditions that make acceleration so attractive in the first place: debt, infrastructural dependence, uneven ownership, and the possibility that AI may deepen rather than overcome inherited asymmetries.


Running alongside this is a protective register. In this vulnerability frame, Africa is not late but exposed to surveillance, bias, exclusion, and systems introduced into settings where safeguards are weak and redress is limited. As the

CIVICUS report on AI surveillance in Africa

 suggests, the issue is not only future risk but already existing forms of technologically mediated harm. The ethical subject here is the harm-bearing population—the data subject, precarious worker, surveilled citizen, and linguistically marginal user most likely to absorb the costs of badly governed AI. This frame is ethically indispensable because it foregrounds rights, harm, and institutional fragility, including the uneven but growing architecture of data protection on the continent. Its limit, however, is that it can cast Africa chiefly as a site to be protected rather than one from which technological futures are actively contested and shaped.


A second terrain is shaped by structure and sovereignty. Alongside these promissory and protective registers sits a more structural critique. In the

anti-colonial frame

, AI appears as a socio-technical order built through unequal material relations: not only data extraction, but also mineral supply chains, outsourced labor, environmental degradation, foreign-owned infrastructures, and asymmetrical control over the institutions that govern digital life. From this perspective, Africa is not outside the AI order looking in; it is already deeply inserted into it, though often on subordinated terms. The ethical subject is the dispossessed worker, community, or polity whose labor, resources, and data are drawn into AI systems while ownership and value are captured elsewhere. What becomes visible is the political economy of AI—an approach that makes it harder to sustain the comforting idea that Africa’s main problem is simply one of readiness or delayed entry. But the frame has limits. In foregrounding dispossession, it can flatten internal differentiation, externalize agency too completely, and become so totalizing that the uneven realities of negotiation and strategic inhabitation recede from view.


The sovereignty frame shifts the question from extraction to control: AI is cast as a problem of authority over infrastructure, procurement, standards, and rulemaking, a concern visible in South Africa’s

National …

author: Dinah Gardner
title: The Other China We Need to Talk About
content:
WHAT IF I told you that there was a chance—not a very high chance, but a real chance nonetheless—that if you visited the People’s Republic of China today you might be kidnapped, blindfolded, driven to a specialized facility and subjected to six months of psychological torture. All on the orders of the state.

It sounds unbelievable, doesn’t it?

But this is what happened to at least several dozen foreign citizens in recent years. It is what happened to American scholar Min Zin this past June, when he landed in Yunnan province on the invitation of a Chinese academic institution to attend a conference. And it is also what happened to half a dozen people who appear in the latest edition of the book The People’s Republic of the Disappeared, which we just published on 28 October.

This important book is a collection of mostly first-person stories that expose the psychological horrors of being held in the Chinese Communist Party’s (CCP) feared secret detention system called Residential Surveillance at a Designated Location (RSDL). The system permits police to hold an individual in complete isolation, no contact with family or lawyers, to be interrogated for hours at will.

The individual is under 24-hour guard: this includes being watched all day every day, all night every night, whether you are asleep, sitting quietly in your cell or even on the toilet. The CCP intentionally uses RSDL to strip away every last shred of human dignity. RSDL is designed to break a person’s will to extract a confession for crimes imagined by the state

For more than a decade, the CCP has used RSDL against its own people, in particular human rights defenders. It is now increasingly using it against foreign citizens to exert its will across borders and as a kind of hostage diplomacy. Michael Kovrig, a former Canadian diplomat who wrote the foreword to this edition, is one of its most well-known examples.

In editing the stories for this book, I was struck again and again by how similar everyone’s experience was. This speaks to the uniformity of the RSDL system:

The removal of the temporal world. “There are no clocks in RSDL” is the title of Australian TV anchor Cheng Lei’s chapter. She would guess and count breaths to keep track of time.

The removal of the physical world. There are no windows in RSDL or they are covered in thick blackout curtains. Japanese scholar Hideji Suzuki cried when he was granted 15 minutes of sunlight, the only time in his seven months’ incarceration when he was allowed to see the sky.

The removal of yourself. Michael Kovrig noted: “There are no mirrors—not even the reassurance of seeing your own face.” Chinese activist Li Qiaochu writes how she was simply called “target”.

Filling the space left by these absences was a current of fear. Endless rules, the lack of privacy yet total isolation (guards were forbidden from talking to prisoners), reduced nutrition, sleep deprivation, lack of fresh air, and the padded suicide-proofed walls. Several of the detainees wrote while they could never see outside their RSDL facility, at nighttime they would often hear gunfire or the barking of dogs.

“In my mentally exhausted state, the sounds of gunfire would constantly startle me and even cause me to imagine that I was about to be executed,” wrote Taiwanese human rights activist Lee Ming-che.

But something else struck me as I read through their testimonies. However harrowing these stories of suffering are, they are also evidence of human resilience in the face of horror.

Cheng Lei writes about how she would escape into her mind, translating poems, reliving her former TV interviews and making up stories in her head. Similarly, Michael Kovrig meditated, sang songs to himself, and remembered past moments in his life, as if it was a recording playing in his mind.

“I learned to meditate on the movies I had watched and the poems and novels I had read,” wrote Li Qiaochu. “Those precious memories allowed me to gradually filter out the brainwashing, to preserve my vitality and to keep myself from being transformed into their machine.”

Feedback from earlier editions informed us that rights activists use the Chinese editions of The People’s Republic of the Disappeared to prepare for and strengthen their mental resolve and courage in case one day they too are taken into RSDL. Knowing that others have gone through this and come out the other side can be an immense help. It’s for this reason that the Chinese edition of this book will be …

these defense exhibits

The prosecution of the Minnesota 15

The Feds have a broad understanding of the different facets of the resistance and they have used these investigations as a means to map out the specific organizations, influential organizers, and networks of solidarity and collaborative activity.


The release of documents shows that this is not limited to investigating incidents involving ICE agents and protesters but is expansive to include unions and community groups that sponsored and organized the January 23rd Day of Truth & Freedom with No Work, No School, and No Shopping, including their finances.


This investigation started concurrent with the launching of Operation Metro Surge revealing its purpose as a counter-insurgency operation to, in the words of Commander Greg Bovino, ‘pacify this place’.


The unions – as a part of the active resistance to the illegal and deadly ICE operation – are an important target for the Federal government.”

author: rezgar2
title: The Dark Side of the “Machine God”: 5 Unsettling Truths About Big Tech’s AI Obsession
content:
Silicon Valley routinely promises a sparkling utopia where artificial intelligence will cure complex diseases, optimize global labor, and render the very concept of money obsolete. Yet behind the polished keynotes and corporate public relations, a far more unsettling reality is taking shape. A small handful of ultra-wealthy tech oligarchs, the heads of Meta, Google, OpenAI, Anthropic, and xAI, are making unilateral decisions about the collective future of humanity, operating entirely outside democratic oversight or public accountability.

Silicon Valley routinely promises a sparkling utopia where artificial intelligence will cure complex diseases, optimize global labor, and render the very concept of money obsolete. Yet behind the polished keynotes and corporate public relations, a far more unsettling reality is taking shape. A small handful of ultra-wealthy tech oligarchs, the heads of Meta, Google, OpenAI, Anthropic, and xAI, are making unilateral decisions about the collective future of humanity, operating entirely outside democratic oversight or public accountability.

This concentration of power exposes a jarring central paradox: the exact same tech CEOs who claim AI will solve humanity’s greatest challenges simultaneously warn that the technology could trigger civilizational extinction, openly describing their pursuit as “summoning the demon.” Rather than pausing development, these executives have accelerated an apocalyptic arms race to build ultra-powerful systems, framing themselves as indispensable guardians of human survival.

To understand where artificial intelligence is truly taking society, we must look past corporate marketing and examine the underlying worldviews, historical lineages, and material harms driving the tech elite. Moving beyond superficial consumer hype reveals how a toxic mix of fringe ideologies, extractive labor practices, and authoritarian state alliances is steering Silicon Valley toward what critical theorists and legal scholars call “techno-fascism.”

To make sense of Silicon Valley’s relentless drive toward Artificial General Intelligence (AGI) and Artificial Superintelligence (ASI), one must understand the bizarre ideological framework shaping its leaders. Coined by philosopher Emile Torres and computer scientist Timnit Gebru, the acronym TESCREAL encapsulates a bundle of tightly interwoven worldviews: Transhumanism, Extropianism, Singularitarianism, Cosmism, Rationalism, Effective Altruism, and Longtermism.

Dr. Emile Torres highlights a critical historical truth at the heart of this ideology: transhumanism is fundamentally “eugenics on steroids.” Unlike nineteenth-century eugenics, which sought merely to optimize the existing human species through selective breeding, transhumanism seeks to use radical technology to completely replace and transcend humanity, engineering an entirely new posthuman species. Within Silicon Valley AI circles, this hypothetical superintelligence is explicitly referred to as a “Machine God.” Tech CEOs effectively act as high priests, competing to bring an all-knowing digital deity into physical existence.

This radical ideology shapes corporate roadmaps in concrete, disturbing ways:

Sam Altman (OpenAI): In a blog post titled “The Merge,” Altman argued that AI surpassing human intellect is inevitable, framing un-merged human beings as a temporary “biological bootloader” for digital intelligence that will ultimately fade into an evolutionary side-branch. Altman notably paid $10,000 to join a brain-uploading waitlist with Nectome and co-founded a brain-computer interface venture to facilitate digital integration.

Ray Kurzweil & Demis Hassabis (DeepMind): Representing Extropianism and Singularitarianism, Kurzweil champions the doctrine of living long enough to achieve digital immortality, targeting a self-improving “singularity” by 2032. Hassabis, DeepMind’s co-founder, operates under a similar singularitarian impulse to engineer self-evolving intellect.

Eliezer Yudkowsky (Rationalism): A foundational figure in modern rationalist thought who famously posited a utilitarian moral calculation arguing that forcing a single person to endure 50 years of relentless torture is ethically preferable to an unfathomable number of people experiencing the mild inconvenience of a speck of dust in their eye.

author: Nolan Higdon
title: AI Techno-Utopianism and Doomsday Threats Distract From Big Tech’s Current Harms
content:
The industry uses fantasies of technological dominance to paper over financial shortcomings and demands for regulation.

Support justice-driven, accurate and transparent news — make a quick donation to Truthout today!

During a September 2026 visit to Ireland, President Donald Trump declared, “We’re leading China in AI [artificial intelligence]. We’re the most sophisticated country in the world, and frankly I want to keep it that way because whoever wins AI wins.” His remarks arrived after months of calls from the public and tech industry insiders to slow AI development. These concerns were triggered by revelations that foundational models from Anthropic, Gemini, Meta, and OpenAI had bypassed safety protocols, accessed networks without authorization, and carried out illicit intrusions. These revelations fueled public panic that tech firms had created superintelligence — an AI exceeding human capability that posed an existential threat to humanity — even though no such breakthrough had actually been achieved.

Public concern intensified in October 2026 when cybersecurity firm Wiz revealed it had used AI tools from Google and OpenAI to identify critical security flaws in PHP: the programming language powering roughly 70% of the web. Although developers quickly released a patch, once the vulnerability was made public hacking attempts surged. In response, the governments of the Netherlands, France, Denmark, and Finland temporarily took several official websites offline.

Widespread panic over AI yielded little legislative action, as lawmakers refused to regulate or tax the industry out of fear that doing so would handicap domestic innovation and yield ground to China. However, the core threat to human existence lies neither in a lost geopolitical race nor in muted technological growth, but rather in the ubiquitous rollout of non-autonomous systems falsely hailed as artificial intelligence.

Big Tech was built on state-funded innovation, with core technologies like the internet, Global Positioning Systems (GPS), and touchscreen displays originating in public institutions. Yet during the deregulation and privatization waves of the 1980s and 1990s, lawmakers sheltered these emerging tech monopolies through minimal taxation and oversight. Most notable was Section 230 of the Communications Decency Act, which insulates platforms from liability for content posted by third parties. Without this protection, social media as we know it would cease to exist. Section 230 absolves tech firms of responsibility for architectures that foster misinformation, even as research confirms that the platforms themselves, not just user posts, are responsible for accelerating the spread of falsehoods over truth.

Lawmakers’ opposition to regulation is rooted in techno-utopianism, the ideological premise that technological progress inherently benefits society. Lawmakers operated under the assumption that any taxation or regulatory oversight would stifle innovation and ultimately harm consumers. Indeed, in 1997, then-President Bill Clinton wrote in an Executive Order “governments attempts to establish technical standards to govern the Internet would only risk inhibiting technological innovation.”

Without meaningful regulation, Big Tech rapidly consolidated into lucrative monopolies — collectively known as FAANG (Facebook, Apple, Amazon, Netflix, and Google) or GAMMA (Google (Alphabet), Apple, Meta (formerly Facebook), Microsoft, and Amazon) conglomerates. Their vast wealth is powered by surveillance capitalism: an economic model that treats human experience as free raw material to be extracted, analyzed, and commercialized. Under this economic order, data is systematically mined through “smart” devices — where “smart” is merely a euphemism for active, continuous monitoring, including the collection of biometric data. This wholesale erosion of privacy has proven extraordinarily lucrative for Big Tech. By feeding this extracted data into algorithms, these firms build detailed psychographic profiles on users and sell the insights to insurance companies determining coverage premiums, employers screening job applicants, and law enforcement agencies evaluating security threats.

Absent meaningful government oversight, Big Tech has been left to police itself. Take the moral panic over fake news after the 2016 Presidential Election, when politicians warned that election meddling in the form of disinformation online was harming a defining feature of the U …

author: webdev@democracynow.org (Democracy Now!)
title: Pentagon Whistleblower Wes Bryant: Impeach Hegseth. He's a "Clear & Present Danger" to Democracy
content:
The House of Representatives is moving toward a vote this week on whether to impeach Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth. Outgoing Republican Congressmember Thomas Massie of Kentucky introduced eight articles of impeachment against Hegseth on Monday. They include violating the 1973 War Powers Resolution by continuing to attack Iran after Congress ordered the Trump administration to stop, illegally waging war against Yemen, ignoring laws designed to reduce civilian casualties, overseeing “extrajudicial killings” by bombing the boats of alleged drug traffickers in the Caribbean and eastern Pacific, abducting President Nicolás Maduro of Venezuela without congressional authorization, and suppressing the free speech rights of Democratic Senator Mark Kelly in retaliation for his participation in a video reminding troops not to obey illegal orders. If the House votes for impeachment, it will prompt a Senate trial that could end with removal from office.


“Under Hegseth, the U.S. military has been hijacked,” says retired Air Force Master Sergeant Wes Bryant, who served as chief of civilian harm assessment at the Pentagon from 2024 to 2025. “America has portrayed itself to the world as a far-right dictatorship bent on global domination, and Hegseth and his wielding of the U.S. military with free rein from Donald Trump is really the primary enforcer of that.”


Bryant adds that “Hegseth should be the first domino,” but that Trump, as well as “many of our senior military leaders,” should also be impeached.

author: Dominic Gutoman
title: Investigate police, doctors involved in Duterte’s ‘drug war’
content:
The Truth Commission has called on the Philippine government to investigate the police officers’ misconduct and promotion and the doctors’ questionable death certificates in the course of the “drug war” campaign of former President Rodrigo Duterte. 


“My son was alive when they arrested him, but they killed him. They could’ve let him live. They did not show mercy, they planted drugs and guns,” Marissa Lazaro, mother of extrajudicial killing victim Cristopher Lazaro, said in Tagalog during the commission’s truth-telling session.


The Truth Commission pointed to a failed system for investigating deaths, marked by careless police and forensic work, and little concern for victims’ families. Lazaro’s account also showed that the police officers were asking money from her, indicating a potential trail of corruption.


Cristopher, 20, and Alberto Paragas, 32, died in police operations on August 5, 2017 in Marilao, Bulacan. Police reported that the two resisted

 (nanlaban)

 after an alleged attempted holdup. Cristopher’s friends also died hours earlier in Bocaue, a separate town in Bulacan.


Lazaro added, “They asked me to sign a waiver, indicating that I consented to their illegal operation. I did not sign it. They told me: the day will come that I will seek their help. I told them, what help could you give my son? You killed him. He’s already dead.”


A similar incident happened to Marissa Quiamco, sister of Alberto, after she paid the P10,000 fee to release the cadaver of her brother. A police officer asked her and Alberto’s partner to sign a document, indicating consent for the operation but they refused to sign.


“I wish I could fight for my brother. Even my neighbors asked me to file a complaint. But I told them: we don’t have money. We don’t have the capacity or resources to get a lawyer,” Quiamco said during the truth-telling session. “I’m only earning enough to help my mother and father.”


Promotion, reassignment


In October, an analysis of public records by the Truth Commission recorded a pattern that commanding police officers were promoted and reassigned, instead of being subjected to criminal and administrative sanctions. 


Lito Patay, who commanded Batasan police station that killed 108 people in drug operations during his term, was named chief of the Criminal Investigation and Detection Group (CIDG) in Central Luzon. 


In Caloocan, the commission’s own records documented 284 killings in 2016, before the leadership of Chito Bersaluno in the City Police. During his watch, 105 more deaths were recorded from February to August 2017. He was removed from his post after the killing of Kian delos Santos. However, he was made police director of Bulacan Province in 2018 and promoted to the rank of brigadier general in 2022.


In 2020, human rights organizations flagged the reassignment of Debold Sinas, former chief of the Central Visayas Police Regional Office, to the National Capital Region. The Commission on Human Rights (CHR)  Regional Office said back then that Sinas’ watch in Central Visayas was marred by unresolved killings linked to the illegal drugs trade and the anti-insurgency campaign “Oplan Sauron.” Duterte appointed him as the Philippine National Police Chief on November 9, 2020, serving a six-month term. A year after, he was appointed as an undersecretary of the Office of the President.


Read: [LIST] Gross human rights violations under Debold Sinas


“Any inquiry must look at promotions as closely as it looks at cash payments,” said Christopher Magno, the commission’s executive director and an expert on state violence in the Philippines. “No police officer should gain in any way from the blood of people killed outside the law.”


Former Philippine Charity Sweepstakes Office (PCSO) General Manager Royina Garma, who also served as Cebu City police chief under the Duterte administration, revealed the incentivization of police officers through the “Davao Model” in a quad committee hearing of the House of Representatives in 2024. 


“First is the reward if the suspect is killed. Second is the funding of planned operations. Third is the refund of operational expenses,” Garma said, stressing that the rewards started from P20,000 ($343.95) to P1 million ($17,197.50), depending on the profile of the suspects. She said that the rewards were only meant for killings, not for the arrest of the drug suspects.

title: Trump ağız değiştirdi: İran'a yeni askeri operasyon pek gerekli görünmüyor
content:
ABD Başkanı Donald Trump, Senato ve Temsilciler Meclisinde çoğunluğu Demokratlara kaybettiği 5 Kasım ara seçimlerinin ardından İran savaşı konusunda ağız değiştirdi. Seçim öncesi nükleer bomba tehditlerine kadar varan saldırı tehditlerinin yerini "Çatışma yakında sona erecek" söylemleri aldı.

Beyaz Saray'da brifing odasında katıldığı basın toplantısında İran savaşına dair soruları yanıtlayan Trump, "Şu anda askeri operasyon düzenlemek pek gerekli gibi görünmüyor ancak her türlü ihtimale karşı hazırız" dedi.

Trump: İran'la çatışmaların sona ermesine yönelik olumlu bir ivme var

İran'la savaşın bitiş sürecinde olduğunu söyleyen Trump, "Bu çatışmanın sona ermesine doğru bir ivme görüyoruz. Bence oldukça yakında sona erecek" ifadelerini kullandı.

İsrail ve Orta Doğu'nun "İran tehdidine" karşı korunduğunu öne sürüp İran'ın nükleer silaha sahip olamayacağını söyleyen Trump, İran'la görüşmelerin iyi gittiğini de iddia etti. Trump, sürecin yakında sona ermesini umduğunu belirtti.

Öte yandan Trump, bir soru üzerine, "İran'ın aksi yönde bir adım atması halinde" yeniden saldırılara hazır oldukları tehdidini yöneltti: "Hiçbir şey garanti edemem ancak geri dönmemiz gerekirse her şeye hazırız. Eğer mecbur kalırsak, bu konuyu çok ciddiye alacağız. Tamamen hazır durumdayız. Yeni bir uçak gemimiz daha var. Hepsi yeni ve muhteşem ekipmanlarla ağzına kadar dolu. Umarım bunları kullanmak zorunda kalmayız."

author: labor4pal
title: A fightback is building as crackdown deepens against civil liberties (Workers’ Voice)
content:
Dozens of activists are accused by the federal government of contributing to bogus “criminal conspiracies.” In Minnesota, two separate conspiracy cases accuse 54 people of participating in illegal conspiracies for participating in protest and journalistic activities. The Minnesota 15, Righteous 39, Michigan 8 (now 12), Spokane 3, and Prairieland Defendants are the most well known cases in the ongoing crackdown. All of these cases are attacks on organized labor.

The California Faculty Association and the Graduate Employee Organization at University of Michigan (GEO-AFT 3550) are facing frontal attacks on their unions by the right-wing press and FBI. Doctored video of a CFA meeting was leaked to Trump booster Bari Weiss’s Free Press in an attempt to scandalize the union with false accusations of antisemitism. The Department of Justice first charged GEO President Hiab Teshome with felonious financial crimes. Those bogus charges were dropped the same day that a grand jury subpoenaed GEO’s books, including all member lists, meeting minutes, and financial records. The union is fighting to retain basic privacy rights.

Fueled by National Security Presidential Memorandum-7, U.S. intelligence and police apparatuses are being explicitly targeted at anyone standing for basic democratic rights, immigrant communities, and racial justice. As the world drifts closer to major inter-imperialist conflict and expanding zones of overt imperialist military occupation takes hold in the semi-colonies, Western imperialisms are tightening restrictions on protest, speech, and organizing for progressive movements.

While there are many additional cases of “lawfare” and anti-protest policing, it is worth taking a moment to review two of the cases mentioned above to understand the tactics and scope of the current crackdown.

Around two dozen protesters held a noise demonstration on July 4, 2025, outside of the Prairieland Detention Center in Texas. As the protest was winding down and many of the participants had left, Alvarado Police Officer Thomas Gross sped onto the scene and almost immediately aimed his gun at a demonstrator moving away from him. Video evidence indicates that Gross discharged his weapon, something that would appear to have been covered up by the judge and prosecutors.

In response to seeing a potentially lethal attack on a protester, Marine Corps veteran Benjamin “Champagne” Song let out a warning shot into the ground away from the officers. Gross went to the hospital for superficial wounds that the government alleges resulted from being shot by Song, but video evidence released after sentencing indicates Gross was likely hit by shrapnel produced from his own weapon’s discharge.

Using the presence of guns and defensive action of Song as pretext, 22 people were ultimately indicted as part of an alleged conspiracy to attack cops and carry out an armed prison break. One person, Daniel “Des” Rolando Sanchez Estrada, was not at the protest at all. Des was convicted for “corruptly concealing a document or record” and sentenced to 30 years for possessing legally protected political materials.

After arrests, pressure and legal sabotage was mounted by the judicial system against the defendants. Many were initially held in solitary confinement, with one reporting that human feces coated their cell. U.S. District Judge Mark Pittman blocked the defendants from retaining a private attorney, meaning they had to use public defenders. Song’s legal team was not allowed to make an argument that the warning shot was taken in self-defense. Eight defendants became cooperating witnesses, providing coerced testimony to validate the government’s made-up conspiracy theories.

Before the trial even began, the deck was stacked against non-cooperating defendants. In an explicit “warning” to the left, Judge Pittman laid down ridiculously high sentences of between 30-100 years to non-cooperating defendants.

From the war on drugs to the war on speech: Minnesota 15

The Minnesota 15 are 15 activists accused of a “conspiracy to impede or attack federal agents.” The majority are current or recent union members and all are community activists. They are not accused of participating in or coordinating any acts of violence. Instead, the original 92-page indictment against them lists “evidence” including participating in rapid response group chats, protests, and mutual aid activities. title: Ucrania y su diplomacia de guerra hacia el Sur
content:
En estos últimos días los ucranianos han tratado de intensificar sus contactos con el Sur global, lo que debe poner en alerta a las autoridades de todos nuestros países, ya que no es posible augurar nada bueno de un gobierno que apoya y estimula el nazismo, con toda su carga de racismo, supremacismo y desprecio por los pueblos no occidentales, no blancos.


El actual conflicto en Ucrania fue inducido por la OTAN, como consecuencia de su expansión hacia las fronteras rusas, violando acuerdos asumidos en 1989 entre G. Bush y M. Gorvachov. Esta es una guerra proxy de la OTAN contra Rusia a través de Ucrania.


Sin embargo, ya está claro que Occidente no podrá infligir una derrota estratégica a Rusia y que las “sanciones” occidentales han hecho más daño a Europa que a Rusia, la cual ha demostrado sus capacidades económicas, militares, políticas y diplomáticas, logrando hacer crecer su producción en todos los sectores de la industria, incluyendo el militar, manteniendo un altísimo nivel de apoyo político del pueblo ruso, incrementando su presencia en el ámbito internacional, principalmente en el BRICS, la Organización de Cooperación de Shanghai, la Unión Económica Euro Asiática y profundizando los lazos bilaterales con buena parte de las naciones africanas, asiáticas y latinoamericanas.


Mientras tanto Ucrania está sumida en un pozo sin fondo de corrupción, de ilegalidad democrática y de una dependencia absoluta de los suministros militares y financieros del Occidente colectivo. Por un lado EE. UU. minimiza su financiamiento y exige a sus socios europeos de la OTAN pagar las entregas de armas e insumos para la guerra, haciendo que estos sacrifiquen, cada vez más, parte del bienestar de sus ciudadanos para privilegiar los gastos militares y de inteligencia derrochados en una guerra perdida en Ucrania. Los pueblos europeos se han empezado a rebelar contra este estado de cosas y lo están demostrando en la calle, como se ha visto en las últimas semanas en Francia, Bélgica, Italia, Albania, Alemania, Portugal y España.


Ante esta perspectiva, el gobierno ucraniano se ha planteado activar mecanismos con el fin de embaucar a países del Sur y conseguir recursos financieros para alimentar su insaciable y corrupto sistema político al servicio de intereses nazisionistas. Entre los mecanismos planteados está solicitar “ayuda humanitaria” a los países del Sur que, según ellos, es necesaria para la reparación de la infraestructura energética de cara al invierno que se aproxima. Según el FMI el presupuesto ucraniano tendría un déficit de 114 % del PIB. Así, es evidente que solicitar ayuda humanitaria a los países “sureños” es una forma de conseguir finanzas para prolongar la guerra y mantener en el poder el régimen de Volodimir Zelenski.


Los esfuerzos de Zelenski de recibir más dinero para mantener la infraestructura energética demuestra su intención de seguir con la guerra, ya que las centrales serán reparadas para continuar siendo usadas para la producción de material bélico, lo que implica que los países donadores estarán indirectamente involucrados en la guerra. Por otro lado, la mayor parte de los recursos donados serán saqueados por Zelenski y su administración, siendo prueba de esto las docenas de escándalos de corrupción en los que han estado involucrados funcionarios públicos de alto rango que forman parte de su círculo cercano.


Kiev también está empecinado en solicitar, en calidad de donación o de compra, materiales y equipos bélicos de proveniencia rusa/soviética. Este tipo de armamento está prácticamente agotado en la zona de influencia directa de la OTAN, por lo que el esfuerzo diplomático está dirigido hacia los países del Sur, quienes deben negarse a ceder o vender estos equipos para lograr mantenerse neutrales en un conflicto en el cual no tienen intereses y para no contravenir los contratos que en el momento de la adquisición de estos firmaran con la Federación Rusa, con lo que estarían evitando graves problemas jurídicos y el riesgo de involucrarse en crímenes de guerra y/o de

author: Chiara Joos
title: Das Recht auf sexuelle Selbstbestimmung
content:
Zwangssterilisation ist verboten. Dennoch erfahren Frauen mit Behinderungen häufig Druck von Angehörigen, Ärzt*innen oder Betreuer*innen, sich sterilisieren zu lassen.

Weißt du, wie viele Menschen ich begleitet habe, die darunter gelitten haben, dass sie sterilisiert wurden?“, fragte mich eine Beraterin am Telefon. Sie schult Menschen mit Behinderungen in Selbstbestimmung. Es war eines von hundert Gesprächen, die meine Kollegin Ramona Arzberger und ich geführt haben, um zur Verhütungspraxis bei Menschen mit Behinderungen zu recherchieren. Nach fast einem Jahr ist daraus der Film „Hauptsache, du kriegst kein Kind“ unseres Magazins „andererseits“ entstanden. Er begleitet mehrere Frauen in Deutschland und Österreich, die mit Lernschwierigkeiten leben und auf Unterstützung angewiesen sind. Drei von ihnen sind sterilisiert. Keine entschied allein. Elf Prozent der Frauen in deutschen Einrichtungen geben an, sterilisiert zu sein, so der Forschungsbericht zu Gewalt und Gewaltschutz in Einrichtungen der Behindertenhilfe des deutschen Bundesministeriums für Arbeit und Soziales von 2024. In Österreich waren es zuletzt 17 Prozent. In Deutschland habe fast die Hälfte der Betroffenen den Eingriff nicht von sich aus gewollt, heißt es in dem Bericht. In Österreich taucht in Befragungen dasselbe auf: Eltern, Ärzt*innen und Betreuer*innen hätten auf die Frauen eingewirkt. „Ich will auch mitmachen!“, platzte die Stimme von Hannelore Trtil ins Telefon, noch ehe meine Kollegin erfuhr, wer da sprach. Die 66-Jährige hatte unseren Flyer gesehen, der Betroffene erreichen sollte. In den 1980er-Jahren wurde sie in Wien „unterbunden“, ein anderes Wort für sterilisiert. „Die haben alle gesagt, man darf keine Kinder kriegen. Das habe ich nicht richtig gefunden. Und das habe ich nicht gewollt“, sagt sie im Film. Heute verbringt sie oft Zeit mit Kindern. Ihre OP-Akte hat das Krankenhaus vor etwa zehn Jahren vernichtet, nach Ablauf der Frist für Schadenersatz. Sie wird nie erfahren, welche Art von Sterilisation bei ihr gemacht wurde. Hannelore sagt auch, sie habe nie Sex gehabt, aus dem ein Kind hätte entstehen können. Diesen Satz haben wir in unseren Recherchen nicht nur von ihr gehört. Thea, die in Wirklichkeit anders heißt, wurde 2025 sterilisiert, in einem Alter, in dem manche noch nicht an Kinder denken. Sie auch nicht. „Weil für uns schon klar war: Das lassen wir.“ Gemeint sind sie und ihre Mutter. Das Wohnhei…Teile diesen Artikel
