author: Unknown
title: ‘Her Şey Ortada’ vizyonda: Gerçek kimin hikâyesi, kimin kamerasında?
content:
Her Şey Ortada filminden bir sahne

Bir insanın anlattıklarına ne kadar güvenebiliriz? Peki ya o insanın hikayesini kayda alanlara? Kameranın karşısındaki kişi kadar kamerayı tutanların da anlatının bir parçası olduğu bir yerde, izlediğimiz şeyin ne kadarının hakikat, ne kadarının kurgu olduğunu nasıl ayırt edebiliriz? Nathan Fielder ve Lance Oppenheim’ın yönettiği Her Şey Ortada (You Can See Everything), tam da bu soruların peşinden gidiyor. Kurmaca ile belgesel arasında gidip gelen, ancak ağırlığını belgesel sinemadan yana koyan film, izleyiciyi sürekli bu iki alanın sınırında tutuyor. Bir noktadan sonra anlatılan hikayeden çok, hikayeyi kimin, nasıl ve hangi amaçla anlattığıyla ilgilenmeye başlıyoruz.

Her Şey Ortada filmi ne anlatıyor? Herkes Elizabeth Holmes'a inanmıştı, gerçek bambaşka çıktı

Yapımın merkezinde, yakın dönem teknoloji dünyasının en büyük dolandırıcılık vakalarından biriyle gündeme gelen Theranos’un kurucusu Elizabeth Holmes var. Holmes, parmak ucundan alınan birkaç damla kanla çok sayıda sağlık testini gerçekleştirebileceğini iddia ettiği teknolojisiyle Silikon Vadisi’nin en çok konuşulan girişimcilerinden birine dönüşmüştü. Ancak şirketin teknolojisinin vadedilen sonuçları vermediği ortaya çıktı. Yatırımcıları dolandırmaktan suçlu bulunan Holmes, 11 yıl 3 ay hapis cezasına çarptırıldı.

Yapım, Holmes’un cezaevine girmesine 34 gün kala başlıyor. Holmes, kendisinin ve ailesinin gündelik hayatını kayda almaları için Nathan Fielder ve ekibini evine davet ediyor. Başlangıçta bir portre çalışması gibi görünen anlatı, üç yıla yayılan çekim süreci içinde bambaşka bir yere evriliyor.

You Can See Everything adlı belgeselden bir sahne.

You Can See Everything adlı belgeselden bir sahne.

Belgesel sinemanın en temel meselelerinden biri, kameranın gerçekliği ne ölçüde kaydedebildiği, ne ölçüde dönüştürdüğüdür. Kamera yalnızca olup biteni kaydetmez; varlığıyla davranışları, ilişkileri ve anlatıyı da etkiler. Her Şey Ortada, bu meseleyi filmin merkezine yerleştiriyor. Holmes’u izlerken onun kendisini nasıl sunduğunu, Fielder’ın sorularına nasıl karşılık verdiğini ve kameranın varlığında nasıl bir kişiliğe büründüğünü düşünüyoruz. Fakat bir süre sonra aynı sorgulamayı yönetmen için de yapmaya başlıyoruz. Fielder’ın soruları ne kadar kendiliğinden? Onun şaşkınlığı, sessizliği ve müdahaleleri ne kadar gerçek?

Yapımın asıl başarısı, bu sorulara kolay yanıtlar vermemesinde. Holmes’un geçmişini ve Theranos skandalını biliyoruz. Buna rağmen karşımızdaki insanın anlattıklarını dinlerken, bir yandan da onun hangi noktada kendisini savunduğunu, hangi noktada gerçekten inandığı şeyleri dile getirdiğini anlamaya çalışıyoruz. Üstelik yalnızca Holmes’u değil, onu izleyen Fielder’ı da izliyoruz. Ardından kameranın ve kurgunun bu karşılaşmayı nasıl biçimlendirdiğini sorguluyoruz. Böylece seyirci, yalnızca hikayeyi takip eden kişi olmaktan çıkıyor; kendi izleme eyleminin de farkına varıyor.

Bu açıdan yapım, İranlı Yönetmen Abbas Kiarostami’nin sinemasını da hatırlatıyor. Özellikle Yakın Plan (Close-Up, 1990), gerçek ile kurmaca arasındaki sınırın nasıl geçirgenleşebileceğini gösteren en güçlü örneklerden biri. Ancak Kiarostami’nin yaklaşımı, Her Şey Ortada’dan farklı olarak kurmacaya daha yakın duruyor.

Kiarostami’nin Zeytin Ağaçları Altında ve Hayat Devam Ediyor filmlerinde de karşılaştığımız bu yaklaşım, Her Şey Ortada ile farklı bir noktada kesişiyor. Kiarostami gerçekliği kurmacanın olanaklarıyla yeniden kurarken, Fielder ve Oppenheim belgesel olarak başladıkları anlatının içinde kurmacanın ve performansın alanını giderek genişletiyor. Ancak Her Şey Ortada, Kiarostami’nin aksine, seyirciyi daha uzun süre belgesel gerçekliğinin içinde tutuyor; bu gerçekliğin ne zaman ve nasıl bir performansa dönüştüğünü anlamaya çalışmak da filmin temel gerilimlerinden birini oluşturuyor.

You Can See Everything adlı belgeselden bir sahne.

You Can See Everything adlı belgeselden bir sahne.

Anlatının bu denli ilginç bir sorgulamaya dönüşmesinde Nathan Fielder’ın yönetmen ve anlatının içindeki bir karakter olarak konumu belirleyici. Kanadalı Komedyen Fielder, özellikle Nathan for You ve HBO yapımı The Rehearsal ile tanınıyor.

Fielder’ın mizahı, çoğu zaman karşısındaki insanın söyledikleriyle ortaya çıkan çelişkiler arasındaki mesafeden besleniyor. Onun kamerası ve soruları, sıradan görünen durumları giderek tuhaflaştırıyor. Her Şey Ortada’da da bu yaklaşımı sürdürürken, alışık olduğumuz komedi anlayışını çok daha rahatsız edici bir …

author: Aallyah Wright
title: Mississippi Ballot Monitors Say They’re Being Shut Out of Vote Counting
content:
Volunteers say they are navigating confusion and obstacles while trying to ensure a transparent counting process.

Truthout is an indispensable resource for activists, movement leaders and workers everywhere. Please make this work possible with a quick donation.

It took Natt Offiah an hour to realize he had arrived at the wrong location to monitor the provisional and absentee ballots in the Mississippi U.S. Senate race. He drove to Madison County Circuit Clerk’s Office on Wednesday, but the building was under construction.

After a phone call, Offiah, director of organizing for the People’s Advocacy Institute, and his colleague finally reached the temporary clerk’s office. They were redirected again, shared Offiah, still unable to locate officials.

At the next building, one woman said, “I haven’t seen them in an hour or so,” before directing the organizers down a hallway.

Offiah said he banged on the door, to no avail. The duo sat outside the room for 45 minutes before heading back to the front desk. A receptionist then told Offiah about two dozen staffers had left 15 minutes before his initial arrival.

No one could provide him any information on when they would return to continue counting votes.

“There is no standardized process for counting. Each county can pick and choose when they want to start counting. So, we’re running into this runaround issue,” Offiah said.

His experience mirrors the dozens of other volunteers who say they didn’t sign up for chaos and confusion, but to protect the democratic process. Some — who reported their concerns in group chats shared with Capital B — say they’ve been denied a seat to observe the process, while others struggle to find information.

With the nation’s close eye on Mississippi, advocates say it’s even more critical to ensure election officials “do the right thing.” Voters have been on edge since Election Day, waiting to see who will become the state’s next U.S. senator.

Despite no early voting or online registration, turnout and absentee ballots have surged. As of Nov. 6, Democrat Scott Colom leads Republican Cindy Hyde-Smith by over 2,500 votes.

Yet, there are still thousands of mail-in and affidavit ballots outstanding.

Issues like voter ID laws and inoperable machines have fueled delays, said Lydia Grizzell, policy and advocacy manager of ACLU of Mississippi.

“It is appalling the number of issues that we’ve seen and we had on Election Day, and now we’re seeing the extension of that post-Election Day in a way that is not great,” she said.

The Mississippi secretary of state’s office did not address the monitors’ allegations of being shut out of the vote counting process, but told Capital B the public is entitled to be present for the counting of ballots, the process where election commissioners announce which affidavit ballots are accepted or rejected, according to state statute. This does not include the preliminary work commissioners do to determine a voter’s eligibility.

There is no uniform process on how officials conduct affidavit ballot counting. In some counties, where ACLU dispatched attorneys, election officials had a closed door process, Grizell added.

“The best thing that we can do is have people watching, witnessing, and doing their best to gather as much information as possible as to what is happening,” she said.

Volunteers across the state are being deployed in a widespread effort prompted by several grassroots organizations. The NAACP has also deployed national legal, policy, and field staff to the state to make sure every vote is counted.

Both candidates sent their own groups to monitor the process and assembled a group of lawyers who are prepared to take legal action if necessary. Lawyers for Hyde-Smith sent a letter to election commissioners requesting “immediate separation, secure custody and preservation of all affidavit ballots.” Following Hyde-Smith’s legal team’s response, Colom’s legal counsel sent a letter to all 82 counties, calling the GOP senator’s demand unlawful.

Ahead of the election, thousands of Mississippians were moved to inactive status because the secretary of state’s office paid $50,000 to use unverified data from credit bureau Experian to clean out voter rolls. Secretary of State Michael Watson told Mississippi Today that the rollout of the commercial data was “wildly successful.”

This unprecedented number of inactive voters led to more affidavit ballots, prolonging the count, Tarekegn said. These ballots must be …

author: Jon Queally
title: Flooding in Gaza Destroys 70,000 Tents as Israel Continues to Block Aid
content:
The Palestinian Health Minister warned of “a catastrophic deterioration in health and environmental conditions” in Gaza.

Honest, paywall-free news is rare. Please support our boldly independent journalism with a donation of any size.

The suffering of the people of Gaza went from horrific and beyond comprehension to something worse on Saturday after storm waters overnight destroyed tens of thousands of tents and flooded tens of thousands of people into further desperation, all while the US and Israeli governments continue to maintain a cruel blockade on life-saving supplies despite a fast-approaching winter and a military occupation with no end in sight.

“At least 70,000 tents have been flooded & blown away by the torrential downpour and tempestuous wind in Gaza since last night,” reported Palestinian journalist Abubaker Abed, citing statements from health and media officials. “Families are shelterless. Food prices are soaring. Children are starving and shivering with cold. Caravans and mobile homes must enter Gaza now to avert this cataclysm.”

Gaza’s Government Media Office on Saturday, holding Israel wholly responsible for the disaster, said initial losses from flooded and destroyed tents were estimated at $3 million and that dozens of walls of homes had collapsed, resulting in injuries, while the threat of broader building collapse remained a serious risk.

In a statement, Palestinian Health Minister Dr. Majed Abu Ramadan said, “What is happening in Gaza is not a passing winter crisis. I urgently call on the international community, the United Nations, and health, humanitarian, and relief organizations to intervene immediately to save the lives of hundreds of thousands of displaced people in the Gaza Strip, following the flooding of thousands of tents with rainwater and the absence of basic safe shelter conditions.”

According to the United Nations Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA), about 950,000 displaced people in Gaza are living in areas exposed to flooding. Low-lying locations and sites near the coast are particularly vulnerable, with more than 400,000 people living in areas considered at high risk of flooding.

About 44,000 Palestinians are living in structurally unsafe buildings, while more than 4,000 buildings across the territory are estimated to require full or partial demolition due to damage caused by Israeli air strikes. About 294,250 families need shelter assistance ahead of winter, but the available supplies cover only 18 percent of their needs.

Ramadan further warned of “a catastrophic deterioration in health and environmental conditions, alongside growing risks of the spread of diseases and epidemics” if an emergency response was not rapidly and comprehensively deployed.

This is the worst morning ever. No one in Gaza City slept last night. The rain completely flooded the tents, soaking mattresses and destroying families' belongings. We are underwater. Thousands of families have been trying for hours to save what little they have left, with…

Video footage and eye witness accounts offered a heartbreaking picture of the suffering by those hit by the floods.

“We woke up and found ourselves surrounded by water,” a man named Mansour al-Sakni, 33, told the Middle East Eye. “The children were crying. I did not know what to do, and I started crying too.”

“We stood inside the tarpaulin shelter waiting for the rain to stop so we could try to push the water out of the room,” he said. “We are poor people in Gaza. We want to live. We do not want to die from the bombing or the cold. Enough. Have mercy on us.”

The territory’s civil defence service said it had received 1,500 distress calls from displaced residents. Three abandoned houses collapsed without causing injuries, it added.

At a tent encampment in Gaza City, some people tried to repair their tents, ⁠while others used sand to reinforce them and prevent water from entering. ⁠Some were busy getting their children out of flooded tents.

Olfat Magdoub, a Gaza resident, tried in vain to sweep water away from her tent.

“This is the first day of rain, and of course ⁠we are already flooded. What will happen if it rains again the next day? This is only the first day and ⁠we’re already overwhelmed,” said the woman.

“Two weeks ago when it rained, I swear to God, I spent four days sleeping on blankets spread on the floor because the rainwater had flooded the bedding. Same now, the mattresses are wet so we sleep on the ground.” …

author: Ashley Smith
title: As AI Threatens Tech Workers, Their Workplaces Become Sites of Class Struggle
content:
We must develop new modes of organizing that go beyond a narrow focus on labor law and shop floor issues.

Truthout is an indispensable resource for activists, movement leaders and workers everywhere. Please make this work possible with a quick donation.

A political and economic battle against today’s robber barons — the billionaire and trillionaire class of tech bosses — is unfolding on many fronts as tech workers agitate against these oligarchs’ complicity with the U.S. military, the cops, Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE), and the Israeli occupation of Palestine.

In their new book, Against Tech Oligarchy: Workers Resistance in the World’s Most Powerful Industry, JS Tan and Clarissa Redwine recount the emergence of the tech workers’ movement over the last two decades, from the political campaigns they have launched to the heroic strikes they have staged against companies like Kickstarter and The New York Times.

No armchair analysts, Tan and Redwine are tech worker leaders who have been at the heart of many of these fights. In this interview, they discuss the rise of the movement, the workers’ turn to unionization, and the oligarchs’ adoption of authoritarianism and austerity to crush it. And they draw lessons from this struggle not only for tech workers, but for the entire labor movement.

The interview that follows has been lightly edited for clarity and length.

Ashley Smith: The tech workers’ movement was first spurred into action by the radicalization and social movements triggered by the Great Recession. Workers launched campaigns against their companies’ contracts with, for instance, the U.S. military and ICE. What strategies and tactics did workers use?

JS Tan: After the Great Recession, corporate America thought the tech sector was going to rejuvenate the U.S. economy. The tech bosses were aligned with the Democratic Party and embraced things like identity politics and put forth a progressive, democratic vision of the future.

But the industry’s workers realized that the tech sector was not living up to its mission statements and public pronouncements. They were making software for the U.S. military, ICE, and police. And their internal culture was rife with sexism and racism.

So, tech workers launched campaigns to expose their bosses’ hypocrisy. A good example of this is the Google workers’ campaign against the company’s Project Maven, which used AI to analyze military drone footage.

Workers mobilized their radical co-workers and went public with an open letter [to Google CEO Sundar Pichai] in The New York Times. That exposure forced the company to concede to their demand not to renew its Project Maven contract. Simplifying greatly, the tech movement as a whole adopted this strategy of mobilization behind open letters.

This provoked opposition from the tech oligarchy. It abandoned its California liberalism, which included opposition to Donald Trump in his first term, and instead largely backed him in his second term. What caused this political reorientation? How did it change their companies and treatment of workers?

Tan: In our book, we show how the battle in the tech industry led both workers and bosses to acquire class consciousness. It was a process of radicalization on both sides. Initially, the bosses expressed sympathy with the upsurge of tech worker activism, conceded to their workers’ demands, and implemented DEI [diversity, equity, and inclusion] initiatives.

But they got fed up with being told how to run their businesses and started retaliating against their workers for writing open letters, participating in walkouts, and starting union drives. Then, after the pandemic, the Federal Reserve Bank ended its zero-interest rate policy to combat the sharp rise in inflation.

Suddenly, the tech companies lost access to cheap credit and lost billions of dollars in market valuation. To restore their profit margins, they enacted mass layoffs (being asset-light businesses, employee salaries were their largest costs), return-to-work orders, and speed-ups of the remaining workforce.

Elon Musk’s takeover of Twitter is a paradigmatic example. He fired 80 percent of the workforce. He combined that with an ideological assault on the company, targeting teams that oversaw human rights, AI ethics, and content moderation — the teams he believed housed the most progressive, pro-union workers. Seeing this, other tech bosses followed suit, imposing a new normal of authoritarianism, austerity, and …

author: Henry A. Giroux
title: Global Youth Rising Up Know There’s No Democracy Without Economic Justice
content:
Youth around the world are rising up against capitalism and for democracy.

Honest, paywall-free news is rare. Please support our boldly independent journalism with a donation of any size.

Young people are taking to the streets across France, Italy, Belgium, India, Serbia, and Albania, refusing to surrender their futures to a capitalist system that has abandoned them or to a politics that Naomi Klein and Astra Taylor have described as “end times fascism.”

These protests are fueled by mounting anger over deteriorating schools, economic insecurity, unaffordable housing, political corruption, and a ruling class increasingly indifferent to the needs and voices of the young. As far right governments in Europe, the United States, and Latin America cancel out a future plagued by endless wars, climate catastrophe, staggering inequality, deepening poverty, and deteriorating public institutions, young people are rethinking the language of politics, resistance, and hope.

A 21-year-old student protesting in Milan captured this spirit of resistance in an interview with Reuters, declaring: “It’s vital to take part in people’s spontaneous movements born from an explosion of rage that made collective action possible.” She added, “I think the worst damage this ruling class has done to my generation is stealing even the ability to imagine a future, to dream.” Rather than address these grievances, governments have increasingly responded with curfews, protest bans, and brutal police repression, treating the democratic aspirations of young people as threats to be crushed rather than demands for justice to be heard.

These uprisings are driven by more than economic grievances. They express a growing refusal to accept the moral and political cruelty of a system that has declared the young disposable. At their core is a recognition that neoliberal capitalism has robbed an entire generation of the promise of a better future and that austerity is class warfare disguised as economic necessity. As reported in Rolling Stone, Mathys Le Coz Ndzié, a 17-year-old Parisian student, noted: “The current government hasn’t managed to give us a clear picture of the future, or the world we’re heading into. So we feel completely lost. … We haven’t been prepared for the world that’s coming. The one they’ve prepared us for no longer exists.” This war on youth is intensified by the destruction of social protections and the rise of governments that increasingly rely on surveillance, criminalization, and police repression to enforce obedience, especially among the poor and racially marginalized.

Yet out of these conditions of abandonment and repression, something more profound is emerging: a moral and political awakening rooted in the struggle for economic justice and a collective refusal to accept a world in which human dignity is sacrificed to private profit, democracy is hollowed out, and the very possibility of imagining and creating a different future is stolen from an entire generation.

Carlotta Magoga, writing in European Democracy Hub, is right in stating that, “From Serbia to Bangladesh and Senegal, young people are becoming a driving force for a more democratic world. … In search of alternative routes, they are developing new forms of civic engagement — through artistic protest, online campaigns and storytelling — and rewriting the rules of political participation.” Through their courageous presence in the streets, they are fashioning a form of activism “as a way to rethink how democracy works.”

For example, in France, students have challenged overcrowded classrooms, teacher shortages, and a university admissions system that reinforces class inequality. In Italy, students have joined workers in protests over low wages, unaffordable housing, deteriorating public services, and increased military spending. In Genoa, port workers and students have also protested the use of ports for arms shipments. In Serbia, where opposition to government corruption has been central, students have demanded investigations into public contracts, government spending, and the political control of public institutions. These movements do not all embrace an explicitly anti-capitalist agenda, but their demands expose conflicts over who controls public resources, whose interests governments serve, and how economic and political power is organized and maintained.

Capitalism, in one of its more disingenuous moments, celebrates youth rhetorically as the future but denies …

author: Unknown
title: Constitutional Court orders retrial of Mazlum İçli after ten years in prison
content:
Mazlum İçli has already spent more than ten years of his life in prison. He was accused of involvement, at the age of 14, in the killing of four people during the Kobanê protests in Amed (Turkish: Diyarbakır) in October 2014. He was sentenced to a total of 124 years and eight months in prison. However, evidence that could exonerate him was not adequately considered during the trial. Turkey’s Constitutional Court has now confirmed serious deficiencies in the reasoning behind the verdict and ordered a retrial. İçli’s defense team intends to seek his immediate release.


The ruling, issued on September 16, 2026, could mark a decisive turning point in a case that has been fraught with contradictions for years. At the heart of the case is the question of why İçli was convicted despite several witnesses confirming that he was attending a wedding in the district of Kulp, approximately 140 kilometers away, at the time of the alleged crime. Video footage and an expert report also support his alibi.


The Constitutional Court particularly criticized the criminal court’s failure to provide a reasoned assessment of conflicting expert reports. While one examination suggested that İçli might be identifiable in footage from the crime scene, another report by the same expert confirmed with a high degree of probability that he was present at the wedding. It remained unclear why the court had relied on the incriminating report while failing to give appropriate consideration to the exculpatory evidence.

author: Unknown
title: Women organize symposium on social memory and trauma in Amed
content:
A symposium titled “Speaking Out: Social Memory, Testimony and Trauma” began at the Ali Emiri Conference Hall in cooperation with Amed Metropolitan Municipality, the Trauma Studies Association, and the Forum for Social Peace and Freedom.


Speaking during a session titled “Waiting at Ground Zero: Trauma, Unresolved Grief and the Power of Testimony in Enforced Disappearances,” moderated by social worker İrfan Ekinci, Sebla Arcan, a member of the Human Rights Association’s (İHD) Commission on Disappearances in Custody, said, “A person experiencing trauma due to the disappearance of a loved one can neither move forward nor go back. They remain trapped in that moment.”


Highlighting the trauma caused by enforced disappearances, Arcan said, “The effects continue for two or three generations after an enforced disappearance. But other things are also passed down through generations in connection with enforced disappearances. A sense of justice, the determination to struggle, and the spirit of resistance are also transmitted. What is passed down from generation to generation is not only trauma and grief but also political consciousness.”


Emphasizing the importance of testimony, Sebla Arcan said, “Your account of what happened is denied. Some people come and take your child into custody, but when you go to inquire about their detention, the authorities deny it ever happened. Denial is the most severe form of state violence and the most profound form of trauma.”


İHD Women’s Secretary Handan Çoşkun spoke in a session titled “The Perception of Space and the Body in the Intergenerational Transmission of Grief: Sur.” Çoşkun said they had been conducting research since the 1990s into issues including the forced evacuation of villages, enforced disappearances, suicide, and numerous other subjects.


Speaking on the topic “Disenfranchised Grief: Unrecognized Suffering,” neuropsychologist Masum Aydın said, “Witnessing is fundamental to existence. We cannot become ‘us’ without the other.”


Participants then shared their testimonies and asked questions of the panelists.


The third session of the symposium was moderated by sociologist Didem Aydemir. TJA (Free Women’s Movement) activist and psychological counselor Esra Kahraman spoke on “Geography, Body and Mother Tongue: The Transmission of Memory and Healing Mechanisms among Displaced Kurdish Women in the Middle East,” while TJA activist Rojda Bedia Akkaya addressed “From Oppressed Lives to Collective Healing: The Historical Legacy of Resistance, Communal Life and Distinctive Coping Mechanisms of the Kurdish Women’s Movement.”


Referring to the Peace and Democratic Society Process, Esra Kahraman emphasized the importance they attached to the process and stated that confronting the past and ensuring justice were essential to building lasting peace.


Discussing their work with women who came to Amed following the attacks on Rojava, Kahraman said they had observed how women collectively resisted suffering and hardship.


Rojda Bedia Akkaya highlighted the struggle of Kurdish women and the methods they have developed.


The symposium will continue with presentations titled “What Remains in the Body: Rights Violations, Bodily Memory and the Conditions for Healing,” “Traumatic Silence and States of Subjecthood: From Perpetration to Involvement,” “Tracing the Unspoken: The Speaking Body,” and “Traces Left in Memory and Nature: Destruction and Possibilities for Healing.”
